questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario
Correctly reverses the recommendation for the high-write scenario with reasoning
Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes deadlock (1205) from ordinary blocking
Describes SQL Server's automatic deadlock detection and victim rollback
Names a real diagnostic method for capturing the deadlock graph
Identifies inconsistent access order as the root cause
Proposes a concrete redesign (consistent order, shorter transactions, retry logic)
Clear, structured troubleshooting narrative

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here

questions.title: A Nightly Staging Query's Runtime Quietly Tripled
questions.prompt: A nightly ETL step that filters Sales.SalesOrderHeader by a date range used to finish in under a minute. After a recent, unrelated application release, it now takes over 20 minutes most nights, even though nobody touched the query text itself. Walk through your full diagnostic process, in the order you'd actually do it, to find the real cause and prove your fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd work outward from the query itself before looking anywhere else, because the fact that nobody touched this query's text doesn't mean nothing that affects it changed.

First, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run it, looking specifically for whether an operation that used to be an Index Seek is now a Scan -- that's the single most common visible signature of a regressed query. I'd also compare estimated vs. actual row counts on each operator; a big gap there points at stale statistics giving the optimizer bad cardinality estimates, which can push it toward a much worse plan even though the query text is identical.

Second, I'd capture SET STATISTICS TIME and SET STATISTICS IO output and compare it mentally against what I'd expect for this table's size. If CPU time and elapsed time are close, it's genuinely doing more logical work; if elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, something else -- blocking, waits, disk I/O contention -- is adding wait time on top of comparable actual work, and I'd pivot to sys.dm_exec_requests / sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks to see what wait type is dominating.

Third, I'd specifically check whether the query's WHERE clause is still SARGable the way it was before. The "unrelated application release" detail is a flag: if the application layer changed how it passes the date parameter -- say, switching from a DATETIME parameter to a string that now gets implicitly converted, or wrapping the column in a function somewhere upstream that got introduced in the release -- that alone can silently turn a seek into a scan without anyone touching this specific query's text.

Fourth, if this runs as a parameterized query or inside a stored procedure, I'd consider parameter sniffing: if the release changed what date ranges get passed first after a recompile, SQL Server may have cached a plan optimized for a very different-sized result set than what's typically requested now. I'd check sys.dm_exec_query_stats for that procedure's cached plan and compare it against a fresh OPTION (RECOMPILE) run.

Fifth, I'd check whether an index this query relied on was changed, disabled, or had its fill factor/maintenance schedule altered as part of the release, and whether statistics were updated recently -- a large data load with no corresponding stats update is a very common, very quiet cause of exactly this symptom.

Finally, I'd correlate the actual onset against the release timeline and any index maintenance job history, form a specific hypothesis from whichever of the above turned up concrete evidence, apply the fix (rebuild/update statistics, restore a missing index, fix an implicit conversion, add OPTION (RECOMPILE) or a plan guide for parameter sniffing), and then prove it with a direct before/after comparison of logical reads via SET STATISTICS IO -- that number is the most reliable proof a fix genuinely reduced work, independent of how busy the server happened to be at the moment I measured it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't jump straight to 'rebuild the index' or 'update stats' -- I'd want to actually see what changed first. So step one for me is always the actual execution plan, Ctrl+M, run the query, and look specifically for a scan where I'd expect a seek, plus a big gap between estimated and actual row counts, because that gap is basically SQL Server telling you its statistics are lying to it.

Step two, I'd pull SET STATISTICS TIME and IO and look at whether CPU time and elapsed time line up. If they're close, the engine's genuinely doing more work. If elapsed time is way bigger than CPU time, I know to go look at waits and blocking instead of the query logic itself.

The detail that really jumps out at me in this scenario is 'an unrelated application release' right before this started. That's exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks SARGability without anyone touching the SQL -- maybe the app now sends the date as a string instead of a proper date, and now there's an implicit conversion happening on every row. I'd check that specifically.

If this lives inside a stored procedure, parameter sniffing is next on my list -- the first execution after a recompile caches a plan shaped for whatever parameter came in that first time, and if the typical date range changed after the release, that cached plan might be wrong for almost every call since. And I'd double check whether an index got dropped, disabled, or just went stale from a big data load with no corresponding stats update around the same time as the release.

Whatever I land on, I don't call it fixed until I've got a before-and-after comparison of logical reads from STATISTICS IO -- that number doesn't lie the way timing can when the server's under different load each time I test.

Jumping to 'rebuild all the indexes' without first checking the actual plan for a scan-vs-seek regression
Ignoring that an unrelated application change can break SARGability through implicit conversion

Declaring victory based on a single wall-clock timing instead of logical reads before/after

questions.title: Choosing Between #Temp Tables, Table Variables, and CTEs Inside a Stored Procedure
questions.prompt: You're writing a complex reporting stored procedure. Partway through, you compute an intermediate result set of roughly 200,000 rows that gets referenced three separate times later in the procedure, filtered differently each time, and would benefit from its own index on one of its columns. A junior developer on your team used a CTE for it because 'that's what we always use.' Explain why that choice is likely to hurt performance here, what you'd use instead and why, and the one scenario where a table variable would actually be the better choice over a temp table.
questions.modelAnswer:
A CTE isn't a stored, materialized result at all -- it's inlined into the statement that references it, and if you reference the same CTE three separate times, SQL Server may well re-run its underlying query three separate times (unless it happens to decide to spool the result on its own, which isn't something you can rely on or control). For a 200,000-row intermediate result referenced three times with different downstream filters, that risks recomputing the same expensive logic three times over, and a CTE also can't carry its own index -- so if the column you'd filter or join on isn't already well-served by indexes on the base tables, every one of those three references pays that cost independently.

A #temp table is the right choice here. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, which means two things that matter directly to this scenario: SQL Server maintains real statistics on it, so the optimizer can build a genuinely informed plan for each of the three later queries against it (rather than guessing), and you can explicitly CREATE INDEX on it -- so the column those three downstream queries filter or join on can actually be indexed, turning three potential scans into three seeks. At 200,000 rows, this is squarely the 'thousands of rows, reused more than once, might need its own index' case.

A table variable would be the better choice only when the intermediate set is small -- a handful to a few hundred rows -- and you're specifically trying to avoid statement recompilation inside a stored procedure. Historically, SQL Server assumed a table variable held exactly one row for costing purposes (pre-2019 compatibility levels, or without the newer deferred-compilation improvements), which is actually fine when the set really is tiny, but would badly under-allocate resources at 200,000 rows -- the opposite of what you want here. Table variables also aren't rolled back by an enclosing ROLLBACK, which occasionally matters for specific logging/auditing patterns, but that's a narrower reason to choose one and isn't the deciding factor in this scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior developer: the CTE choice makes sense as a habit, but it's working against them here specifically because of how many rows there are and how many times it gets used. A CTE doesn't actually store anything -- every time you reference it, SQL Server might just re-run the query behind it from scratch, and it has no index of its own. If we're touching this 200,000-row set three separate times with three different filters, we could be paying for that underlying computation three times, and none of those three references get to use an index on it even if one would help a lot.

My recommendation is a #temp table instead: dump that intermediate result into it once, put an index on whatever column the three downstream queries actually filter or join on, and now each of those three references gets a real seek against real statistics instead of SQL Server guessing. That's exactly the profile -- meaningful row count, reused multiple times, benefits from its own index -- where a temp table wins clearly.

I'd also tell them table variables aren't wrong, just wrong for this case -- they're great when the set is genuinely small and you're inside a procedure trying to avoid a recompile every time row counts shift. The catch is that SQL Server has historically assumed a table variable holds about one row when it's building a plan, which is totally fine for a small set but would be a disaster at 200,000 rows -- the optimizer would badly under-allocate for a set that size, and the plan quality would suffer for every one of those three references, not help it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a CTE out of habit regardless of row count or reuse pattern
Not realizing a CTE referenced multiple times may re-run its underlying query each time
Assuming a table variable always outperforms a temp table because it 'sounds lighter weight'
Putting a large, reused intermediate set into a table variable and getting a poor plan from the one-row cardinality assumption
Forgetting that only a #temp table supports an explicit CREATE INDEX statement after the fact
keyPoints: CTEs are inlined and re-evaluated per reference, not materialized or indexed
#Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and support explicit indexes
200,000 rows reused three times with filtering is a textbook #temp table case
Table variables historically get a one-row cardinality assumption, poor for large sets
Table variables fit small sets inside procedures where avoiding recompilation matters most

Recommends a #temp table and justifies it with statistics/indexing
Explains the risk of recomputation across three CTE references

Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Implementing a Type 2 Slowly Changing Dimension Update in T-SQL
questions.prompt: Given a DimProduct-style dimension with a surrogate ProductKey, a natural/business key ProductAlternateKey, EnglishProductName, StartDate, EndDate, and Status columns, write the T-SQL that correctly expires the current row and inserts a new current row whenever EnglishProductName changes for a given ProductAlternateKey -- preserving every fact table row's link to the historically-correct version of the product. Explain why this design absolutely requires a surrogate key rather than reusing the natural key, and what would break if you used Type 1 (overwrite) instead for this column.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Type 2 SCD update has two required actions, and they have to happen as one atomic unit: expire the old current row (set its EndDate to now and Status to a non-current value), and insert a brand-new row with a new surrogate ProductKey, the updated EnglishProductName, a fresh StartDate, a NULL EndDate, and Status marked current. Both actions share the same ProductAlternateKey, but deliberately do not share the same ProductKey -- that's the entire mechanism.

The surrogate key is non-negotiable because fact table rows join to the dimension by ProductKey, not by the business key. If I instead tried to do this with only the natural key, I'd have to overwrite the single existing row to change its name -- there would be nowhere to put a second, distinct row representing 'the same product, but as it used to be described,' because the natural key is the same for both versions by definition. The surrogate key is what lets two rows coexist that are 'the same real-world product' but represent two different points in time -- old fact rows keep pointing at the old ProductKey (and so report the old name, correctly, for sales that happened under that name), while new fact rows get the new ProductKey going forward.

If I used Type 1 (overwrite in place) for this column instead, the practical consequence is that I lose the ability to report history accurately: every fact row, past and present, would join to the same single DimProduct row and show whatever the current EnglishProductName happens to be right now -- including sales that occurred back when the product had a different name. A report of 'sales by product name, by month, for the last two years' would silently misattribute historical revenue to the product's current name, which is exactly the kind of error that's invisible until someone reconciles against an old static report and the numbers don't match.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd build this: when I detect that EnglishProductName has changed for a given ProductAlternateKey, I do two things in the same transaction -- I update the existing row to set its EndDate to right now and flip its Status off of current, and I insert a brand-new row for that same ProductAlternateKey with a new surrogate ProductKey, the new name, a fresh StartDate, a NULL EndDate, and Status set to current. Both rows share the business key, but they deliberately do not share the surrogate key, and that's really the whole trick.

If someone asked me why the surrogate key matters so much here, I'd say: because fact tables join on ProductKey, not on the business key, having two distinct surrogate keys is what lets two 'versions' of the same real product coexist in the dimension table at the same time. Old sales keep pointing at the old key and keep showing the old name forever; new sales point at the new key. If I only had the natural key to work with, there'd be nowhere to put that second row -- I'd be forced to just overwrite the one row that exists.

And that's exactly what goes wrong with Type 1 here: if I just overwrite the name in place instead, every fact row ever written against this product -- including years-old sales -- now joins to a row showing today's name. Any historical report broken out by product name would be quietly wrong for anything before the rename, and nobody would notice until they tried to reconcile against an old snapshot and the totals didn't match up.
commonMistakes: Reusing the business key as the dimension's join key instead of a dedicated surrogate key
Overwriting the existing row in place (Type 1 behavior) when history needs to be preserved (Type 2)
Forgetting to wrap the expire-and-insert as a single atomic transaction
Not setting EndDate/Status consistently, leaving two rows both marked 'current'
Assuming fact rows automatically re-point to the new surrogate key, when they should keep the old one for historical accuracy
keyPoints: Type 2 SCD = expire the old row, insert a new row with a new surrogate key
Fact tables join on the surrogate key, enabling two 'versions' of one business entity to coexist
Natural/business key stays the same across versions; surrogate key does not
Type 1 on this column would silently misattribute historical facts to the current attribute value
StartDate/EndDate/Status track which version was active at any point in time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct expire + insert logic as a single atomic operation
Correctly explains why a surrogate key (not the natural key) is required
Correctly explains the consequence of using Type 1 instead
Explains how fact rows preserve historical accuracy via the surrogate key
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Covering, Filtered Index for a High-Frequency Reporting Query
questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint runs this query hundreds of times per minute: SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product WHERE Color = 'Red' AND SellEndDate IS NULL ORDER BY ListPrice. Design the single nonclustered index you'd create to best serve it -- specifying key column order, included columns, and any filter -- and explain exactly how you'd confirm in the execution plan that it's actually being used as a fully covering seek rather than falling back to a scan or a key lookup.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query filters on Color (equality) and SellEndDate IS NULL, then orders by ListPrice, and selects ProductID, Name, ListPrice. I'd build the index key on Color first, since it's the equality predicate the optimizer can seek on directly, then ListPrice second, since that both satisfies part of the ORDER BY and keeps rows pre-sorted within each color -- letting the engine potentially avoid a separate sort operator entirely. ProductID and Name don't belong in the key at all; they're only ever selected, never filtered or sorted on, so they belong as INCLUDE columns, which attaches their data to the index's leaf level without making them part of the search key (keeping the key itself narrow). Finally, since this query only ever cares about currently-active products, I'd add a filter: WHERE SellEndDate IS NULL, so the index only covers the subset of rows this specific query pattern actually needs -- smaller, faster to scan, and still perfectly usable by any other query matching that same filter condition.

To confirm it's working as intended, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run the exact production query. I'm looking for a single Index Seek operator with no accompanying Key Lookup and no separate Sort operator afterward -- that combination means the index is fully covering (every selected column came straight from the index, no trip back to the clustered index) and pre-sorted for the ORDER BY. If I instead see an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup, that tells me I missed an included column the query actually needs. If I see a Sort operator after the seek, either my key column order doesn't match the ORDER BY the way I assumed, or the optimizer decided sorting was cheaper than using the index's physical order for some other reason. And if I see a Scan instead of a Seek at all, I'd first check that the filter predicate on the index exactly matches the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server will only use a filtered index when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter, and a subtle mismatch (like comparing against a variable instead of a literal in some SQL Server versions) can silently prevent that match and fall back to scanning the base table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through the query, I see one equality filter (Color), one IS NULL filter that's really describing 'currently active products' (SellEndDate), an ORDER BY on ListPrice, and three columns actually being selected. So my index key is Color first, because that's the equality predicate, then ListPrice second, because that handles the sort and keeps things grouped nicely within each color. ProductID and Name never show up in a WHERE or ORDER BY here, so I don't want them cluttering the key -- they go in as INCLUDE columns instead, just along for the ride so the index can hand back the full row without touching the base table. And since this query only ever wants active products, I'd make the whole index filtered on SellEndDate IS NULL -- there's no reason to carry the weight of retired products in an index built specifically for this access pattern.

To prove it's actually helping, I turn on the actual plan and run the real query, and I want to see exactly one operator: an Index Seek, nothing else hanging off it. If there's a Key Lookup tagging along, that tells me I forgot to include a column the query needed. If there's a Sort sitting after the seek, my key order isn't lining up with the ORDER BY the way I thought it would. And if I'm staring at a Scan instead of a Seek, my first suspicion is that the filter on the index doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server is strict about that match for a filtered index, and small mismatches are a classic reason the optimizer quietly falls back to ignoring it.
commonMistakes: Putting ProductID/Name in the index key instead of as INCLUDE columns, widening the key unnecessarily
Forgetting the ORDER BY column when choosing key column order, leaving a Sort in the plan
Leaving off the filter, indexing retired products the query never actually needs
Assuming an Index Seek alone proves full coverage without checking for an accompanying Key Lookup
Writing a filter predicate that doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause, causing SQL Server to ignore the filtered index
keyPoints: Equality predicate columns go first in the index key, ahead of sort/range columns
ORDER BY columns in the key can eliminate a separate Sort operator
Select-only columns belong in INCLUDE, not the key, to keep the key narrow
A filtered index should match the query's WHERE clause as closely as possible
Verify with the actual execution plan: single seek, no Key Lookup, no Sort = fully covering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct key column choice and order (Color, ListPrice)
Correctly places ProductID/Name as INCLUDE columns
Correctly applies the SellEndDate IS NULL filter
Describes verifying via actual execution plan (seek, no key lookup, no sort)
Explains what a Key Lookup or Sort in the plan would each indicate is wrong

questions.title: Choosing a Lookup Transformation Cache Mode for a High-Volume Fact Load
questions.prompt: You're loading 20 million fact rows nightly in SSIS, and every row needs a Lookup against an 80,000-row Product dimension to translate a business key into a surrogate key. The dimension almost never changes during the load window. Which cache mode do you choose, and why? Then explain what changes about your recommendation if a separate process is actively updating that same dimension table concurrently, during the same window your fact load is running.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the base scenario, Full cache is the clear choice. Full cache queries the entire 80,000-row reference dataset exactly once, up front, and loads it into memory before the Lookup starts processing any of the 20 million fact rows -- after that one-time cost, every single lookup during the run is a fast in-memory check with no additional round trip to the database. At 80,000 rows, the memory footprint is trivial, and against 20 million fact rows needing a lookup each, the per-row savings compound enormously compared to either Partial cache (which still queries live for every cache miss) or No cache (which queries live for every single row, with 20 million round trips to the database being the worst possible outcome for throughput).

If a separate process is actively updating that same dimension table concurrently during the load window, the calculus changes, but not necessarily toward abandoning Full cache. The real problem Full cache introduces here is a staleness window: the cache is built once, at the start of the Lookup's execution, from a single point-in-time query -- any dimension changes committed after that snapshot are invisible to every row processed for the rest of the run, no matter how long the load takes. If those concurrent changes are things this fact load genuinely needs to see (new products being added that today's fact rows might reference), Full cache could silently route rows that should have matched into the No Match output instead, simply because the matching dimension row didn't exist yet at the moment the cache was built.

The practical fix is usually not to switch to No cache across the board, since that reintroduces the full per-row round-trip cost at 20-million-row scale. Instead, I'd look at the actual pattern of the concurrent updates: if new dimension rows are added early and rarely mid-run, Full cache is probably still fine with a well-handled No Match output (redirecting unmatched rows to a holding area, or to the inferred-member pattern from the SCD Transformation, rather than failing the load). If updates are frequent and the fact load genuinely can't tolerate any staleness, Partial cache becomes the more defensible choice -- it starts empty and populates on demand, so at least every cache miss re-queries live, at the cost of some per-row overhead for whatever fraction of rows aren't already cached.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the straightforward version of this -- 20 million fact rows, an 80,000-row dimension that's stable during the load -- I go with Full cache without much hesitation. You pay one query up front to pull the whole dimension into memory, and at 80,000 rows that's basically free, memory-wise. After that, every one of those 20 million lookups is just an in-memory check, no database round trip. Compare that to No cache, where you'd be hitting the database 20 million separate times, and it's not even close.

Where it gets more interesting is your second question -- a concurrent process updating that same dimension while my load is running. The thing people miss about Full cache is that it's a snapshot: it's built once, right when the Lookup starts, and nothing that changes in the source table after that point is visible to the rest of the run, however long that run takes. So if new products are landing in that dimension mid-load and my fact rows need to match against them, Full cache can quietly send rows to the No Match output that really should have matched -- not because anything's broken, just because the cache is frozen in time.

I wouldn't automatically jump to No cache to fix that, though, because at 20 million rows that's a real throughput hit. I'd first ask how often and how urgently those concurrent updates actually need to be visible. If it's rare, I'd keep Full cache and make sure the No Match output is handled gracefully instead of just failing the package. If it's frequent and staleness genuinely isn't acceptable, that's when I'd move to Partial cache -- it starts empty and fills in as it goes, so at least every miss gets a live check, even if that costs a bit more per row than a pure in-memory lookup.

-- Lookup Transformation Editor settings for the base scenario:
-- General page:
--   Cache mode: Full cache
--   Connection type: OLE DB connection manager (or Cache connection manager
--     if sharing the cache across multiple packages)
--   Specify how to handle rows with no matching entries: Redirect rows to no match output
--
-- Connection page:
--   Use a table or view: Production.Product (or a narrower SQL query
--     selecting only BusinessKey, SurrogateKey to minimize cache size)
--
-- Columns page:
--   Join on BusinessKey -> BusinessKey
--   Add SurrogateKey to output as ProductKey
commonMistakes: Choosing No cache by default 'to be safe,' ignoring the throughput cost at 20-million-row scale
Not realizing Full cache is a point-in-time snapshot taken once at the start of execution
Letting unmatched rows fail the package instead of redirecting to a handled No Match output
Assuming Partial cache eliminates all live queries, when it still queries live on every cache miss
Caching every column from the reference table instead of narrowing the query to only what's needed
keyPoints: Full cache: one upfront query, then fast in-memory lookups for the rest of the run
Full cache is ideal when the reference dataset is large-row-count-manageable and stable during the run
Full cache's cache is a frozen snapshot -- it does not see changes committed after it's built
No cache queries live every row -- worst throughput at high fact-row volume
Partial cache is the middle ground when some freshness is required without full per-row live cost
Unmatched rows should be redirected to a handled No Match output, not left to fail the package

Explains the memory/performance tradeoff across all three cache modes
Correctly identifies the staleness/snapshot risk introduced by concurrent updates
Proposes a reasonable adjustment (Partial cache or handled No Match) for the concurrent-update case
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing an Incremental Load Pipeline for a 50-Million-Row Source Table
questions.prompt: You need to load a 50-million-row OLTP sales table into a staging table nightly, but a full reload every run is no longer acceptable. Design the incremental (delta) load pipeline step by step, using only standard SSIS tasks and transformations: where the watermark lives, how each run reads and updates it safely, which transformation decides new vs. changed rows, and what specifically happens on the Lookup's No Match output. Also explain what would go wrong if the watermark update ran before the data flow finished loading, instead of after.
questions.modelAnswer:
The pipeline has four stages, built entirely from standard tasks: read the watermark, extract the delta, classify new vs. changed, save the new watermark -- and the order those last two happen in matters a lot.

First, an Execute SQL Task runs at the start of the Control Flow and reads the last successful run's watermark value -- typically the maximum ModifiedDate (or an equivalent monotonically increasing change-tracking column) that was successfully processed last time -- out of a dedicated control/watermark table, into a package variable.

Second, a Data Flow Task's OLE DB Source uses a parameterized query referencing that variable to pull only source rows where the change-tracking column is greater than the saved watermark -- this is the actual extract step that makes the load a delta instead of a full reload, and it's the step that should be doing the heavy row-count reduction: instead of reading 50 million rows every night, it reads only however many actually changed since last time.

Third, inside that same data flow, a Lookup transformation checks each extracted row's business key against the staging/destination table to determine whether it already exists. I'd configure it to redirect rows with no match to the No Match output rather than letting the Lookup treat them as errors by default -- that No Match output is exactly the set of genuinely new rows. The Lookup's Match output (rows that do already exist in the destination) feeds into a Conditional Split, or more simply, the two Lookup outputs themselves route directly to two different destinations: Match output -> an OLE DB Command doing a row-by-row UPDATE (or a staging table feeding a downstream MERGE), and No Match output -> an OLE DB Destination doing a straight INSERT.

Fourth -- and this is the step order that matters -- only after the data flow task has completed successfully does a second Execute SQL Task run, updating the watermark control table with the new maximum value extracted this run.

If the watermark update ran before the data flow finished instead of after, and the data flow then failed partway through (a bad row, a connection drop, a destination constraint violation), the control table would already record the new watermark as successfully processed -- even though some of those rows never actually made it into the destination. The next run would read that already-advanced watermark, extract only rows newer than it, and permanently skip the rows that failed in the previous run. Those rows would never be picked up again by any future incremental run; they'd simply be silently lost from the pipeline, which is exactly the failure mode the watermark pattern exists to prevent if sequenced correctly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through this as four stages, and I'd be deliberate about the order because that's where the real risk lives. First, an Execute SQL Task at the top of the Control Flow reads the last watermark -- usually the max ModifiedDate we successfully processed last time -- out of a small control table, into a package variable.

Second, the Data Flow's OLE DB Source uses a parameterized query built around that variable, so it only pulls rows newer than the watermark -- that's the piece that actually turns this from a 50-million-row reload into something proportional to just what changed overnight.

Third, inside the data flow, I put a Lookup against the destination's business key, configured to redirect unmatched rows to the No Match output instead of treating them as errors -- that's genuinely new rows. The Match output -- rows that already exist -- goes to an update path, an OLE DB Command or a downstream MERGE; the No Match output goes straight to an insert destination.

The part I'd really call out, though, is the fourth step: updating the watermark. That Execute SQL Task has to run after the data flow succeeds, never before. If you flip that order and the data flow fails halfway through, you've already told the control table 'everything up to this point is safely loaded' when it isn't -- and the next run will start from that advanced watermark, which means whatever didn't make it in during the failed run just vanishes. Nothing ever extracts those rows again. That's the one sequencing detail in this whole pattern I'd never let someone get backwards.
questions.example:
-- Stage 1: Execute SQL Task - read watermark into a package variable
SELECT ISNULL(MAX(LastWatermark), '1900-01-01')
FROM dbo.ETL_Watermark
WHERE SourceTable = 'Sales.SalesOrderHeader';
-- (Result Set mapped to User::LastWatermark)

-- Stage 2: OLE DB Source, parameterized query
SELECT SalesOrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue, ModifiedDate
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE ModifiedDate > ?;  -- parameter bound to User::LastWatermark

-- Stage 3: Lookup (business key = SalesOrderID) against Staging.SalesOrderHeader
--   No Match output -> OLE DB Destination (INSERT)
--   Match output     -> OLE DB Command (UPDATE)

-- Stage 4: Execute SQL Task - runs ONLY after the Data Flow Task succeeds
UPDATE dbo.ETL_Watermark
SET LastWatermark = ?   -- the new MAX(ModifiedDate) extracted this run
WHERE SourceTable = 'Sales.SalesOrderHeader';

Letting the Lookup treat unmatched (new) rows as errors instead of redirecting to No Match
Doing a full table scan extract and filtering the watermark in SSIS instead of pushing the filter into the source query
Storing the watermark only in a package variable with no persistent control table, losing it between runs
Using a non-monotonic or nullable column as the change-tracking column, causing rows to be missed
keyPoints: Execute SQL Task reads the watermark before the data flow starts
The source query's WHERE clause, parameterized by the watermark, is what makes the extract incremental
Lookup against the destination's business key classifies new vs. existing rows
No Match output = new rows (insert); Match output = existing rows (update)
Watermark update must run only after the data flow succeeds, never before
Running the watermark update too early causes silent, permanent data loss on a mid-run failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sequences all four pipeline stages
Correctly explains the parameterized extract as the actual delta mechanism
Correctly describes the Lookup's role and No Match output handling
Identifies that the watermark update must run after the data flow succeeds
Correctly explains the silent data-loss consequence of the wrong order

questions.title: Choosing Fixed, Changing, or Historical for Each Column in the SCD Wizard
questions.prompt: You're configuring the Slowly Changing Dimension Wizard against a DimCustomer table with these columns: EmailAddress, BirthDate, City, and LoyaltyTier. Assign each one to Fixed, Changing, or Historical attribute type and justify each choice. Then explain what happens when a fact row arrives referencing a CustomerKey that doesn't exist yet in the dimension, including which SCD Transformation output is involved and what happens later when the real customer record finally arrives.
questions.modelAnswer:
BirthDate: Fixed attribute. A customer's birth date should never genuinely change once recorded; if an incoming row tries to update it, that's far more likely a data-quality problem than a real change, so flagging it as an error is the correct, safe behavior.

EmailAddress: Changing attribute (Type 1). An email address update is a correction or a genuine change to current contact information, and there's essentially no reporting value in knowing someone's old email address -- overwrite in place, no history needed.

City: Historical attribute (Type 2). Where a customer lived at the time of a given purchase is often analytically meaningful -- regional sales trend reports, territory analysis -- so I want the old value preserved in an expired record rather than silently overwritten, with the new city starting a new current record.

LoyaltyTier: Historical attribute (Type 2), arguably the most important one to get right here. If LoyaltyTier were Type 1, every historical fact row would retroactively show the customer's current tier, which would corrupt any report analyzing 'did loyalty tier correlate with purchase behavior' or 'how many Gold-tier sales did we have last quarter' -- the whole point of that analysis depends on knowing what tier the customer actually held at the time of each purchase, not their tier today.

For the inferred member case: when a fact row arrives referencing a CustomerKey with no matching row yet in DimCustomer, the SCD Transformation (when configured to support this) generates an inferred member -- a minimal placeholder dimension row containing just the key, with every other attribute null or defaulted, so the fact row has something valid to join to immediately rather than being rejected or held back. This flows through the transformation's Inferred Member Updates Output, which is wired by the wizard to its own OLE DB Command. Later, when the real customer data actually arrives from the source system, that same row is recognized by its business key and updated in place through that same Inferred Member Updates Output path -- filling in the previously-null attributes -- rather than inserting a second, duplicate dimension row for the same customer.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Going column by column: BirthDate I'd mark Fixed, because that value just shouldn't change -- if it ever tries to, I want the wizard to flag it as an error so we investigate, not quietly accept it. EmailAddress I'd mark Changing, Type 1 behavior -- if someone updates their email, I just want the current value, there's no analytical reason to keep the old one around. City I'd mark Historical, Type 2, because where someone lived when they made a purchase can genuinely matter for territory or regional analysis, and I don't want that information to disappear the moment they move. And LoyaltyTier I'd also mark Historical -- honestly, that's probably the one I'd be most insistent about, because if we overwrote it in place, every past sale would suddenly look like it happened under the customer's current tier, which would wreck any report trying to connect loyalty tier to purchase behavior over time.

On the inferred member question -- this comes up more than people expect, when a fact row shows up for a customer the dimension hasn't caught up to yet. The SCD Transformation handles that by generating a minimal placeholder row, just the key with everything else null, through its Inferred Member Updates Output, so the fact load doesn't have to stall or fail waiting on a dimension that hasn't synced yet. Then later, when the real customer record does show up from the source, it comes through that exact same output path and updates that placeholder in place -- filling in the real attributes -- instead of creating a second row for the same person.
questions.example:
-- The real Type 2 tracking columns this produces, inspectable afterward:
SELECT CustomerKey, CustomerAlternateKey, City, LoyaltyTier,
       StartDate, EndDate, Status
FROM dbo.DimCustomer
WHERE CustomerAlternateKey = 'AW00011000'
ORDER BY StartDate;

-- An inferred member looks like this immediately after creation:
-- CustomerKey = 9001, CustomerAlternateKey = 'AW00099999',
-- City = NULL, LoyaltyTier = NULL, Status = 'Current'
-- (filled in later via the Inferred Member Updates Output)
commonMistakes: Marking a column like BirthDate as Changing, silently accepting bad data as a real update
Marking an analytically important column like LoyaltyTier as Changing (Type 1), corrupting historical analysis
Forgetting that a Historical attribute needs Start/End date or current-flag columns configured in the wizard
Not realizing an inferred member is a real, if minimal, row -- not a special null placeholder outside the table
Inserting a second dimension row for the same customer when the real data arrives, instead of updating the inferred member in place
keyPoints: Fixed = value should never change; flagged as an error if it tries
Changing (Type 1) = overwrite, no history, for attributes with no reporting value in their history
Historical (Type 2) = keep expired version, insert new current version, for analytically meaningful attributes
Inferred members let fact loads proceed even when the matching dimension row hasn't arrived yet
The real customer data later updates the inferred member in place via the same Inferred Member Updates Output

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, justified attribute-type assignment for all four columns
Correctly explains why LoyaltyTier/City warrant Historical treatment
Correctly describes inferred member creation and the output involved
Correctly describes how the inferred member is later updated, not duplicated
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Five-Task Nightly Package Fails on Task 4 — Designing a Safe Restart
questions.prompt: A nightly package runs five sequential tasks (three Execute SQL Tasks, then two Data Flow Tasks) and fails intermittently on task 4 due to a transient timeout. Explain exactly which package and task properties you'd configure to let the package restart cleanly from task 4 without redoing tasks 1 through 3, the real restart granularity limit you have to design around, and why you would deliberately avoid also wrapping the entire package in one transaction here.
questions.modelAnswer:
On the package itself, I'd set SaveCheckpoints to True (the master switch that actually writes a checkpoint file as the package runs), CheckpointFileName to a real file path, and CheckpointUsage to IfExists -- so the package restarts from the checkpoint file if one exists from a prior failed run, but still starts clean from task 1 on a normal night with no leftover file. On every one of the five tasks, I'd set FailPackageOnFailure to True -- without that property set on a task, that task's failure doesn't register correctly as a checkpoint boundary, and the restart mechanism won't know to resume after it.

With that in place, if task 4 fails, tasks 1-3 are recorded as complete in the checkpoint file; fixing whatever caused the transient timeout and rerunning the package causes SSIS to skip 1-3 entirely and resume starting at task 4.

The real granularity limit to design around: a package can only restart at the control-flow level, at task-host-container boundaries. You cannot restart partway through a single task -- if task 4 is itself a Data Flow Task that fails five minutes into a ten-minute run, the whole Data Flow Task reruns from its own beginning on restart, not from wherever it got to. If that granularity genuinely matters -- say, task 4's data flow is actually doing two logically separate loads -- the real fix is to split it into two separate Data Flow Tasks in the Control Flow, each one its own restart point, not to look for a finer-grained checkpoint option that doesn't exist.

I would deliberately not also wrap the whole package in one enclosing transaction here, because checkpoints and transactions actively fight each other. If a container is both covered by a transaction and inside a checkpoint's reach, a restart can replay a transaction that already committed successfully the first time around -- Microsoft's own guidance describes mixing the two as something that 'could cause unexpected results.' Given that this package already has a working checkpoint-based restart strategy, layering a package-wide transaction on top of it would introduce exactly that risk for no real benefit -- if I needed transactional atomicity for a specific task, I'd scope that transaction narrowly to just that task, kept separate from the checkpoint mechanism rather than wrapping everything together.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For this one, I'd set three things on the package itself: SaveCheckpoints to True, which is really the on/off switch for writing the checkpoint file at all, CheckpointFileName pointing at a real path, and CheckpointUsage set to IfExists -- so it restarts from the checkpoint if one's sitting there from a failed run, but still runs clean from the top on a normal successful night. Then on every one of the five tasks, I'd flip FailPackageOnFailure to True, because without that, a task's failure just doesn't register as a real restart boundary for the checkpoint mechanism.

With all that set, if task 4 fails from the timeout, I fix whatever caused it, rerun the package, and it skips straight past tasks 1 through 3 and picks up at task 4 — exactly what we want.

The thing I'd make sure whoever's reviewing this understands: you can only restart at the task level, never partway through one. If task 4 were a ten-minute data flow and it died at the nine-minute mark, restarting doesn't resume from minute nine -- it reruns that whole data flow task from scratch. If that's a real problem, the fix is splitting that one data flow into two separate tasks in Control Flow, not hunting for a setting that restarts mid-flow, because that setting doesn't exist.

And I'd specifically push back if someone suggested also wrapping the whole package in one transaction on top of this. Checkpoints and transactions genuinely don't play well together -- if you restart a package that's both checkpointed and transactional, you risk replaying a transaction that already committed the first time through, which Microsoft flat out says can cause unexpected results. Since the checkpoint approach already solves our restart problem cleanly, adding a package-wide transaction on top of it would just be introducing a new risk for nothing.
questions.example:
-- Package Properties (Control Flow background -> Properties):
--   SaveCheckpoints     = True
--   CheckpointFileName   = C:\ETL\Checkpoints\NightlyLoad.chkpt
--   CheckpointUsage      = IfExists

-- On EACH of the five tasks (Properties):
--   FailPackageOnFailure = True

-- Result on a task-4 failure + rerun:
--   Task 1 (Execute SQL) - skipped, already recorded complete
--   Task 2 (Execute SQL) - skipped, already recorded complete
--   Task 3 (Execute SQL) - skipped, already recorded complete
--   Task 4 (Data Flow)   - re-executed from its own beginning
--   Task 5 (Data Flow)   - runs normally after Task 4 succeeds

Using CheckpointUsage = Always, which fails the package outright if no checkpoint file exists yet
Assuming a restart can resume partway through a single Data Flow Task
Layering a package-wide transaction on top of checkpoints without realizing they can conflict
Not splitting a long-running task into smaller ones when finer restart granularity is actually needed

FailPackageOnFailure=True on each task is required for it to register as a checkpoint boundary
Restart granularity is limited to the task-host-container level, never mid-task
Splitting a long task into smaller ones is the real fix for finer restart granularity
Checkpoints and package-wide transactions can conflict, risking a replayed already-committed transaction
