questions.title: Triaging an Unfamiliar SSIS Failure at 2 AM
questions.prompt: You get paged with a SQL Server Agent job failure for a nightly SSIS package. The only detail in the alert is a generic error referencing a destination table and a truncation message. Walk through how you'd categorize this failure among the four recurring SSIS failure patterns, what you'd actually check first given that one clue, and which Chapter 6 mechanism -- if it had been in place beforehand -- would have made this diagnosis far faster than reading the raw error message at 2 AM.
questions.modelAnswer:
A truncation error naming a destination table sorts cleanly into the data type mismatch category, not connection, permission, or dependency failure -- the error text itself is the tell: this isn't a 'can't reach the server' or 'access denied' message, it's specifically about a value not fitting the shape the destination expects.

Given that single clue, I wouldn't start by reading transformation logic broadly -- I'd go straight to the Data Conversion or Derived Column transformations feeding into that specific destination, and check the metadata on the path closest to the failure (right-click the data flow path, View Data, or inspect the column lengths/types in the destination's mapping). The most common real cause behind a sudden, previously-fine truncation failure is that an upstream source value grew past whatever fixed length a column was defined with -- a product description that used to max out at 50 characters and just didn't that night, or a source system change that widened a column SSIS wasn't told about.

The Chapter 6 mechanism that would have made this a five-minute diagnosis instead of guesswork: error outputs on the data flow component, configured to redirect failing rows (rather than failing the whole package) and capture ErrorCode and ErrorColumn into a dedicated error table or file. If that had been configured ahead of time, I wouldn't be reverse-engineering which column and which row caused this from a generic Agent job failure message at all -- I'd query the error-capture table directly and see the exact row, the exact column, and the exact error code in seconds, which is the entire point of building error outputs into a package before you need them at 2 AM instead of after.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The second I see 'truncation' and a destination table name, I know which bucket this falls into -- that's a data type mismatch, not a connection problem, not a permissions problem, not some upstream dependency that didn't show up. The wording of the error itself tells me that; it's not complaining about reaching anything, it's complaining about a value not fitting.

So my first move isn't to start reading through the whole package -- it's to go straight to whatever Data Conversion or Derived Column sits right before that destination and check the actual column widths against what's coming through right now. Nine times out of ten with truncation, something upstream just got a little wider than it used to be -- a description field, a name field, something that used to always fit and one night didn't.

But honestly, the bigger point I'd make is about what should have already been in place before this page ever went out. If this package had error outputs configured on its data flow components -- redirecting bad rows instead of blowing up the whole run, and capturing the error code and which column caused it into a table somewhere -- I wouldn't be doing any of this detective work at 2 AM. I'd just query that error table and have the exact row and column in front of me immediately. That's the whole reason that mechanism exists, and this is exactly the kind of 2 AM page it's meant to prevent you from having to solve from scratch.
questions.example:
-- Without error outputs configured ahead of time, you're reverse-engineering
-- the failure from a generic Agent job message at 2 AM.

-- With error outputs configured on the OLE DB Destination beforehand,
-- the failing rows land here instead of failing the package:
SELECT ErrorCode, ErrorColumn, SourceRowData, CapturedAt
FROM dbo.ETL_ErrorLog
WHERE PackageName = 'NightlyProductLoad'
ORDER BY CapturedAt DESC;

-- ErrorColumn maps directly to the lineage ID of the failing column,
-- turning a vague truncation message into an exact, queryable answer.
commonMistakes: Treating every SSIS failure the same way instead of sorting it into connection/data-type/permission/dependency first
Starting a broad search through the whole package instead of the specific destination named in the error
Assuming 'just rerun it' will fix a data type mismatch, which is not a transient failure
Not having error outputs configured ahead of time, forcing a slow manual reconstruction of what failed
Overlooking that an upstream source schema or data-width change, not the package itself, is often the real cause
keyPoints: A truncation error naming a destination table is a data-type-mismatch failure, not connection/permission/dependency
Look first at the Data Conversion/Derived Column feeding the named destination, and check column metadata
Upstream source values growing past a fixed destination column width is the classic real cause
Error outputs on data flow components, configured ahead of time, turn this into a fast, queryable diagnosis
ErrorCode and ErrorColumn captured into an error table identify the exact row and column immediately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly categorizes the failure as a data type mismatch
Describes a sensible, targeted first investigation step
Identifies the likely real-world cause (upstream value exceeding column width)
Correctly identifies error outputs as the preventive Chapter 6 mechanism
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Refactoring a 40-Task Monolithic Package into a Master/Child Orchestration
questions.prompt: You inherit a single SSIS package with over 40 tasks loading an entire warehouse refresh -- several dimension loads followed by two fact table loads -- and it's become hard to maintain and hard to isolate when something fails. Propose a master/child redesign: how you'd split the work, which children can run in parallel versus which absolutely must run sequentially, and how a value like a shared batch/run ID gets passed from the master down into each child.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd split the monolith along the natural unit of work: one child package per dimension (ChildLoadDimCustomer, ChildLoadDimProduct, ChildLoadDimGeography, and so on), and one child package per fact table (ChildLoadFactInternetSales, ChildLoadFactResellerSales), with a new, much smaller master/orchestrator package whose Control Flow consists almost entirely of Execute Package Task entries, one per child, referencing them via Project Reference.

For parallelism: dimensions that have no dependency on each other -- DimCustomer and DimGeography, say, since nothing about loading one requires the other to already exist -- get their Execute Package Tasks left completely unconnected on the Control Flow canvas. With no precedence constraint between them, SSIS's engine runs them concurrently, and the whole dimension layer finishes in roughly the time of the slowest single dimension load rather than the sum of all of them.

Sequencing is mandatory wherever a genuine dependency exists: every dimension load must complete successfully before any fact table load starts, because the fact loads' Lookup transformations resolve dimension surrogate keys, and a fact row can't correctly resolve a key that doesn't exist yet. So I'd connect the last dimension child's Execute Package Task to the first fact child's Execute Package Task with a standard success precedence constraint -- the fact layer as a whole waits on the dimension layer as a whole. Within the fact layer, if FactInternetSales and FactResellerSales are independent of each other (not of the dimensions, but of one another), those two can again run in parallel.

For passing a shared batch/run ID: on the Project Deployment Model, the master package would read or generate the batch ID early (an Execute SQL Task, or a parameter set at execution time), hold it in a package variable or parameter, and each Execute Package Task's Parameter Bindings tab maps that parent value directly to the matching child package parameter -- so every child package declares a BatchID parameter, and the master's Parameter Bindings page wires its own BatchID value into each child's parameter at the moment that Execute Package Task runs, with no Package Configuration layer needed. Each child then uses its own BatchID parameter value consistently in its own logging and any control-table writes, so every row loaded across every child in that night's run can be traced back to the exact same batch.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My approach here is to split this along what each piece of work actually is: a child package per dimension, a child package per fact table, and then a new master package that's mostly just a sequence of Execute Package Task entries pointing at each one through a Project Reference. That alone makes each piece testable and debuggable on its own, instead of hunting through one 40-task package to isolate a failure.

For what can run in parallel -- any two dimensions that don't depend on each other, like Customer and Geography, I'd just leave their Execute Package Tasks unconnected on the canvas. No precedence constraint between them means SSIS runs them at the same time, so the whole dimension layer finishes a lot faster than running everything one after another.

What has to stay sequential is anything with a real dependency, and the big one here is: every dimension has to finish before any fact table starts, because the fact loads are doing lookups against those dimensions to resolve surrogate keys -- you can't resolve a key for a dimension row that isn't there yet. So I'd put a precedence constraint from the last dimension child into the first fact child. If the two fact tables themselves don't depend on each other, those two can run in parallel just like the dimensions did.

For the batch ID, I'd generate or read it once in the master package early on, hold it in a variable, and then on each Execute Package Task's Parameter Bindings tab, map that value straight into the child's own BatchID parameter. Every child package declares that same parameter, so every single one of them -- whether it's loading a dimension or a fact table -- logs and writes against the exact same batch ID for that night's run, which makes tracing an entire run after the fact really straightforward.
questions.example:
-- Master package Control Flow:
--   [Execute SQL Task: Get New BatchID] -> User::BatchID
--
--   (unconnected, run in parallel)
--   [Execute Package Task: ChildLoadDimCustomer]
--   [Execute Package Task: ChildLoadDimGeography]
--   [Execute Package Task: ChildLoadDimProduct]
--        |
--        v  (success precedence constraint -- dimensions must finish first)
--   (unconnected, run in parallel)
--   [Execute Package Task: ChildLoadFactInternetSales]
--   [Execute Package Task: ChildLoadFactResellerSales]
--
-- Each Execute Package Task's Parameter Bindings tab:
--   Child Package Parameter: $Package::BatchID
--   Binding (parent value): User::BatchID
commonMistakes: Splitting children by task type instead of by logical unit of work (one dimension/fact per child)
Running fact table children in parallel with dimension children instead of after them
Assuming all dimensions must run sequentially even when none of them depend on each other
Using the older Parent Package Variable configuration instead of Parameter Bindings on the Project Deployment Model
Forgetting to give every child the same BatchID parameter, breaking cross-package traceability for a single run
keyPoints: Split by logical unit of work: one child per dimension, one child per fact table
Independent dimensions left unconnected on Control Flow run in parallel
All dimension loads must complete before any fact load starts (surrogate key resolution)
Independent fact table loads can run in parallel with each other
Parameter Bindings on the Execute Package Task maps a parent value into each child's parameter
A shared BatchID parameter across all children makes a full run traceable end to end

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly splits the monolith into logical per-dimension/per-fact child packages
Correctly identifies which children can run in parallel
Correctly identifies the mandatory dimension-before-fact sequencing and why
Correctly describes passing the batch ID via Parameter Bindings
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Making One Package Process Every File in a Folder Without Hardcoding Paths
questions.prompt: You need a package that processes every flat file dropped into a folder each night, without knowing the file names or how many there will be until the package actually runs. Describe the full end-to-end mechanism -- container, variable, property expression -- that makes this work, and explain specifically why a connection manager's property expressions have to be reached through a different UI path than a task's own Expressions page.
questions.modelAnswer:
The mechanism has three pieces working together, each covered earlier in the course, combined into the one pattern that makes 'process every file in a folder' possible without hardcoding anything.

First, a Foreach Loop Container using the Foreach File Enumerator, pointed at the target folder, with its enumerator configured to map each file it finds, one at a time, into a package variable -- say User::varFilePath. On every iteration of the loop, SSIS updates that variable with the next file's full path.

Second, a Flat File connection manager whose ConnectionString property is not set to a fixed value at design time, but instead has a property expression attached to it: @[User::varFilePath]. A property expression is an expression assigned to a read/write property that gets recalculated at run time instead of staying fixed -- so every single time the Foreach Loop updates varFilePath on a new iteration, the connection manager's ConnectionString recalculates right along with it, with zero changes needed to the Data Flow Task sitting inside the loop that actually reads from that connection manager.

Third, a Data Flow Task placed inside the Foreach Loop, reading through that same Flat File connection manager -- on iteration one it reads file A's contents, on iteration two it reads file B's, and so on, because the connection manager it's pointed at is the same object each time, just reconfigured by the expression underneath it.

On why connection managers need a different path to their property expressions: most tasks and containers have their own Expressions page right in their editor (for example, the Execute SQL Task Editor has an Expressions tab, with an ellipsis next to the Expressions collection that opens the Property Expressions Editor directly). Connection managers don't have an equivalent editor tab for this -- they're reached a different way: select the connection manager in the Connection Managers area first, then use the Properties window and click the ellipsis next to its Expressions row from there. Both paths ultimately open the same Property Expressions Editor and, from it, the same Expression Builder -- it's genuinely the identical underlying mechanism, just entered through a UI surface specific to connection managers rather than through an Expressions tab they simply don't have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this with three pieces stacked on top of each other. First, a Foreach Loop Container using the Foreach File Enumerator, pointed at the folder, mapping whatever file it finds on each pass into a package variable -- call it varFilePath. Second, a Flat File connection manager whose ConnectionString isn't hardcoded at all -- instead it has a property expression on it pointing at @[User::varFilePath], so every time the loop updates that variable on a new iteration, the connection manager's actual connection string updates right along with it automatically. Third, a Data Flow Task sitting inside the loop, reading through that same connection manager -- it doesn't need to know or care which file it's reading this time, because the connection manager underneath it is quietly pointed somewhere new on every pass.

On why connection managers are reached a different way for this: most tasks have their own Expressions tab built right into their editor -- you open the task, click Expressions, and there's an ellipsis that gets you straight to the Property Expressions Editor. Connection managers just don't have that tab. So the way in is: select the connection manager over in the Connection Managers area, open the Properties window for it, and the Expressions row there has the same ellipsis. It lands you in the exact same dialog either way -- it's really the same underlying feature, just a different doorway because connection managers don't come with their own Expressions page the way tasks do.
questions.example:
-- 1. Foreach Loop Container (Foreach File Enumerator)
--    Folder: C:\ImportDrop\
--    Files: *.csv
--    Variable Mappings: 0 -> User::varFilePath

-- 2. Flat File Connection Manager 'FF_NightlyImport'
--    Properties window -> Expressions -> (...) -> Property Expressions Editor:
--    Property: ConnectionString
--    Expression: @[User::varFilePath]

-- 3. Data Flow Task (inside the Foreach Loop):
--    Flat File Source -> FF_NightlyImport -> ... -> OLE DB Destination
--    (No changes needed inside the Data Flow between iterations --
--     the connection manager's ConnectionString changes underneath it)
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a single file path in the Flat File connection manager instead of driving it from a variable
Putting the Data Flow Task outside the Foreach Loop instead of inside it
Forgetting that the enumerator's variable mapping is what actually feeds the loop variable each iteration
Looking for an Expressions tab on the connection manager's own editor, which doesn't exist
Confusing a variable's own expression (set once via Expression Builder on the variable) with a property expression attached to a different object's property
keyPoints: Foreach Loop Container (File Enumerator) updates a package variable with each file's path per iteration
A property expression on the connection manager's ConnectionString recalculates every iteration
The Data Flow Task inside the loop needs no changes -- it just reads through the same connection manager object
Property expressions are reached via a task's own Expressions page, or via the Properties window for objects without one
Connection managers specifically lack an Expressions tab, so they're reached only through the Properties window

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Foreach Loop + File Enumerator + variable mapping
Correctly describes the property expression on ConnectionString
Correctly explains the Data Flow Task's role inside the loop
Correctly explains why connection managers are reached via the Properties window
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Promoting an SSIS Project From Dev to Production via the SSIS Catalog
questions.prompt: Your SSIS project runs fine from SSDT on your laptop, pointed at dev connection strings. Explain the full real path to running it reliably in production through the SSISDB catalog: what has to exist on the target server before you can deploy anything, how environments let the exact same deployed project point at different connection strings per environment without touching the project itself, and one genuine operational gotcha around the catalog's setup that catches people the first time they do this.
questions.modelAnswer:
Before anything can be deployed, the SSISDB catalog itself has to exist on the target SQL Server instance -- it is not created automatically when Integration Services is installed. Someone with sysadmin rights has to right-click Integration Services Catalogs in Object Explorer and run Create Catalog once per instance, which provisions a real database named SSISDB with its own purpose-built schema. That dialog requires enabling CLR integration (non-optional, since the catalog's internal stored procedures are implemented in .NET) and setting a master key password that protects the database master key SSISDB uses to encrypt sensitive parameter and connection values -- that password (or a backup of the master key) is what you'd need later to recover or move the catalog to a different instance.

Once SSISDB exists, deployment lands your project as a folder containing one or more projects (deployed .ispac files, each with its own packages and parameters). Separately, within that same folder, you create one or more environments -- named containers of variables. The key mechanism for dev-to-prod promotion is that you don't touch the deployed project itself between environments: instead, you map the project's parameters (like a connection manager's connection string) to environment variables, and at execution time you tell the catalog which environment reference to use for that specific run. A Dev environment's variables hold dev connection strings; a Prod environment holds prod connection strings; the exact same deployed .ispac is used in both cases, with the catalog substituting the right values at runtime based on which environment reference is active for that execution -- this is precisely what makes 'the same tested code runs in both places' actually true, instead of maintaining separate dev and prod copies of the project.

The real operational gotcha people hit the first time: CLR integration has to be enabled at the instance level before the catalog can even be created, and on a locked-down production instance, that's often disabled by policy -- so the Create Catalog step can fail or get blocked by a DBA/security review the first time someone tries it on a real production server, well before anyone even gets to the deployment or environment configuration. The master key password is the second trap: if it isn't recorded and backed up somewhere secure, recovering the catalog (or moving it to a new instance during a server migration) later becomes a real problem, since that password protects the encryption of every sensitive value the catalog holds.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd tell someone who's only ever run this from SSDT on their laptop is: there's a whole real database that has to exist on the server before any of this works, and SQL Server doesn't create it for you automatically just because Integration Services is installed. Someone with sysadmin rights has to go into Object Explorer, right-click Integration Services Catalogs, and run Create Catalog -- and that dialog asks for two things that matter: enabling CLR integration, which isn't optional because the catalog's internals are built on .NET stored procedures, and a master key password that protects everything sensitive the catalog stores. I always tell people to write that password down somewhere safe, because you'll need it if you ever have to move or recover the catalog later.

Once SSISDB actually exists, deploying your project puts it into a folder as a set of packages and parameters. The piece that actually solves the dev-to-prod problem is environments -- named buckets of variables, separate from the project itself. You map your project's parameters, like a connection string, to variables living in an environment, and then at execution time you just pick which environment reference to run against. Same exact deployed project, dev environment gives you dev connection strings, prod environment gives you prod connection strings -- you're never maintaining two different copies of the project or editing anything between environments.

The gotcha I'd flag from experience: that CLR integration requirement trips people up constantly on real production servers, because a lot of locked-down instances have CLR disabled by policy, and suddenly creating the catalog itself becomes its own approval process before you've even gotten to deploying a single package. And separately, if that master key password isn't documented and backed up somewhere, you're in real trouble the day you need to recover the catalog or migrate it to new hardware.
questions.example:
-- One-time, per instance (requires sysadmin):
-- Object Explorer -> Integration Services Catalogs -> Create Catalog
--   [x] Enable CLR Integration
--   Password: ********  (protects the SSISDB master key -- back this up)

-- After deployment, per folder:
--   SSISDB
--     \LTV Academy ETL   (folder)
--       \Projects
--         \WarehouseRefresh.ispac
--       \Environments
--         \Dev   (ConnString_Source = 'dev server...', ConnString_DW = 'dev dw...')
--         \Prod  (ConnString_Source = 'prod server...', ConnString_DW = 'prod dw...')

-- Executing the SAME deployed project against different environments:
EXEC catalog.set_execution_parameter_value ...
-- (environment reference selected per execution -- project itself is untouched)
commonMistakes: Assuming SSISDB is created automatically when Integration Services is installed
Forgetting that CLR integration must be enabled before the catalog can be created at all
Losing or never backing up the master key password, blocking catalog recovery/migration later
Editing the deployed project itself between environments instead of mapping parameters to environment variables
Not realizing a production instance's security policy may block CLR integration, stalling the whole rollout
keyPoints: SSISDB must be explicitly created via Create Catalog -- it does not exist by default
CLR integration and a master key password are required to create the catalog
Folders inside SSISDB hold both deployed projects and environments
Environments let the same deployed project use different connection values per environment, with no project changes
CLR-integration policy restrictions and an unbacked-up master key password are real first-time operational gotchas

Correctly describes the folder/project/environment hierarchy
Correctly explains how environments decouple connection values from the deployed project
Identifies a genuine, specific operational gotcha

questions.title: Diagnosing a Partial Data-Driven Subscription Failure
questions.prompt: A data-driven subscription delivers a report by e-mail to roughly 5,000 recipients pulled from a subscriber table every morning. It has run successfully for months. This morning, 200 of those 5,000 recipients never received the report, with no error surfaced anywhere obvious, while everyone else's copy arrived on time. Walk through exactly how you would investigate this.
questions.modelAnswer: Start by recognizing the limit of the obvious signal: the Subscriptions page's Result column reports one aggregate outcome for the whole data-driven run, not a per-recipient delivery status, so 'succeeded' there doesn't rule out 200 individual deliveries failing silently after the query returned. Next, re-run the subscription's dataset query directly in SSMS exactly as the wizard runs it, and diff the row count and e-mail column against the known 5,000 - look specifically at whether the 200 affected rows share something distinctive: NULL or malformed addresses, duplicate rows, trailing whitespace, or a source table that wasn't refreshed by the same ETL job that feeds the rest. Then check the ReportServer trace logs and the ReportServer database around the run's notification/job ID for SMTP-level errors - most 'some recipients never got it' problems at this scale are mail-server-side: a shared relay rate-limiting or greylisting after N messages per connection, a distribution-list change causing bounces, or a corporate gateway blocking a subset of domains. Also check whether the subscriber table's upstream source changed that day - a batch of 200 new or edited rows written by an HR/IT sync job whose addresses weren't valid yet. Finally, check whether the SQL Agent job backing the subscription actually completed all 5,000 iterations within its window, since a data-driven subscription generates one delivery per row and a timeout or service restart partway through would cut off a tail segment of the row set, which would point at execution duration rather than at the recipients themselves. Land on a fix based on whichever of these the evidence actually points to - add retry/backoff at the SMTP layer, fix the data-quality issue upstream, or batch/stagger the subscription - not a guess.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat the Result column as a false sense of security here - for a data-driven subscription it tells you the job as a whole ran, not that every one of 5,000 individual sends succeeded, so I wouldn't stop there. My first real move is pulling the exact subscriber query into SSMS and comparing what it returns against the 5,000 I expect, paying close attention to the 200 rows that are missing or look odd - bad e-mail formatting, duplicates, blanks are common. If the data looks clean, I pivot to the delivery side: the ReportServer trace logs around that run's timestamp, looking for SMTP rejections, because at 5,000 recipients a mail relay throttling or greylisting after a batch size is a very common culprit, as are bounces from a changed distribution list. I'd also ask whether anything upstream fed the subscriber table differently this morning - a sync job that ran late or partially. And I'd sanity-check that the subscription job itself finished cleanly within its time window rather than getting cut off mid-run. Whatever the evidence shows - bad data, a mail throttling limit, or a timeout - that's what drives the fix, not a hunch.
questions.example: Example root cause found in practice: the subscriber table was fed nightly by an AD-group sync; a change to one AD group that day wrote 200 addresses back with a trailing '@contoso.com.' (an extra dot), which passed the subscription's column mapping fine but silently bounced at the mail relay. Re-running the raw query in SSMS and eyeballing the 200 suspect e-mail values caught it in minutes.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Subscriptions page Result column reports per-recipient status for a data-driven subscription, when it only reports the overall job outcome
Blaming SSRS itself before checking whether the subscriber table's data changed
Not re-running the subscription's exact query outside the wizard to isolate data issues from delivery issues
Overlooking SMTP-side throttling/rate limits as a cause when sending to thousands of recipients in one run
keyPoints: Data-driven subscriptions report one aggregate result, not per-row delivery status
Re-run the subscriber query in SSMS to separate data problems from delivery problems
Check SMTP/mail relay logs and throttling behavior for large recipient counts
Check whether the subscriber table's upstream source changed or ran late
Check whether the job completed within its window for all 5,000 rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the limits of the subscription Result column for data-driven subscriptions

questions.title: Choosing Between a Standard and a Data-Driven Subscription
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks you to set up automatic delivery for a monthly commission report. Fifteen minutes in, they mention that each regional sales manager needs the report filtered to just their own region, and the list of managers changes a few times a year. Explain which subscription type you'd use, why, and the two things you need to confirm on the report itself before either kind of subscription is even possible to set up.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a data-driven subscription, not a standard one. A standard subscription has exactly one fixed set of parameter values, one destination, and one schedule - fine for 'the same report to the same person every time,' but it can't vary the recipient or the region parameter per delivery. A data-driven subscription instead queries a subscriber data source every time it runs and generates one delivery per row, mapping columns from that query to the recipient address, the region parameter, and any other delivery settings - so when the manager roster changes, you update the subscriber table, not the subscription. Regardless of type, two prerequisites gate the New Subscription option entirely: the report's data source must use stored credentials or no credentials at all, since the subscription runs unattended with nobody available to type in a login; and every parameter the report uses must have a default value set, since nobody is present to fill one in when the subscription fires. For the data-driven case the mapped query columns feed the parameter instead of a human, but the parameter still needs a valid default defined on the report. I'd also flag that data-driven subscriptions require elevated permissions and generally aren't available for reports sitting in a personal My Reports folder, so this needs to live in a shared folder with proper role assignments.
questions.professionalAnswer: Once they mentioned per-manager filtering and a roster that changes, I immediately rule out a standard subscription - it only supports one fixed parameter set and one destination, so I'd need a separate subscription per manager and I'd have to manually edit it every time someone joins or leaves. A data-driven subscription solves that by querying a subscriber table at run time and generating one delivery per row, with columns mapped to the recipient and the region parameter - so roster changes become a data update, not a subscription edit. Before I can set up either one, though, I'd check two things on the report itself: the data source has to run on stored or no credentials, since nothing's unattended-friendly about prompted or Windows-integrated auth, and every parameter needs a default value, because there's no one there to fill it in when the job fires. I'd also make sure this report lives in a shared folder with the right permissions, since data-driven subscriptions need elevated rights and don't work out of My Reports.
questions.example: Example: build a small Subscribers table (ManagerEmail, RegionCode) maintained by sales-ops; the data-driven subscription's query is SELECT ManagerEmail, RegionCode FROM dbo.Subscribers WHERE Active = 1, with To mapped to ManagerEmail and the report's @Region parameter mapped to RegionCode.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to standard subscriptions and trying to work around per-recipient filtering with many separate subscriptions
Forgetting the default-parameter-value requirement, so New Subscription never offers an option for the report at all
Using Windows-integrated or prompted credentials on the data source, which blocks unattended execution
Assuming updating the subscriber table takes effect immediately rather than on the subscription's next scheduled run
keyPoints: Standard subscription = one fixed parameter set/destination/schedule
Data-driven subscription = one delivery per subscriber-query row, columns mapped to settings
Data source must use stored or no credentials
Report parameters must have default values
Data-driven subscriptions need elevated permissions and a shared (non-My Reports) folder

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies data-driven subscription as the right mechanism
Explains why a standard subscription can't do per-recipient variation
States both prerequisites (credentials, default parameter values) accurately
Mentions permission/folder constraints on data-driven subscriptions
Describes a workable subscriber-table design

questions.title: Designing an Execution Strategy: Cache, Snapshot, or On-Demand
questions.prompt: You're responsible for three reports: (A) a company-wide sales dashboard that roughly 300 employees open every morning between 8 and 9 AM, built on a data source with no per-user security; (B) a finance close report that must reflect the exact state of the ledger at 11:59 PM on the last day of the month, viewed by a handful of people over the following week; (C) a personalized commission report that uses Windows-integrated authentication and shows each viewer only their own numbers. Decide an execution mode for each and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: (A) Cache a temporary copy of the report, backed by a cache refresh plan scheduled around 7:45 AM. Three hundred people requesting the same unfiltered, non-personalized report in a tight morning window is exactly the scenario caching exists for: the first request after the cache expires pays the real query cost, and the rest get the rendered copy instantly; a refresh plan warms the cache proactively so even the first viewer that morning doesn't eat the cost. (B) A report snapshot, captured once right after month-end close finishes, with a default parameter value representing that closed period. A snapshot locks in data and layout at a specific point in time independent of who's viewing - exactly the 'frozen as of 11:59 PM' requirement - and tolerates being viewed sporadically over a week without re-running a heavy close-period query each time; a cache could expire mid-week and re-run against data that's since moved on, which this report can't tolerate. (C) Neither. A report whose output legitimately differs per viewer, or that relies on Windows-integrated authentication, cannot be cached or run from a snapshot at all - there's no single 'right' rendered copy to reuse safely, so it has to run on demand with the most recent data for every viewer, every time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pick a different mode for each because they have genuinely different access patterns. The morning dashboard gets cached, with a refresh plan timed just ahead of 8 AM, because 300 people hitting the same non-personalized report in an hour is the textbook case for serving one rendered copy to everyone instead of running the query 300 times. The finance close report gets a snapshot instead, captured right when close finishes, because it has to represent one frozen point in time no matter when someone looks at it over the following week - a cache could expire and quietly re-run against data that's moved on, which defeats the whole point. The commission report gets neither - it's per-user and uses Windows-integrated auth, so there's no single safe copy to reuse; it has to run live, every time, for every person.
questions.example: Example refresh-plan config for (A): Cache Expiration = on a schedule, 24 hours; Cache Refresh Plan = report-specific schedule at 7:45 AM daily, parameters at their defaults.
commonMistakes: Trying to cache or snapshot the per-user commission report and risking wrong data served to the wrong person
Using plain caching for the month-end report, where an expired cache could re-run against data that's since moved on
Not setting a default parameter value for the snapshot report, which blocks snapshot creation entirely
Confusing 'runs often' with 'benefits from caching' - caching only pays off when many different people request the same rendered output
keyPoints: Caching suits shared, frequently-viewed, non-personalized reports
Snapshots suit point-in-time, infrequently-viewed reports needing frozen data
Per-user/Windows-integrated reports cannot be cached or snapshotted
Cache refresh plans pre-warm the cache so the first real viewer doesn't pay the cost
Snapshots require a default parameter value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct mode chosen for each of the three reports
Justification ties mode to the report's actual access pattern/personalization
Correctly identifies that per-user reports can't be cached/snapshotted
Mentions refresh plan / default parameter mechanics

questions.title: Triaging a Sudden Report-Server-Wide Slowdown
questions.prompt: Starting this morning, every report on your Report Server is taking noticeably longer to render, not just one. Walk through how you'd investigate, and explain why the fact that it's affecting every report (not just one) changes where you look first.
questions.modelAnswer: The first diagnostic question for any SSRS slowdown is 'is it every report, or just one?' because that answer points to a completely different class of fix. When it's every report at once, it's almost never any single report's query or design - a single bad dataset doesn't get slower across dozens of unrelated reports simultaneously. That pattern points to infrastructure: the report server or its database running low on memory or CPU, the server and database competing for resources on the same box, a recent patch or restart, backup/antivirus contention, or the server simply being past its load capacity for the current concurrent-user count. Concretely: check resource counters (CPU, memory, disk queue length) on both the report server and its database for the affected window; check whether report server and ReportServer database are co-located and whether that's new; check the Windows/SQL Server error logs and the ReportServer service's trace logs for anything starting around when the slowdown began; and pull ExecutionLog3 for an objective before/after comparison - average processing and rendering time across all reports today vs. the same hour on a normal day - to confirm it's genuinely uniform rather than concentrated on a handful of reports. If ExecutionLog3 shows the slowdown is actually concentrated in a narrow time window across many reports, the real cause might be a scheduling collision - several cache refresh plans or snapshots firing at once - rather than a pure capacity problem. If the server is genuinely at capacity and the growth is real rather than a one-off, the structural fix is a scale-out deployment: multiple report server instances sharing one ReportServer database with load balanced across them, rather than tuning any individual report.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I check is whether this is truly every report or just feels that way - because if it really is every report at once, I know not to waste time opening up any one report's dataset query, since a single query problem doesn't drag down unrelated reports simultaneously. That points me at infrastructure: I'd look at CPU, memory, and disk counters on the report server and its database around the time this started, check whether they're sharing hardware, and check the service logs for anything that lines up with when things got slow - a patch, a restart, a backup job. I'd also pull ExecutionLog3 and compare today's average processing time across reports against a normal day, so I'm working from a number instead of a feeling. If that data shows the slowness clustered in a specific window rather than spread evenly, I'd suspect several scheduled refreshes or snapshots colliding rather than raw capacity. And if it turns out the server's genuinely maxed out for good, I'd be looking at a scale-out deployment rather than trying to tune my way out of a capacity problem one report at a time.
questions.example: Example query sketch against ExecutionLog3: compare AVG(TimeDataRetrieval+TimeProcessing+TimeRendering) grouped by day, filtered to the last 7 days, to confirm today's average jumped across the board rather than being dragged up by one report.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into tuning one report's dataset query when the real problem is server-wide
Not checking whether the report server and its database are competing for the same hardware
Skipping ExecutionLog3 and relying on anecdote ('it feels slower') instead of a measured comparison
Assuming a scale-out deployment fixes a problem that's actually a scheduling collision (snapshots/caches refreshing at the same time)
keyPoints: Server-wide slowness points to infrastructure, not one report's design
Check CPU/memory/disk on report server and its database
Use ExecutionLog3 to measure objectively, not anecdotally
Consider scheduling collisions (simultaneous snapshot/cache refreshes) as a server-wide cause
Scale-out deployment is the structural fix when capacity, not one report, is the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why 'every report vs one report' changes the investigation path
Proposes concrete infrastructure checks (CPU/memory/co-located DB)
Uses ExecutionLog3 to measure objectively
Considers scheduling/concurrency collisions as a cause
Recommends scale-out as the structural fix when warranted

questions.title: Rewriting an Inefficient Report Dataset
questions.prompt: A report's dataset is `SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader` with no WHERE clause, and the report body uses a visibility expression to hide rows outside the selected date range plus a tablix sort to order by OrderDate. The report is slow and the server is under memory pressure when multiple people run it concurrently. Rewrite the approach and explain each change.
questions.modelAnswer: Push every piece of work currently happening inside the report body back into the dataset query, because a report can only render as fast as its slowest dataset query plus whatever extra work is layered on top in the report engine. Concretely: filter at the source with a WHERE clause tied to the report's date parameters instead of pulling every row and hiding some with a visibility expression - every hidden row still had to be retrieved, held in memory, and evaluated; presort with ORDER BY OrderDate in the query instead of sorting inside the tablix, since sorting at the data source is cheaper than sorting after the fact in the report engine; select only the columns the report actually displays instead of SELECT *, since every extra column is memory the report doesn't need; aggregate with GROUP BY at the source if the report only ever shows a rollup, instead of pulling every detail row and summing client-side; and tie the report's date parameters to the dataset's query parameters so the query plan only ever touches the needed rows instead of retrieving everything and filtering it client-side. Only after the query itself is efficient does it make sense to layer in caching, if many different people request the same parameter combination often, or a snapshot, if it's driven by a genuinely heavy nightly aggregation - caching a slow query still pays the slow cost on the first request of each cache cycle, so query tuning comes first, not as a substitute for it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is getting rid of the SELECT * and the WHERE-less query entirely - everything that's currently happening in the report body with a visibility expression and a tablix sort should be happening in the query instead. I'd add a WHERE clause tied to the date parameters so the database only ever sends back the rows actually needed, add an ORDER BY so sorting happens at the source rather than after rendering starts, and trim the column list down to only what the report displays. If the report's really just showing a summary, I'd push a GROUP BY into the query too rather than pulling every detail row. I'd also make sure the report's date parameters are wired to the dataset's query parameters directly, not just used for display-side filtering. Only once that query is actually efficient would I think about caching or a snapshot on top - caching a slow query just means the first person each cycle still waits the full time, so the query has to be fixed first regardless.
questions.example: SELECT SalesOrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, TotalDue FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader WHERE OrderDate >= @StartDate AND OrderDate < @EndDate ORDER BY OrderDate; -- @StartDate/@EndDate tied to the report's date parameters as query parameters, not filtered after the fact in the tablix
commonMistakes: Hiding rows with a visibility expression instead of filtering at the source - the engine still retrieves and holds every row
Using SELECT * and pulling columns the report never displays
Sorting inside the tablix instead of with ORDER BY in the query
Reaching for caching/snapshots before tuning the query itself, so the first request of every cache cycle still pays the full slow cost
keyPoints: Filter, sort, and aggregate at the data source, not in the report body
Select only needed columns
Tie report parameters to dataset query parameters
Query tuning comes before caching/snapshots, not instead of them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies filtering-at-source as the primary fix
Identifies presorting and column pruning
Mentions tying report parameters to query parameters
Correctly sequences query tuning before caching/snapshots
Rewritten query is syntactically sound and reflects the fixes

questions.title: Granting a New BI Analyst Access to the Report Server
questions.prompt: A new analyst joins the team. They need to view and run every report under the Sales folder, and they also need to use Report Builder to author new ad hoc reports against a shared data source. Explain, in terms of role assignments, exactly what you have to configure and why one assignment alone won't cover both needs.
questions.modelAnswer: This needs two separate role assignments because item-level and system-level security are mutually exclusive scopes in Reporting Services - neither substitutes for the other. First, an item-level role assignment on (or inherited down to) the Sales folder, granting the Browser role, which covers viewing and running reports there - this is what gets the analyst into the content itself. Second, a system-level role assignment granting the System User role, the predefined role covering use of Report Builder and shared schedules - this is scoped to the server as a whole and doesn't by itself grant access to any folder or report; without it, Report Builder simply won't be usable even though the analyst can see Sales reports fine. If the analyst also needs to publish the ad hoc reports they build back to the Sales folder rather than just author them, the item-level assignment needs to move up from Browser to Publisher on that folder specifically. I'd also confirm whether Sales currently inherits its security from Home or has already had security customized on it - if it's still inherited, adding the role assignment at Home would affect every other folder beneath it too, which is probably not the intent; the right move is to customize security specifically at the Sales folder level so the grant stays scoped to where it's needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up as two distinct grants, because in Reporting Services item-level access and system-level access don't overlap at all - one doesn't imply the other. For the folder access, I'd add an item-level role assignment scoped to the Sales folder specifically - not at Home, where it would leak into every other folder - giving the analyst Browser so they can view and run what's there, or Publisher if they'll also be saving reports back into that folder. Separately, for Report Builder, I'd add a system-level role assignment granting System User, since Report Builder access is a server-wide capability that has nothing to do with folder permissions - without that second grant, they'd see the Sales reports fine but Report Builder just wouldn't work for them. I'd also check first whether Sales is still inheriting security from Home, so I know whether I'm customizing it fresh or adding to an existing override.
questions.example: Item-level: New Role Assignment on the Sales folder for user@contoso.com with Browser (or Publisher if they'll save reports back). System-level: Site Settings → Security → New Role Assignment for user@contoso.com with System User.
commonMistakes: Assuming a system-level role assignment grants access to folders/reports
Assuming full control/administrator anywhere implies system-level rights elsewhere automatically
Granting the role at Home when it should be scoped to the Sales folder specifically, accidentally widening access
Forgetting Report Builder access is a system-level concern, not an item-level one
keyPoints: Item-level and system-level role assignments are mutually exclusive scopes
Item-level controls access to folders/reports/data sources
System-level authorizes server-wide operations like Report Builder and shared schedules
Granting full access to a new analyst is typically a two-part configuration
Check whether security should be customized at a specific folder rather than at Home

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains item-level vs system-level distinction
Identifies both assignments needed (Browser/Publisher + System User)
Addresses inheritance and scoping the grant to the right folder
Clear, specific configuration steps

questions.title: Why the New Subscription Button Won't Appear
questions.prompt: A report uses three cascading parameters - Region, then State (filtered by Region), then Store (filtered by State) - and works fine interactively. A user asks you to set up a subscription for it and the New Subscription option isn't available at all. Diagnose why, and explain the fix without breaking the cascading behavior for people who still run it interactively.
questions.modelAnswer: New Subscription is unavailable for one of two reasons: either the data source isn't using stored/no credentials, or one or more parameters has no default value - a subscription runs unattended, so it can't be created for a report where nobody will be present to pick values. With a three-level cascading chain, it's very common for only the top-level parameter (Region) to have an explicit default while State and Store are left with no default, because interactively a user always picks them in sequence and nobody ever noticed the gap running it by hand. The fix is to set a valid default for every parameter in the chain, including State and Store, consistent with the defaults already set further up - default Region to a specific region, set State's default-values query to resolve against that default Region, and Store's default to cascade the same way from State's default. This doesn't break interactive use: a user can still change Region and still re-filter the State and Store available-values lists exactly as before - the only thing being added is what happens when nobody touches the controls at all, which is exactly the subscription's unattended path. I'd also double-check the credentials setting at the same time, since that's the other common gate, even though missing cascading defaults is the more likely cause given the symptom here.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess with a cascading chain like this is that the defaults only go one level deep - Region has one, but State and Store were never given defaults because nobody ever needed them interactively; you always pick your way down the chain by hand. That alone blocks New Subscription, since every parameter needs a default for an unattended run. The fix is to actually give State and Store real defaults, and to make sure those defaults are consistent with each other - State's default needs to resolve correctly under the default Region, and Store's default under that default State, so the chain doesn't end up pointing at an invalid combination. None of that touches how the parameters behave when a person is actually clicking through them interactively, since I'm only defining what happens when nobody does. I'd also glance at the data source credentials while I'm in there, just to rule out the other common cause, but with cascading parameters specifically, missing defaults past the first level is almost always the story.
questions.example: Example: Region defaults to 'West'; State's available-values AND default-values queries both filter on @Region, so with Region defaulted to 'West' the State parameter's default resolves to a real state (e.g. 'WA') instead of being blank; Store cascades the same way from State's default.
commonMistakes: Only checking the top-level parameter's default and missing that State/Store have none
Assuming the credentials setting is always the cause and not checking parameter defaults
Hardcoding a default value for State that isn't actually valid under the default Region, breaking the cascade logic
Forgetting that 'has a default' and 'has a default that's actually reachable through the cascade' are two different things
keyPoints: New Subscription requires stored/no credentials AND every parameter having a default value
Cascading parameters often have defaults only on the top level, breaking subscription availability
Set defaults consistently through the whole cascade chain, not just the parameter that's missing one
Interactive cascading behavior is unaffected by adding defaults

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing parameter defaults as the likely cause
Explains why cascading parameters are especially prone to this
Proposes a fix that preserves interactive cascading behavior
Mentions checking the credentials prerequisite too

questions.title: Designing a Cache Refresh Plan for a Morning Dashboard
questions.prompt: Roughly 200 executives open the same company dashboard report between 7:30 and 9:00 AM every weekday; the underlying query takes about 90 seconds to run and the report has no per-user data. Design the caching configuration you'd put in place, including what you'd set the cache expiration and refresh plan to, and explain what happens for the person who opens it at exactly 7:30.
questions.modelAnswer: Set the report's execution mode to Cache copies of this report and use them when available, with Cache Expiration on a daily schedule rather than a short fixed-minutes timeout, since the goal is 'fresh once a day,' not re-run every twenty minutes. Then add a Cache Refresh Plan on a report-specific schedule at around 7:15 AM every weekday, running with the report's default parameter values. That refresh plan proactively fires the 90-second query at 7:15, before the 7:30 traffic starts, and the resulting rendered copy becomes the cache. Without the refresh plan, the first person to open the report after the cache expires or after a server restart would be the one stuck waiting the full 90 seconds while the query runs live - that's what 'cache copies and use them when available' means literally: it only has something to serve once a first request, or a refresh plan, has populated it. With the 7:15 refresh plan in place, the person who opens it at 7:30 gets the already-rendered cached copy back essentially instantly, same as everyone who opens it afterward, because the cache was warmed before anyone requested it. I'd also set the cache to expire once daily rather than never, so the report picks up genuinely new data each morning instead of serving yesterday's cached copy indefinitely.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd switch the report to cached execution with a daily expiration, since this data really only needs to refresh once a day, not on some short timer. The key piece is the refresh plan - I'd schedule it for about 7:15, a little ahead of when the real traffic starts, so the 90-second query has already run and the cache is sitting there warm by the time the first executive opens it at 7:30. Without that refresh plan, whoever happens to be first each day would be the unlucky one stuck waiting the full 90 seconds while the cache populates live. With it scheduled ahead of time, the 7:30 person and everyone after them just get the already-rendered copy back almost instantly. And I'd still have the cache expire daily so it's not serving stale data indefinitely.
questions.example: Caching page: Cache copies of this report and use them when available; Cache Expiration = Schedule, daily at midnight. Cache Refresh Plan: report-specific schedule, 7:15 AM every weekday, parameters at default values.
commonMistakes: Using Always run with the most recent data, which makes all 200 executives pay the 90-second cost every time they open it
Setting cache expiration to a short fixed-minutes window instead of a daily schedule, causing unnecessary re-runs mid-morning
Forgetting the refresh plan, so the first person each day still waits the full 90 seconds
Trying to cache a report that has per-user data, which isn't legal/safe to cache at all
keyPoints: Cache copies + a proactive refresh plan avoids making anyone pay the live query cost
Refresh plan timing should precede the real traffic window
Cache expiration schedule should match how often the underlying data actually changes
Caching only benefits non-personalized, frequently shared reports

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Chooses the correct caching execution mode
Designs a refresh plan timed ahead of the traffic window
Sets a sensible cache expiration schedule
Correctly explains what the 7:30 user experiences and why

questions.title: Writing the Dataset Query for a Regional Manager Subscription
questions.prompt: Design and write the subscriber dataset query for a data-driven subscription that e-mails a sales report to each active regional manager, with the report's @Region parameter set to that manager's own region, and a Bcc to a sales-ops distribution list on every delivery. Assume a table dbo.RegionManagers(ManagerEmail, Region, IsActive).
questions.modelAnswer: The query only needs to return the columns the subscription will map to delivery fields and parameters - here, the manager's e-mail, mapped to To, and their region, mapped to the @Region parameter - filtered to active managers only, since inactive ones shouldn't generate a delivery row at all. The Bcc doesn't need a column from this query because it's the same literal value on every single delivery, so in the wizard I'd set Bcc's Source of value to a literal value, the distribution list address, instead of mapping it to a dataset column - there's no reason to repeat a constant in every row of the query. I'd validate this exact query in SQL Server Management Studio first, confirm the row count matches the expected active-manager count, and confirm there are no NULL or duplicate e-mail addresses before ever pasting it into the wizard - a duplicate ManagerEmail row would quietly generate two deliveries to the same person. In the wizard: To maps to ManagerEmail from the dataset; Bcc is set as a literal value; the report's Region parameter maps to Region from the dataset.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the query as narrow as possible - just ManagerEmail and Region, filtered to IsActive = 1, since those are the only two things the wizard actually needs to map: To and the @Region parameter. The Bcc address doesn't belong in the query at all since it's the same value on every single delivery - I'd just type it in as a literal in the wizard rather than carrying a constant through every row. Before I ever touch the wizard, I'd run this exact query in SSMS, check the row count lines up with how many active managers I expect, and specifically look for duplicate e-mail addresses, since a duplicate silently means someone gets the report twice. Once that's clean, the mapping itself is straightforward: To from ManagerEmail, the Region parameter from Region, Bcc as a fixed literal.
questions.example: Validation query to catch the duplicate-row trap before pasting into the wizard: SELECT ManagerEmail, COUNT(*) FROM dbo.RegionManagers WHERE IsActive = 1 GROUP BY ManagerEmail HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
commonMistakes: Adding a Bcc column to the query for a value that's actually constant across every row
Not filtering IsActive = 1, generating deliveries to former managers
Not checking for duplicate ManagerEmail rows, which silently doubles some deliveries
Pasting an untested query straight into the wizard instead of validating it in SSMS first
keyPoints: Query only returns columns actually needed for mapping (To, Region)
Filter to active recipients only
Constant values across every delivery belong in the wizard as a literal, not as a repeated query column
Validate row count and check for duplicates in SSMS before using the query in the subscription

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Query correctly filters to active managers and returns only needed columns
Correctly identifies Bcc as a literal value rather than a mapped column
Describes the field-mapping steps in the wizard accurately
Includes a validation step (row count/duplicate check) before deployment

questions.title: Diagnosing Unexpected Totals From CALCULATE Inside SUMX
questions.prompt: A measure written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100)), where [Customer Measure] itself calls CALCULATE on Sales, returns totals that shift unexpectedly when a product-category slicer is applied - numbers that don't match a hand-calculated expectation. Walk through how you'd diagnose the context-transition behavior causing this.
questions.modelAnswer: The core thing to check is what happens to [Customer Measure] inside that FILTER. FILTER(Customer, ...) iterates the Customer table row by row - that's row context. [Customer Measure] is a measure reference, and every measure reference is implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE, which means context transition fires for every single customer row: the current customer's row context gets converted into a one-customer filter context before [Customer Measure] evaluates. Critically, that implicit CALCULATE also inherits whatever filter context is already active outside, including the product-category slicer. So [Customer Measure] isn't being evaluated against 'this customer, all products' per row; it's being evaluated against 'this customer, intersected with whatever category the slicer currently has selected.' That's almost certainly the source of the shifting numbers: as the slicer changes, the per-row result of [Customer Measure] changes for every customer, which changes which customers pass the >100 threshold inside FILTER, which changes the set of customers the outer SUM runs against - a compounding effect, not a simple scaling. To diagnose concretely: temporarily rewrite [Customer Measure] as a plain CALCULATE expression inline so the context transition is visible instead of hidden behind a measure reference; use a VAR to capture [Customer Measure]'s value for one specific, known customer under two different slicer selections and compare them directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching into the per-row evaluation via context transition, which is expected behavior, not a bug; then decide whether that's actually wanted - if the threshold should be evaluated against each customer's all-time total regardless of the slicer, wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL(Product) or REMOVEFILTERS(Product) to deliberately cut it off from the slicer, rather than letting it inherit by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd zero in on is that FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100) is evaluating [Customer Measure] once per customer row, and since that's a measure reference sitting inside row context, it's implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE - so context transition fires for every row, and that implicit CALCULATE picks up whatever filter context is already active, including the category slicer. So the per-customer threshold check isn't really 'does this customer's all-time value exceed 100,' it's 'does this customer's value under the currently selected category exceed 100' - and that set of qualifying customers shifts every time the slicer changes, which compounds into the outer SUM. To prove that's what's happening, I'd isolate one known customer with a VAR, evaluate [Customer Measure] for them under two different slicer states, and compare the numbers directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching inside the per-row evaluation. Then it's a design decision: if the threshold is supposed to ignore the slicer, I'd wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL or REMOVEFILTERS on the category column so it stops inheriting that context.
questions.example: Debug step: VAR TestCustomerValue = CALCULATE([Customer Measure], Customer[CustomerKey] = 123) RETURN TestCustomerValue - evaluated once with the category slicer set to 'Bikes' and once cleared, to see directly whether the per-customer value is slicer-dependent.
commonMistakes: Assuming a measure reference inside FILTER behaves like a plain column and ignores outer filter context
Not realizing context transition means the implicit CALCULATE inherits the active filter context, including slicers
Treating the shifting totals as a bug instead of correct (if unintended) behavior that needs a deliberate ALL/REMOVEFILTERS fix
Debugging by staring at the final number instead of isolating one row's value with a VAR

Context transition inherits the currently active filter context, including slicers, unless explicitly overridden
FILTER iterating a table creates row context for every measure called inside it
Isolate one row's value with VAR under different filter states to confirm the behavior
Use ALL/REMOVEFILTERS inside the inner measure if the threshold should ignore the slicer
