questions.title: Explaining Context Transition in a Calculated Column
questions.prompt: A colleague doesn't understand how this calculated column can possibly work, since a calculated column is supposed to only see row context: Customer Segment = IF(CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey])) < 2500, "Low", "High"). Explain, step by step, what actually happens for one customer row.
questions.code:
Customer Segment =
IF (
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] ),
        ALLEXCEPT ( Customer, Customer[CustomerKey] )
    ) < 2500,
    "Low",
    "High"
)
questions.modelAnswer: Context transition is exactly the bridge that makes this work. For one specific customer row: the formula starts in row context, since DAX is evaluating this expression for one particular CustomerKey. The moment CALCULATE is invoked, it triggers context transition - the current row context, this one customer, is converted into an equivalent filter context, as if a filter had been applied limiting the whole model to that one CustomerKey. ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey]) then clears every other filter that might be active on the Customer table while deliberately preserving the context-transition filter just created on CustomerKey - this matters because it's what protects the expression from unrelated filters if this logic were ever reused in a visual, even though a calculated column itself has no report-level filters to begin with. SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) now aggregates across whatever rows of Sales are reachable through the Customer-Sales relationship under that one-customer filter - that is, all of that customer's sales, nothing else. IF compares the result to 2500 and labels that row. This repeats independently for every row in Customer - row context in, filter context out, one customer at a time - which is exactly why a calculated column, which is 'supposed to' only see row context, can still produce a result that depends on aggregating an entirely different table: CALCULATE is what converts between the two context types, and it's invisible/automatic for a bare measure reference but explicit here because CALCULATE is written directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk them through it one customer at a time. We start in row context - DAX is sitting on one specific CustomerKey. As soon as it hits CALCULATE, that row context gets converted into a filter context scoped to just that one CustomerKey - that conversion is context transition, and it's the whole reason this works. ALLEXCEPT then strips away any other filters on the Customer table but specifically keeps the one context transition just created, so the filter context going into SUM is exactly 'this one customer.' SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) then totals every sale tied to that customer through the relationship, and IF labels the row based on that total. Every row repeats this independently. So the calculated column isn't magically seeing filter context on its own - CALCULATE is explicitly converting its row context into one, which is the same thing that happens invisibly whenever you reference a plain measure from inside a calculated column.
questions.example: Simpler illustration of the same mechanism without ALLEXCEPT: a calculated column Row Total = [Some Measure] works for the same reason - referencing a measure from row context implicitly wraps it in CALCULATE, triggering context transition automatically, with no CALCULATE visible in the formula at all.
commonMistakes: Saying calculated columns 'can't see filter context' without explaining that CALCULATE is what bridges the two
Missing that a bare measure reference in row context triggers the same mechanism implicitly, without a visible CALCULATE
Thinking ALLEXCEPT is what causes context transition, rather than CALCULATE itself
Describing the behavior without walking through it per-row
keyPoints: Context transition converts row context into an equivalent one-row filter context
It is triggered specifically by CALCULATE evaluating inside row context
A bare measure reference inside row context triggers it implicitly via an invisible wrapping CALCULATE
ALLEXCEPT here preserves the context-transition filter while clearing other filters on the table
The whole calculation repeats independently for every row

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the trigger for context transition (CALCULATE in row context)
Walks through the five-step mechanism accurately
Explains the implicit-CALCULATE case for bare measure references
Clear, row-by-row framing

questions.title: Writing a Revenue Measure That Plain SUM Can't Express
questions.prompt: Sales[Quantity] and Sales[UnitPrice] exist as separate columns, but there's no stored Revenue column. Write a measure that totals revenue, filtered to only rows where the related SalesTerritory[Country] isn't the United States, and explain why SUM alone cannot do this.
questions.modelAnswer: Plain SUM only aggregates a single existing column directly - it has nothing to point at here, because revenue is a per-row computation (Quantity times UnitPrice), not a stored value. SUMX is an iterator: it walks the table row by row, evaluates an expression using that row's own values, then adds up the results - exactly what's needed to compute Quantity times UnitPrice fresh for each row before summing. Combining SUMX with FILTER handles the country condition: FILTER returns the subset of Sales rows where the related country isn't 'United States,' reached via RELATED since Country lives on the territory table, and SUMX then iterates only that filtered subset rather than the whole table. SUM alone can express neither the per-row multiplication nor the conditional subset - both require row-by-row evaluation, which is the entire reason the X-suffixed iterator functions exist.
questions.professionalAnswer: SUM can only point at a single column that already exists, and revenue here doesn't exist as a column - it only exists as Quantity times UnitPrice computed per row. That's exactly what SUMX is for: it goes row by row, computes that multiplication fresh each time, and adds the results together. To handle the country exclusion, I'd wrap the table argument in a FILTER that uses RELATED to reach the territory table's Country column from each Sales row, and SUMX then only iterates over the rows that pass. There's really no way to get SUM to do either of those two things - the per-row math or the conditional subset - because SUM was never built to evaluate an expression, only to add up a column that's already there.
questions.code:
Non-USA Revenue =
SUMX(
    FILTER(
        Sales,
        RELATED(SalesTerritory[Country]) <> "United States"
    ),
    Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]
)
questions.example: Contrast: Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) with no FILTER would total revenue across every country; adding the FILTER narrows the exact rows SUMX iterates.
commonMistakes: Trying to write SUM(Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) directly - SUM doesn't accept an expression, only a single column
Forgetting RELATED is needed to reach the country column on a different table from inside the row-by-row FILTER condition
Not realizing FILTER's second argument is itself evaluated in row context per row of Sales
Using a calculated column instead of a measure, pre-computing per-row revenue and losing the ability to recompute dynamically under different filter contexts
keyPoints: SUMX evaluates an expression row by row, then sums the results
Use SUMX whenever the needed value isn't a single stored column
FILTER inside SUMX's table argument narrows which rows get iterated
RELATED reaches a related table's column from inside row context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SUMX + FILTER + RELATED expression
Explains why SUM alone cannot express this
Explains the role of FILTER narrowing the iterated rows
Explains RELATED's role in reaching the related table

questions.title: AVERAGEX vs. a Plain AVERAGE Measure
questions.prompt: A report needs the average order value, where order value is the sum of all line items on an order, not a single stored column. Explain why CALCULATE(AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal])) gives a different (and wrong) answer than an AVERAGEX-based approach, and write the correct measure.
questions.code:
Average Order Value =
AVERAGEX(
    VALUES(Sales[OrderID]),
    CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[LineTotal]))
)
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE(AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal])) averages across line items, not orders - every individual line of every order counts as one data point, so an order with ten small line items pulls the average down and an order with one huge line item pulls it a different way, regardless of what each order actually totaled. That's the wrong grain entirely: the business question is 'average order value,' and the unit of analysis has to be the order, not the line. The fix is to iterate at the order grain: use VALUES to get one row per order, compute each order's total with CALCULATE(SUM(...)) inside that per-order context, and then AVERAGEX that result across orders - AVERAGEX evaluates its expression once per order, the correct grain, and averages those per-order totals rather than the raw line-level column. This is the same 'does the value already exist as one column, or does it need computing per group first' question that distinguishes SUM from SUMX, just applied to AVERAGE: because order value genuinely doesn't exist as a single column anywhere, a plain AVERAGE, even wrapped in CALCULATE, is aggregating the wrong thing from the start - no filter context modifier fixes that, because the problem isn't the filter, it's the grain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem isn't a filter-context issue at all, it's a grain mismatch. AVERAGE(Sales[LineTotal]) is averaging over line items, so an order with a lot of small lines and an order with one big line pull the average in different directions that have nothing to do with what either order actually totaled - CALCULATE wrapped around it doesn't change that, because CALCULATE only changes filters, not what's being averaged. What actually fixes it is averaging at the order grain: I'd use VALUES(Sales[OrderID]) to get one row per order, compute each order's total inside that context with CALCULATE(SUM(...)), and let AVERAGEX average those per-order totals instead of the raw line rows. That's the same idea as SUMX versus SUM, just one level up - the value I need doesn't exist as a column, it exists as a calculation at a specific grain, so I need an iterator that operates at that grain.
questions.example: If Order 1001 has three lines totaling $300 and Order 1002 has one line totaling $900, the wrong measure averages across 4 individual line amounts; the correct measure averages {$300, $900} = $600 - a materially different answer.
commonMistakes: Averaging at the line-item grain when the business question is about orders
Assuming wrapping AVERAGE in CALCULATE fixes a grain problem - it only changes filter context, not the unit being averaged
Forgetting that CALCULATE(SUM(...)) inside AVERAGEX's expression triggers context transition for each OrderID, which is exactly what makes the per-order total correct
Using SUMX instead of AVERAGEX when the goal is specifically an average across the grouped values, not a sum
keyPoints: Plain AVERAGE averages at whatever grain the underlying column exists at - here, line items, not orders
AVERAGEX lets you choose the correct grain by supplying the table to iterate (one row per order)
Context transition inside AVERAGEX's expression (via CALCULATE/SUM) computes each order's total correctly before averaging
No filter modifier fixes a wrong-grain measure - the fix is changing what's being iterated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the grain mismatch as the root cause
Correct AVERAGEX-based measure at order grain
Explains why CALCULATE alone doesn't fix a grain problem
Concrete numeric example showing the discrepancy

questions.title: Choosing Between ALL, ALLEXCEPT, and ALLSELECTED
questions.prompt: A report has a table visual broken out by Product Category and Year, on a page already filtered to Europe via a report-level filter. Write three measures that each answer a different question: (1) each cell's share of the true dataset-wide grand total, (2) each cell's share of the total for everything currently visible given the Europe filter, ignoring only the visual's own category/year breakdown, and (3) a measure that behaves like #1 but written using ALLEXCEPT instead of ALL. Explain the difference between all three.
questions.modelAnswer: These three functions remove filters in different scopes, and picking the wrong one produces a number that's technically correct DAX but answers the wrong business question. ALL(Sales) removes every filter on the Sales table unconditionally, including the Europe report filter and the visual's own breakdown - so dividing by CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales)) always gives the true worldwide grand total, regardless of what's selected anywhere. ALLSELECTED() is different: it keeps filters applied outside the visual, so the Europe report-level filter stays active, and only removes the row/column filters generated by the visual itself, the category/year breakdown. That's what 'visual total' means: the total for everything the user actually selected, just not broken out by category and year. ALLEXCEPT(Sales, <columns to keep>) takes the opposite framing from ALL(Column) - instead of naming the few columns to clear, you name the few columns to keep filtered and everything else on that table gets cleared; written with no columns named to keep, ALLEXCEPT(Sales) behaves equivalently to ALL(Sales) for the grand-total case, so #3 and #1 should produce identical numbers. The real choice between ALL and ALLEXCEPT is about which list, to-clear or to-keep, is shorter and more readable for a given table, not a difference in what gets filtered when neither keeps any columns.
questions.professionalAnswer: Each of these clears filters at a different scope, and that's the whole ballgame here. The ALL version strips every filter off Sales entirely, Europe filter included, so its denominator is always the true worldwide total no matter what's selected on the page. ALLSELECTED is the one that respects the Europe filter - it only clears what the visual itself added, the category and year breakdown, so its denominator becomes the total for Europe specifically, which is what people usually mean by a 'visual total.' ALLEXCEPT, with no columns named to preserve, ends up doing the same thing as ALL in this case - it's really just a different way of writing 'clear everything,' useful when you'd rather list the columns to keep than the columns to clear. So #1 and #3 should match exactly, and #2 is the odd one out because it's the only one that respects the Europe selection.
questions.code:
%% of Grand Total (ALL) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales)))

%% of Visible Total (ALLSELECTED) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLSELECTED()))

%% of Grand Total (ALLEXCEPT) = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(Sales)))
questions.example: With the Europe filter active: the ALL-based measure's denominator is the worldwide total (ignores Europe); the ALLSELECTED-based measure's denominator is the Europe total (keeps the report filter, drops only category/year); the ALLEXCEPT(Sales)-based measure matches the ALL-based one since no columns are named to keep.
commonMistakes: Using ALL when the requirement is actually a 'visual total' that should respect report-level filters
Assuming ALLSELECTED clears all filters like ALL does
Thinking ALLEXCEPT and ALL always differ - with no columns named to keep, ALLEXCEPT(Table) behaves like ALL(Table)
Not checking which total the stakeholder actually wants (true grand total vs. respecting what they selected) before picking a function
keyPoints: ALL clears every filter unconditionally, including report-level filters
ALLSELECTED keeps filters set outside the visual, clears only the visual's own breakdown
ALLEXCEPT names columns to keep filtered; everything else on that table clears
ALLEXCEPT(Table) with nothing named to keep is equivalent to ALL(Table)
The business question - true grand total vs. visual/selected total - decides which function is correct

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ALL-based grand total measure
Correct ALLSELECTED-based visual total measure
Correct ALLEXCEPT equivalent and explanation of when it diverges from ALL
Clearly explains the business-question framing for choosing between them

questions.title: A Percent-of-Total Measure Ignores the Slicer
questions.prompt: A '% of Total' measure was built as DIVIDE([Sales], CALCULATE([Sales], ALL(Sales))). Stakeholders report that when they select a single region in a slicer, the percentages across the visible categories don't sum to 100% - they're much smaller than expected. Diagnose the cause and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is working exactly as ALL is defined to work - the symptom isn't a bug, it's a mismatch between what the measure computes and what the stakeholders actually want. ALL(Sales) clears every filter on Sales unconditionally, including the region slicer, so the denominator is always the worldwide total across every region, every time, no matter what's selected. When a user filters to one region, the numerator shrinks to that region's sales but the denominator stays at the full worldwide total - so the percentages correctly reflect 'this category's share of everyone, everywhere,' which only sums to 100% when nothing is filtered, and sums to something much smaller once a region is selected, exactly as reported. What the stakeholders actually want is a visual total: a percentage of what's currently selected, the one region, not of the whole dataset. That's ALLSELECTED's job specifically - it keeps the filters applied outside the visual, the region slicer, and only clears the breakdown generated by the visual itself. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator fixes it: the denominator becomes 'total sales for the currently selected region,' which the numerators, each category's sales within that region, correctly sum to 100% of.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't actually broken DAX, it's answering a different question than the one being asked. ALL(Sales) wipes out every filter on that table, the region slicer included, so no matter what someone picks, the denominator is always the full worldwide total. That's why, once you filter to one region, the numbers only add up to that region's small slice of the world instead of 100% - the math is doing exactly what ALL tells it to do. What the stakeholders actually want is for the denominator to respect their region selection and only ignore the category breakdown the visual itself creates - that's precisely what ALLSELECTED does. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator means the total becomes 'everything selected, in this case the one region,' and the category percentages go back to summing to 100% of that.
questions.example: Before the fix, selecting 'West' region: numerator = West's category sales, denominator = worldwide total, so percentages sum to roughly West's share of the world, well under 100%. After the fix: denominator = West's total, so percentages correctly sum to 100% of West.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a bug in ALL rather than the wrong function choice for the requirement
Trying to 'fix' it by adding more filter arguments to ALL instead of switching to ALLSELECTED
Not testing the measure with a slicer selection active before shipping it, so the discrepancy wasn't caught earlier
Assuming ALLSELECTED and ALL are interchangeable because they both start with 'ALL'
keyPoints: ALL clears report-level/slicer filters too, not just the visual's own breakdown
A percentage that should respect slicer selections needs ALLSELECTED, not ALL
Always test ratio/percent-of-total measures with a slicer active, not just unfiltered
The underlying DAX wasn't broken - it was answering a different question than the one asked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses ALL as clearing the slicer filter too
Explains why percentages don't sum to 100% once filtered
Correct ALLSELECTED-based fix
Frames it as a requirement mismatch, not a DAX bug

questions.title: Rewriting a YoY Growth Measure With Variables
questions.prompt: Rewrite this measure to follow DAX best practices, and explain each change: Sales YoY Growth % = ([Sales] - CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))) / CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))
questions.code:
Sales YoY Growth %% =
VAR SalesPriorYear =
    CALCULATE ( [Sales], PARALLELPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], -12, MONTH ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( [Sales] - SalesPriorYear, SalesPriorYear )
questions.modelAnswer: Two problems, two fixes. First, CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD(...)) is written twice and evaluated twice - identical work done over again for no reason, which costs real query time on a large model. A VAR computes it once, names it, and both places that need it reference the stored result instead of recomputing it, roughly halving the work for this formula. Second, the plain '/' operator throws an error the instant the denominator is zero or blank, which happens for any period with no prior-year data - a new product line, a new store, the first year of history - and that error surfaces to end users as a broken visual instead of a clean blank. DIVIDE handles a zero/blank denominator gracefully, returning blank by default, or a value you specify, instead of erroring. Naming the variable SalesPriorYear also makes the RETURN line read as plain English instead of a repeated formula, which matters when someone else, or you in six months, has to maintain this.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two things jump out. The same CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression is written twice, which means the engine computes 'sales a year ago' twice for no reason - I'd pull that into a VAR, compute it once, and reference it in both places it's needed, which is real query-time savings, not just tidiness. The other issue is the plain division - the moment there's no prior-year data at all, which happens for anything new, that divide-by-zero throws an error straight into the visual instead of quietly returning blank. I'd swap it for DIVIDE, which handles that gracefully. On top of the performance and correctness fixes, naming the variable SalesPriorYear also just makes the RETURN line readable as a sentence instead of a repeated formula, which matters for anyone maintaining this later, including me.
questions.example: Debugging tip from the same pattern: temporarily change RETURN to just SalesPriorYear to inspect what the variable actually holds for a given filter context, before reinstating the real DIVIDE expression.
commonMistakes: Leaving the repeated CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression evaluated twice instead of once via a variable
Using plain division and letting the report error out on periods with no prior-year data
Naming variables generically (Var1, Result) instead of something that documents what the value represents
Not knowing the VAR-swap-to-RETURN trick for isolating which part of a formula produces an unexpected value
keyPoints: VAR/RETURN computes a repeated subexpression once instead of multiple times
DIVIDE avoids division-by-zero/blank errors that plain / throws
Named variables double as self-documentation
Temporarily returning a variable directly is a fast debugging technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct VAR/RETURN rewrite eliminating the duplicated CALCULATE call
Correct use of DIVIDE in place of /
Explains the performance benefit of computing once vs twice
Explains the zero/blank-denominator failure mode DIVIDE avoids

questions.title: Designing Dynamic RLS for 40 Sales Territories
questions.prompt: A company has 40 sales territories, each with its own manager who should only see their own territory's data, and the territory list changes periodically as the business reorganizes. Design the row-level security approach - don't just name the feature, walk through the actual model changes, the role definition, and how you'd validate it before any real manager is assigned.
questions.modelAnswer: Forty territories rules out a static role per value immediately - that's 40 roles to create and maintain by hand every time the org chart changes, and someone has to remember to add a 41st when the business adds a territory. The right design is a single dynamic role whose filter expression adapts to whoever is signed in, backed by a small user-mapping table added to the model: two columns, UserEmail and TerritoryID, with one row per manager, related to the territory dimension. The role's DAX filter expression is simply [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() on that mapping table - one role, one expression, scaling to any number of territories because the filtering logic never changes, only the rows in the mapping table do. A critical detail: USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return different formats depending on where the report runs - USERNAME() returns DOMAIN\username in Desktop but a UPN in the service, while USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns a UPN-style value, like an email, in both places. Whichever function the role uses, the mapping table's values have to match the format that function actually returns when the report is viewed in the Power BI service, which is where real managers will view it, not necessarily what it shows while testing in Desktop. Before assigning a single real person, I'd validate with Test as role: select the role, confirm the report filters down to exactly one territory's data, and check that it matches the identity shown under 'Now viewing as.' The real limitation to flag: Test as role evaluates the filter using my own identity, so USERPRINCIPALNAME() inside the test returns my UPN, not the UPN of the manager I'm trying to simulate - it genuinely proves the filter logic works, but it can't prove a specific external manager will see the right data once onboarded. For that, the manager has to actually sign in and view it themselves, which I'd do for at least one real manager as a final check before rolling the role out to all 40.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 40 territories, I wouldn't even consider a static role per value - that's 40 things to build and maintain, and it falls apart the moment the org reorganizes. I'd build one dynamic role instead, backed by a small user-mapping table I add to the model: a UserEmail column and a TerritoryID column, related to the territory dimension, with one row per manager. The role's filter is just [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and because that's the only logic, adding or removing a territory becomes a data update to the mapping table, not a model or role change. The detail I'd be careful about is that USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() don't necessarily return the same format in Desktop as they do once published to the service, so whichever function I pick, I need the mapping table's values to match what that function actually returns in the service, since that's where managers will really view it. Before putting a single real person on this, I'd use Test as role to confirm the filter narrows down to one territory correctly - but I'd be upfront that Test as role is checking the logic using my own identity, not proving what an actual colleague will see, so I'd still have at least one real manager sign in and verify their own view before rolling this out to all 40.
questions.example: Mapping table: UserMapping(UserEmail, TerritoryID) with 40 rows, one per manager, related to DimTerritory[TerritoryID]. Role 'Territory Manager' filter: [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Reorg handling: adding/removing a territory is an UPDATE to UserMapping, not a change to the role or the model.
commonMistakes: Building 40 static roles instead of one dynamic role with a mapping table
Assuming USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return the same format in Desktop and the service
Treating a successful Test as role result as proof a specific external manager will see correct data
Forgetting the mapping table needs a real relationship to the territory data for the filter to actually propagate
keyPoints: A single dynamic role with a user-mapping table scales to any number of territories
USERPRINCIPALNAME()/USERNAME() format must match what's stored in the mapping table as seen in the service
Test as role validates filter logic using your own identity, not the target user's
Reorganizations become data updates to the mapping table, not model/role changes
Final validation should include a real manager signing in, not just Test as role

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes a single dynamic role + user-mapping table design
Explains the USERNAME/USERPRINCIPALNAME format gotcha
Describes Test as role validation steps
Correctly states the limitation of Test as role and the real-user validation step
Addresses maintainability as territories change

questions.title: RLS Filter Isn't Reaching the Fact Table in a Complex Model
questions.prompt: A dynamic RLS role filters a user-mapping table that relates to a dimension table sitting on the 'many' side of a relationship relative to the fact table. Test as role shows no rows at all for the test user, even though the mapping table clearly has a matching row. Separately, a measure using USERELATIONSHIP to reach an inactive date relationship started throwing an error after RLS was enabled. Diagnose both issues.
questions.modelAnswer: First issue: by default, an RLS filter only flows in one direction across a relationship, regardless of whether that relationship itself is set to bidirectional filtering in the model. If the user-mapping table sits on the side of the relationship where the filter needs to flow against the default direction to reach the fact table, the RLS filter simply won't propagate - Test as role correctly shows zero rows, because from the engine's perspective there genuinely is no filter reaching the fact table, even though the mapping row exists. The fix is to open that specific relationship in model view and enable 'Apply security filter in both directions,' which lets the RLS filter flow the direction it needs to. Two things to flag before enabling it blindly: it should be turned on specifically because of this dynamic-RLS need, not as a general-purpose fix for unrelated filtering oddities, and if that table participates in more than one bidirectional relationship, only one of them can have this option enabled at all - so if the mapping table already has another bidirectional relationship, that has to be accounted for in the design. It's also worth testing query performance afterward, since bidirectional security filtering can measurably slow queries on larger fact tables, especially once there are many relationships in play. Second issue: this is a known interaction - enabling RLS alongside a measure that calls USERELATIONSHIP to activate an otherwise-inactive relationship can throw unexpected errors. The fix isn't to disable RLS; it's to redesign the DAX so it doesn't depend on USERELATIONSHIP while RLS is active, typically by modeling the role-playing dimension differently, for example with physically separate relationships or tables per date role, so the needed relationship doesn't have to be activated on demand inside a measure that's also subject to a security filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: The zero-rows result tells me the filter genuinely isn't reaching the fact table, not that the mapping data is wrong - by default an RLS filter only flows one direction across a relationship, independent of whatever cross-filter setting is on that relationship generally. If the mapping table sits on the side where the filter has to go against that default direction, it just won't get there, and Test as role is correctly reporting that. The fix is turning on 'Apply security filter in both directions' on that specific relationship - but I'd do that deliberately, only because this dynamic-RLS case needs it, and I'd check first whether that table is already bidirectional on another relationship, since only one can have this enabled. I'd also benchmark performance afterward, since this setting isn't free on a larger fact table. For the USERRELATIONSHIP error, I know that's a documented friction point between RLS and activating an inactive relationship on demand inside a measure - the fix isn't to turn RLS off, it's to stop relying on USERELATIONSHIP there, usually by restructuring the role-playing dimension so the relationship it needs is already active rather than something a measure has to switch on.
questions.example: Relationship fix: Model view, select the UserMapping-to-DimTerritory relationship, check 'Apply security filter in both directions,' then re-run Test as role to confirm non-zero rows for the test user, and benchmark a heavy visual before/after to check the performance cost.
commonMistakes: Assuming a bidirectional relationship setting already covers RLS filter propagation - RLS direction is governed separately from the relationship's own cross-filter direction setting
Enabling bidirectional security filtering broadly instead of only on the specific relationship that needs it for RLS
Not checking whether the mapping table already has another bidirectional relationship, which would block enabling a second one
Trying to fix the USERELATIONSHIP error by disabling RLS instead of redesigning the measure/model
keyPoints: RLS filters flow one direction by default, independent of the relationship's own cross-filter direction setting
Apply security filter in both directions is the specific, deliberate fix - not a default-on setting
A table can only have this enabled on one of its bidirectional relationships
USERELATIONSHIP combined with active RLS can error; the fix is redesigning the DAX/model, not disabling RLS
Always re-test with Test as role after any relationship change, and check performance impact

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the one-directional-by-default RLS filter as the cause of zero rows
Correctly proposes enabling bidirectional security filtering on the right relationship, with its constraints
Flags the performance cost consideration
Correctly diagnoses and resolves the USERELATIONSHIP + RLS interaction without disabling RLS

questions.title: Adding a Returns Process to an Existing Sales Star Schema
questions.prompt: Your warehouse has a mature sales star schema: Fact_Sales at the grain of one row per order line, with conformed Dim_Customer, Dim_Product, and Dim_Date dimensions already in production and feeding live reports. The business now wants to track product returns for the first time. Walk through your grain decision and explain whether returns should be modeled as a new fact table or as a flag/column added to the existing sales fact table.
questions.modelAnswer: Returns is a genuinely different business process from the original sale, not a status on it, so it needs its own fact table at its own grain rather than a column bolted onto Fact_Sales. Run Kimball's four-step method on it: the business process is 'product returns,' not 'sales.' The grain is one row per returned line item. A return can happen weeks or months after the original sale, can be partial (a customer returns 2 of 5 units), can happen more than once against the same original sale line, and carries its own measures (ReturnedQty, RefundAmount) and its own attribute (ReturnReasonKey) that have no home on a sales row. Trying to force this onto Fact_Sales as an 'IsReturned' flag or a ReturnedQty column breaks the grain two ways: it assumes one return event per sale line (false - partial and repeated returns exist), and it assumes the return happens at the same time as the sale (false - the return date is a different date than the order date, and overwriting OrderDateKey or adding a second date to a transaction-grain row mixes two events into one row). The correct design is a new Fact_Returns transaction fact table: one row per return line, with ReturnDateKey and OrderDateKey as role-playing references to the same conformed Dim_Date, ProductKey and CustomerKey referencing the same conformed Dim_Product/Dim_Customer already used by Fact_Sales, a new Dim_ReturnReason dimension, a degenerate dimension column holding the original SalesOrderNumber so a return can always be traced back to its originating sale, and measures ReturnedQty and RefundAmount. Because Fact_Returns reuses the exact same conformed Dim_Product, Dim_Customer, and Dim_Date tables Fact_Sales already uses, you get drill-across for free: 'net revenue by product by month' is computable by joining both fact tables through those shared dimensions, something that would be impossible if returns were buried as an uninspectable flag inside the sales table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as a brand new business process, not a modification of an existing one. Returns happen at a different time than the sale, can be partial, can happen more than once per sale line, and need their own reason code - none of that fits the grain Fact_Sales already has, which is one row per order line at the moment the sale happened. So I'd build a separate Fact_Returns table, transaction grain, one row per returned line. I'd reuse the existing conformed Dim_Product, Dim_Customer, and Dim_Date dimensions rather than building new ones, add a new Dim_ReturnReason, and keep the original sales order number as a degenerate dimension on the return row so I can always trace a return back to the sale it came from. The reason I wouldn't just add a ReturnedQty column to Fact_Sales is that it would silently assume one return per sale line, which isn't true in practice, and it would mix two different events with two different dates into one row. Keeping them as two fact tables that share conformed dimensions actually gives me more power, not less - I can drill across both tables through Product, Customer, or Date to get net sales, which I couldn't do cleanly if returns were jammed into the sales table as a flag.
questions.example:
Fact_Sales(SalesOrderNo, ProductKey, CustomerKey, OrderDateKey, Quantity, LineRevenue)
Fact_Returns(ReturnLineNo, OriginalSalesOrderNo [degenerate], ProductKey, CustomerKey, ReturnDateKey, ReturnReasonKey, ReturnedQty, RefundAmount)
-- Net revenue by product/month via drill-across:
SELECT d.Month, p.ProductName,
       SUM(s.LineRevenue) AS GrossRevenue,
       SUM(r.RefundAmount) AS Refunds,
       SUM(s.LineRevenue) - ISNULL(SUM(r.RefundAmount),0) AS NetRevenue
FROM Dim_Product p
LEFT JOIN Fact_Sales s ON s.ProductKey = p.ProductKey
LEFT JOIN Fact_Returns r ON r.ProductKey = p.ProductKey
JOIN Dim_Date d ON d.DateKey = s.OrderDateKey
GROUP BY d.Month, p.ProductName;
commonMistakes: Adding a ReturnedQty or IsReturned column directly to Fact_Sales instead of modeling a new fact table
Assuming one return per sale line, missing partial or repeated returns
Overwriting or reusing OrderDateKey for the return event instead of a separate ReturnDateKey
Forgetting to carry the original sales order number forward as a degenerate dimension for traceability
Building new, non-conformed copies of Product/Customer/Date dimensions for the returns fact table instead of reusing the existing conformed ones
keyPoints: Returns is a distinct business process with its own grain, not a status on a sales row
Forcing returns onto Fact_Sales violates grain and breaks additivity
New Fact_Returns table at one-row-per-return-line grain, transaction fact type
Reuse conformed Dim_Product/Dim_Customer/Dim_Date to enable drill-across
Keep the original sales order number as a degenerate dimension for traceability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies returns as a separate business process requiring its own grain
Explains concretely why forcing returns onto Fact_Sales breaks grain/additivity
Designs a new fact table reusing conformed dimensions
Addresses traceability back to the original sale

questions.title: Choosing Fact Table Types for a Loan Servicing Pipeline
questions.prompt: You're designing the warehouse for a loan servicing business process: a loan originates, then is serviced over years with monthly payments, and may eventually enter a 'workout' (modification) process before closing. Leadership wants (a) outstanding balance trends month over month across the portfolio, and (b) time-to-close tracking for loans currently going through a workout. Which fact table type(s) would you build, and why won't one table serve both needs?
questions.modelAnswer: These are two different measurement problems with two different grains, so they need two different fact tables, both referencing a conformed Dim_Loan and a conformed, role-played Dim_Date. For the balance trend, build a periodic snapshot fact table, Fact_LoanBalanceSnapshot, with grain 'one row per loan, per month-end,' loaded on a fixed schedule whether or not anything happened to that loan that month. Its OutstandingBalance measure is semi-additive: you can validly sum it across loans within one month-end to get portfolio balance at that point in time, but summing it across months double-counts balance that never moved and produces a meaningless number - the correct cross-month analysis is picking the latest snapshot or averaging, never summing. For the workout time-to-close tracking, build an accumulating snapshot fact table, Fact_LoanWorkout, with grain 'one row per workout process instance,' holding multiple role-playing date keys to the same Dim_Date (RequestedDateKey, ReviewedDateKey, ApprovedDateKey, ClosedDateKey), each nullable until that milestone is reached, with duration measures (DaysRequestToReview, DaysReviewToApprove) computed and updated as the row is revisited at each stage - an UPDATE-based load, not insert-only. A single transaction fact table of 'loan events' would satisfy neither need well: it has no row for a loan that experienced nothing in a given month (so trend reporting has to infer presence, which is fragile and expensive), and it doesn't naturally support milestone-to-milestone duration without expensive self-joins across many event rows. Both new fact tables should reference the same conformed Dim_Loan so a loan's history is queryable consistently across both tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into two fact tables rather than trying to force one table to answer both questions, because the two requests are actually asking for different grains. For the balance trend, I want a periodic snapshot - one row per loan, per month-end, loaded on schedule regardless of activity - because that's the only way to get a clean month-over-month balance series; the balance measure there is semi-additive, so I can sum it across loans within a month but never across months, otherwise I'm double-counting money that just sat there. For the workout tracking, I'd build an accumulating snapshot - one row per workout case that gets inserted when it starts and updated in place as it hits each milestone like requested, reviewed, approved, and closed, using the same physical date dimension referenced several times in different roles. The reason one table can't do both is that a periodic snapshot's whole point is regular, scheduled rows regardless of activity, while an accumulating snapshot's whole point is a single row that mutates as a specific process moves forward - those are opposite load patterns, and mixing them into one table would mean some rows behave one way and some the other, which is exactly the mixed-grain problem that breaks additivity. Both tables share the same conformed loan dimension so I can still connect a loan's balance history to its workout history when I need to.
questions.example:
Fact_LoanBalanceSnapshot(LoanKey, SnapshotDateKey, OutstandingBalance, InterestAccrued)  -- one row per loan per month-end
Fact_LoanWorkout(WorkoutKey, LoanKey, RequestedDateKey, ReviewedDateKey, ApprovedDateKey, ClosedDateKey, DaysRequestToReview, DaysReviewToApprove)  -- one row per workout, updated as milestones occur
commonMistakes: Trying to serve both reporting needs from one transaction-grain fact table
Summing OutstandingBalance across snapshot dates instead of across loans within one date
Making the workout table insert-only instead of designing it to be updated at each milestone
Building three separate date dimensions for the workout milestones instead of one role-played Dim_Date
Not sharing a conformed Dim_Loan across both fact tables
keyPoints: Periodic snapshot for balance trend; accumulating snapshot for workout milestones
Semi-additivity: sum balance across loans, never across time
Accumulating snapshot requires an update-in-place load, not insert-only
Role-playing Dim_Date shared across workout milestone keys
Conformed Dim_Loan links both fact tables together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects periodic snapshot for balance trend and explains semi-additivity
Correctly selects accumulating snapshot for workout tracking and explains the update-based load
Explains concretely why one fact table can't serve both needs
Notes shared conformed dimensions (Loan, role-played Date)

questions.title: Writing a Type 2 SCD Load With a Hybrid Attribute Mix
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL you'd run to load Dim_Customer from a staging table when the customer's MailingRegion attribute changes, while EmailAddress on the same table should be handled as Type 1 (overwritten in place, no new version). Assume CustomerAlternateKey is the natural key, CustomerKey is the IDENTITY surrogate key, and the table has RowStartDate, RowEndDate, and IsCurrent columns.
questions.modelAnswer: A single naive MERGE can't correctly express 'overwrite this column, but version that one' in one UPDATE action, because MERGE's UPDATE branch can only do one kind of change per matched row. The reliable pattern is two explicit steps, run inside one transaction so they commit or fail together: first, apply the Type 1 change (EmailAddress) directly to the current row regardless of whether MailingRegion also changed, since a Type 1 correction never needs a new version. Second, detect rows where the Type 2 attribute (MailingRegion) actually changed, and for exactly those rows, close the current version (set RowEndDate and IsCurrent = 0) and insert a brand-new row carrying the new MailingRegion plus every other current attribute value (including whatever EmailAddress was just set to in step one) forward, with a new surrogate key, a fresh RowStartDate, RowEndDate = '9999-12-31', and IsCurrent = 1. The order matters: apply the Type 1 update first so the new Type 2 version row carries the already-corrected EmailAddress forward, not a stale value.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to do this in one clever MERGE statement, because Type 1 and Type 2 changes need genuinely different actions on the same row, and MERGE's single UPDATE branch can't express both at once. Instead I run it as two steps in one transaction. Step one: update EmailAddress in place on the current row for every customer where it changed - that's pure Type 1, no new row, no date logic. Step two: compare staged rows against the current dimension rows on MailingRegion specifically, and for just the ones that changed, close out the old row by setting RowEndDate and flipping IsCurrent to zero, then insert a new row with a new surrogate key and the new region, carrying forward all the other attributes as they stand right now - which includes picking up the EmailAddress I already corrected in step one, not whatever it was before that update ran. Doing the Type 1 update first and the Type 2 close-and-insert second is what keeps the new version row accurate instead of reintroducing a stale email address.
questions.example:
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

-- Step 1: Type 1 - overwrite EmailAddress on the current row, no versioning
UPDATE d
SET    d.EmailAddress = s.EmailAddress
FROM   dbo.Dim_Customer d
JOIN   stg.Customer s ON s.CustomerAlternateKey = d.CustomerAlternateKey
WHERE  d.IsCurrent = 1
  AND  d.EmailAddress <> s.EmailAddress;

-- Step 2: Type 2 - close the old version where MailingRegion changed
UPDATE d
SET    d.RowEndDate = CAST(SYSUTCDATETIME() AS DATE),
       d.IsCurrent   = 0
FROM   dbo.Dim_Customer d
JOIN   stg.Customer s ON s.CustomerAlternateKey = d.CustomerAlternateKey
WHERE  d.IsCurrent = 1
  AND  d.MailingRegion <> s.MailingRegion;

-- Step 2b: insert the new current version, carrying forward the already-corrected EmailAddress
INSERT INTO dbo.Dim_Customer
  (CustomerAlternateKey, EmailAddress, MailingRegion, RowStartDate, RowEndDate, IsCurrent)
SELECT s.CustomerAlternateKey, s.EmailAddress, s.MailingRegion,
       CAST(SYSUTCDATETIME() AS DATE), '9999-12-31', 1
FROM   stg.Customer s
JOIN   dbo.Dim_Customer d
  ON   d.CustomerAlternateKey = s.CustomerAlternateKey AND d.IsCurrent = 0
  AND  d.RowEndDate = CAST(SYSUTCDATETIME() AS DATE);

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
commonMistakes: Using a single MERGE that overwrites the Type 2 attribute in place, destroying history
Forgetting to carry the already-updated Type 1 attribute value forward into the new Type 2 version row
Not wrapping the close-and-insert in one transaction, risking a half-closed dimension if the insert fails
Comparing the entire row for 'has it changed' instead of comparing Type 1 and Type 2 columns separately
Generating a new version row for a pure Type 1 change
keyPoints: Type 1 and Type 2 changes need separate update logic, not one combined statement
Apply Type 1 updates before detecting/creating Type 2 versions so new rows carry correct values forward
Close old row (EndDate, IsCurrent) and insert new row with new surrogate key for Type 2
Wrap close+insert in a transaction
Natural key stays the same across versions; only the surrogate key changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates Type 1 overwrite logic from Type 2 versioning logic
SQL correctly closes old row and inserts new version with new surrogate key
Explains ordering (Type 1 before Type 2) and why it matters
Addresses transactional integrity of the two-step load

questions.title: Classifying SCD Types Across a Single Customer Dimension
questions.prompt: You inherit a Dim_Customer table with these attributes: DateFirstPurchase, EmailAddress, CustomerSegment, MailingRegion, PreferredContactMethod, and LoyaltyTierAtEnrollment. For each attribute, state which SCD type you'd assign and justify it in terms of what a historical report would actually need.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision rule for every attribute is the same question asked individually: does any report need this value exactly as it was at the time a related fact occurred? DateFirstPurchase is Type 0 - it's fixed the moment it's first recorded and is never a real 'change,' so it should be write-once and excluded from every future UPDATE statement's column list, forever. EmailAddress is Type 1 - a correction or update with no analytical need for the old value; nobody runs 'revenue by email address as of the order date.' CustomerSegment is Type 2 - 'revenue by segment' rollups need the segment as it actually was at the time of each historical order, not today's segment, or a customer who moved from Budget to Premium last month would retroactively show all of last year's orders as Premium. MailingRegion is Type 2 for the same reason - regional sales rollups must reflect where the customer actually was assigned when each historical order happened, otherwise a salesperson's past territory reassignment silently rewrites historical regional totals. PreferredContactMethod is Type 1 - it's purely operational (how to reach the customer today), and no report's historical accuracy depends on knowing what the preferred method used to be. LoyaltyTierAtEnrollment is Type 0 - by definition it's the tier at the moment of enrollment, a fixed historical fact about that customer's signup, distinct from the customer's current loyalty tier (which would itself be a separate, Type 2 or Type 1 attribute if tracked). This mix is exactly the hybrid pattern: a single dimension applying different SCD types to different columns based on each attribute's own history requirement, which means the ETL load logic has to branch per column rather than applying one rule to the whole table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go attribute by attribute and ask the same question each time: would any report need this value exactly as it was back when a related sale happened? DateFirstPurchase and LoyaltyTierAtEnrollment are both Type 0 in my mind - they're facts fixed at a specific moment by definition, a signup date and an enrollment-time tier, and they should never be touched again once they're loaded. EmailAddress and PreferredContactMethod I'd call Type 1 - those are just current contact details, corrections or updates with zero analytical weight on history, so overwrite them in place. CustomerSegment and MailingRegion are the two I'd insist on Type 2 for, because both feed real historical rollups - if a customer's segment or region gets overwritten instead of versioned, every past order they're tied to silently gets relabeled as if they'd always been in that segment or region, which quietly corrupts last year's reporting without throwing any error. So the dimension ends up as a genuine hybrid, and that means my ETL load has to compare each column against its own rule rather than treating the whole row as one block - some columns update in place, some trigger a brand-new versioned row, and one group never gets touched after the initial insert.
questions.example:
| Attribute | SCD Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| DateFirstPurchase | 0 | Fixed at first load, never a real change |
| EmailAddress | 1 | Correction, no historical need |
| CustomerSegment | 2 | Segment-based rollups need historical accuracy |
| MailingRegion | 2 | Regional rollups need historical accuracy |
| PreferredContactMethod | 1 | Purely operational |
| LoyaltyTierAtEnrollment | 0 | Fixed fact about enrollment moment |
commonMistakes: Classifying the entire dimension as one SCD type instead of per attribute
Confusing Type 0 (never changes, by design) with Type 1 (changes, but history isn't kept)
Making CustomerSegment or MailingRegion Type 1, silently corrupting historical rollups
Making low-value operational attributes like PreferredContactMethod Type 2, bloating the dimension with meaningless versions
Not recognizing the ETL implication: hybrid dimensions need column-by-column comparison logic
keyPoints: Per-attribute decision rule: does a report need this value as of the fact's time?
Type 0 for permanently fixed facts, Type 1 for corrections, Type 2 for attributes driving historical rollups
Hybrid SCD dimensions are the norm, not an exception, in mature warehouses
ETL load logic must branch per column, not apply one rule to the whole row

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly classifies all six attributes
Justifies each classification in terms of actual reporting need, not just terminology
Articulates the general per-attribute decision rule
Notes the ETL/load-logic implication of a hybrid dimension

questions.title: Snowflaking a Product Dimension at Warehouse Scale
questions.prompt: A retail warehouse's Dim_Product has grown to 40 million rows across a deep category/subcategory/brand hierarchy, and the fully denormalized flat table is becoming expensive to maintain and slow to reload nightly, since every row repeats category and brand text. A teammate suggests snowflaking the dimension. Do you agree, and specifically what would you snowflake versus keep denormalized?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd agree, but partially, because this is exactly the exception case the default guidance calls out, not a reason to abandon the default. Microsoft's own guidance says dimensions should almost always be denormalized, and reaches for snowflaking specifically when a dimension is extremely large and the storage/maintenance savings outweigh the query-performance cost - which is exactly this situation at 40 million rows with a repeated category/brand hierarchy. I'd normalize the hierarchy, not the whole table: pull Category, Subcategory, and Brand into their own Dim_Category, Dim_Subcategory, and Dim_Brand tables, each referenced by a foreign key from Dim_Product. That removes the repeated text from every one of the 40 million rows, which meaningfully shrinks storage and - just as importantly for the nightly reload problem - means a hierarchy-level correction (renaming a brand) touches one row in Dim_Brand instead of potentially millions of rows in Dim_Product. I would not snowflake product-specific attributes like Color, Size, ListPrice, or SKU - those have no redundancy problem and splitting them out would just add join overhead for no storage benefit. To avoid paying a query-performance cost on every single report, I'd expose the normalized pieces back to reporting as a single denormalized view that joins Dim_Product to Dim_Category/Dim_Subcategory/Dim_Brand and flattens them - so Fact_Sales still joins to one object, one hop, exactly as it does today, and report authors never see the normalization underneath. I'd also flag this as something to periodically reassess: if the catalog's growth rate or hierarchy volatility changes, the right line between normalized and denormalized can move.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct is usually to defend the default - denormalized star dimensions - but 40 million rows with a repeated category and brand hierarchy is genuinely the textbook exception, so I'd agree with snowflaking, just not the whole table. I'd specifically pull out Category, Subcategory, and Brand into their own small lookup tables referenced by Dim_Product, because that's where all the redundant text actually lives, and that's also what's making the nightly reload painful - a brand name change today means touching every row that brand appears on. I'd leave the actual product-level attributes, things like color, size, and list price, flat on Dim_Product, since there's no redundancy to save there and normalizing them would just add joins for nothing. The part I wouldn't skip is giving reporting back a denormalized view over the normalized pieces, so Fact_Sales and Power BI still see one simple product table one join away, and nobody querying the warehouse has to know or care that the hierarchy is split underneath for ETL and storage reasons. And I'd treat this as a decision worth revisiting later, not permanent - if the catalog's size or change pattern shifts, the tradeoff might flip back.
questions.example:
Dim_Product(ProductKey, ProductAlternateKey, ProductName, Color, Size, ListPrice, BrandKey, SubcategoryKey)
Dim_Subcategory(SubcategoryKey, SubcategoryName, CategoryKey)
Dim_Category(CategoryKey, CategoryName)
Dim_Brand(BrandKey, BrandName)

CREATE VIEW rpt.DimProductFlat AS
SELECT p.ProductKey, p.ProductName, p.Color, p.ListPrice,
       b.BrandName, sc.SubcategoryName, c.CategoryName
FROM Dim_Product p
JOIN Dim_Brand b ON b.BrandKey = p.BrandKey
JOIN Dim_Subcategory sc ON sc.SubcategoryKey = p.SubcategoryKey
JOIN Dim_Category c ON c.CategoryKey = sc.CategoryKey;
commonMistakes: Snowflaking the entire dimension, including attributes with no redundancy problem
Not providing a denormalized reporting view, forcing extra joins on every report
Treating snowflaking as a style choice rather than a scale-driven exception
Forgetting Fact_Sales should still join to Dim_Product directly, not to the normalized hierarchy tables
Not planning to reassess the decision as data volumes or change patterns shift
keyPoints: This scenario is the legitimate documented exception to default denormalization
Normalize only the redundant, large hierarchy (Category/Subcategory/Brand), not product-level attributes
Expose a denormalized view back to reporting to preserve one-join simplicity
Benefit is storage savings and cheaper hierarchy-level maintenance, not query speed
Revisit the decision periodically as volumes change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this as the legitimate snowflaking exception, not a default-breaking choice
Correctly identifies which parts to normalize vs. keep flat
Proposes a denormalized reporting view to preserve query simplicity
Connects the decision to the stated maintenance/reload problem, not just storage

questions.title: Modeling a Many-to-Many Sales Credit Relationship
questions.prompt: Sales leadership wants to credit a deal to every salesperson who worked on it - some deals have one rep, others are split three ways. Design how you'd model this against an existing Fact_Sales table and Dim_Salesperson dimension, and explain how you'd compute 'total revenue credited per salesperson' without double-counting total company revenue.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a genuine many-to-many relationship - one sale can have multiple salespeople, and one salesperson is credited on many sales - so no amount of fact-table redesign turns it into a clean one-to-many. The fix is a bridge table, Bridge_SaleSalesperson, with one row per sale-salesperson pairing: SalesOrderNo (matching the fact table's degenerate dimension), SalespersonKey, and critically an AllocationPercent column so credit can be split, since the splits must sum to 100% per sale. Without the allocation weight, a naive join from Fact_Sales to the bridge and a SUM of LineRevenue for each matching row causes a fan-out: a sale split three ways produces three bridge rows, and summing SalesAmount across them triples that sale's revenue. The correct per-salesperson revenue query multiplies SalesAmount by AllocationPercent for each bridge row before summing, so a $900 sale split 50/30/20 across three reps credits $450/$270/$180 - which sums back to $900, not $2,700. Just as important: any query computing total company revenue must go straight to Fact_Sales and never join through the bridge table at all, because the bridge table's entire purpose is reallocating existing revenue across people, not generating additional revenue - joining through it for a company-wide total would multiply revenue by however many salespeople happened to be on each deal.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since one sale can have several salespeople and one salesperson touches many sales, I can't model this as a normal one-to-many foreign key - I need a bridge table sitting between Fact_Sales and Dim_Salesperson, with one row per sale-salesperson combination. The detail that actually matters here is adding an allocation percentage to that bridge table, because if I just join Fact_Sales to the bridge and sum revenue, a three-way-split deal shows up three times and I've tripled that sale's revenue by accident - that's a classic fan-out problem. So for 'revenue credited per salesperson,' I multiply each bridge row's share of the sale by its allocation percentage before summing, which makes the per-rep numbers add back up to the real total. And for anything asking about total company revenue, I'd make sure that query never touches the bridge table at all - it goes straight to Fact_Sales - because the bridge exists purely to redistribute credit for a sale that already happened, not to create new revenue every time it's joined.
questions.example:
Bridge_SaleSalesperson(SalesOrderNo, SalespersonKey, AllocationPercent)
-- 3-way split of a $900 sale: (50,30,20)

-- Correct per-salesperson credited revenue (no double counting)
SELECT b.SalespersonKey,
       SUM(f.SalesAmount * b.AllocationPercent / 100.0) AS CreditedRevenue
FROM Fact_Sales f
JOIN Bridge_SaleSalesperson b ON b.SalesOrderNo = f.SalesOrderNo
GROUP BY b.SalespersonKey;

-- Total company revenue: bypass the bridge entirely
SELECT SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalRevenue FROM Fact_Sales;
commonMistakes: Summing SalesAmount through the bridge join without applying an allocation weight, causing fan-out double counting
Treating the bridge table as a true measures-bearing fact table instead of a weighted factless association
Routing total company revenue reporting through the bridge join
Not enforcing that AllocationPercent values sum to 100% per sale
Forgetting the bridge is itself a factless fact table when weights aren't needed for count-based metrics
keyPoints: Genuine many-to-many relationships need a bridge table, not a clever fact-table redesign
Fan-out risk: summing additive measures through an unweighted bridge join multiplies revenue
Allocation percentage weighting makes per-salesperson credit sum back to the real total
Total company revenue must bypass the bridge table entirely
A bridge table without measures is itself a factless fact table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a bridge table resolving the many-to-many relationship
Identifies and explains the fan-out/double-counting risk precisely
Proposes a correct allocation-weighted query for per-salesperson credit
Explains why total company revenue must bypass the bridge

questions.title: Diagnosing a Row-Count Mismatch After a Nightly Warehouse Load
questions.prompt: Every morning your SSIS-based nightly load populates Fact_Sales from staging. This morning, the fact table has 40,000 fewer rows than yesterday's source extract, but the package reported success with no errors. Walk through how you would investigate, in order, and what you'd look for at each step.
questions.modelAnswer: A package reporting success tells you it didn't crash, not that it moved every row correctly, so the first move is to confirm and isolate the discrepancy rather than guess at a cause. First, re-run row-count parity across every stage - source table, staging table, and fact table - to find exactly which hop lost rows; if source and staging match but the fact table is short, the problem is in the transform/load step, not the extract. Second, with the loss isolated to the warehouse load, check every Lookup transformation's 'no match' handling: a Lookup configured to fail the component on no match can sometimes be misconfigured to redirect silently without those rows being captured anywhere, which would explain rows vanishing with no visible error. Third, check whether a dimension table failed to load before the fact load ran, or loaded late - if new dimension members (new products, new customers) hadn't landed yet when the fact Lookup ran, every fact row needing one of those new keys would either fail the Lookup or need inferred-member handling that may not exist, both of which drop or misroute rows. Fourth, pull the SSISDB catalog's All Executions report and check per-component row counts for the specific run - this shows exactly how many rows entered and left each transformation, including any redirected error-output rows nobody is monitoring. Fifth, if the warehouse uses a watermark-based incremental load, check the watermark boundary logic specifically - an upper bound captured before some late-committing source rows finished writing can silently exclude them from today's extract without any error, and they may never get picked up by a future run if the watermark then advances past them. Sixth, check for an overly aggressive deduplication step in the transform that might be collapsing legitimately distinct rows. Once the actual cause is found, the fix isn't just correcting today's load - it's adding a permanent row-count validation check (comparable to Lesson 10's four-check pattern) that fails the batch loudly the next time this happens, instead of silently succeeding.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd remind myself is that 'the package succeeded' only means it didn't error out, not that every row made it where it should - so I start by actually proving where the rows disappeared, not by guessing. I'd run the same row-count check across source, staging, and the fact table to pin down which specific step lost 40,000 rows. If it turns out staging matches the source but the fact table is short, I'm looking at the transform step next - specifically every Lookup transformation's no-match configuration, since a Lookup that's quietly redirecting unmatched rows without anyone capturing that output is a classic way for rows to vanish with zero visible errors. I'd also check load ordering - if dimensions didn't finish loading before the fact load ran, new products or customers wouldn't have surrogate keys yet, and those fact rows would fail or get dropped. From there I'd go straight to the SSISDB catalog's execution report to see per-component counts for last night's specific run, including anything sent to an error output. If this load uses a watermark, I'd check the boundary logic closely, because a watermark captured a moment too early can silently exclude rows that were still committing, and they might never get picked up later if the watermark's already moved past them. Whatever I find, I wouldn't consider it closed until I've also added a permanent check - a row-count threshold that fails loudly - so next time this doesn't happen again without anyone noticing.
commonMistakes: Treating 'package reported success' as proof nothing is wrong
Jumping to a fix before isolating which pipeline stage actually lost the rows
Not checking Lookup transformation no-match/error-output configuration
Overlooking dimension-load ordering as a cause of dropped fact rows
Not checking watermark boundary edge cases on an incremental load
Fixing the immediate problem without adding a permanent validation safeguard
keyPoints: Success status does not guarantee correctness - isolate the discrepancy first
Check row-count parity at every pipeline stage to localize the problem
Inspect Lookup no-match/error-output handling for silently dropped rows
Check dimension-load ordering and watermark boundary logic
Use SSISDB's execution reports for per-component row counts
Add a permanent, loudly-failing validation check after root-causing the issue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly starts by isolating which pipeline stage lost rows rather than guessing
Names specific, plausible root causes (Lookup no-match, load ordering, watermark boundary)
References concrete diagnostic tools/reports (SSISDB executions, row-count queries)
Proposes a permanent safeguard, not just a one-time fix

questions.title: Writing a Watermark-Based Incremental Load
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL a watermark-based incremental load needs for Sales.SalesOrderHeader, which has a ModifiedDate column: reading the stored watermark, finding the current max ModifiedDate in the source, selecting only the new/changed rows, and persisting the new watermark - and explain exactly when in the process the last step is allowed to run.
questions.modelAnswer: The cycle has four steps, in a fixed order, and getting the boundaries and the timing of the last step right is what makes it safe to re-run. Step one reads the previously stored watermark value for this specific table from a control table. Step two reads the current maximum ModifiedDate in the source right now. Step three extracts rows whose ModifiedDate falls strictly after the old watermark and up to and including the new watermark captured in step two - bounding both ends matters, because an unbounded upper edge (just WHERE ModifiedDate > @OldWatermark) can pick up a row that gets modified again in the middle of this very extract, landing it in an inconsistent partial state, or double-processing rows across adjacent runs if the extract takes a long time. Step four persists the new watermark value back to the control table - but only after the rows pulled in step three have been fully loaded and verified successful. If the watermark is updated before confirming the load succeeded, a failure partway through silently and permanently loses whatever didn't make it in, because the next run's lower bound has already moved past those rows and will never request them again. The watermark update belongs as the last statement of a successful transaction, ideally gated behind the same validation checks (row counts, no orphaned keys) used elsewhere in the pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd implement this as four repeatable steps against a control table that stores one watermark value per source table. First I pull the last stored watermark for SalesOrderHeader. Second I ask the source for its current maximum ModifiedDate right now - that becomes this run's new watermark candidate. Third, I extract rows strictly between those two values, bounded on both ends, not just 'greater than the old watermark' - bounding the top edge matters because without it, a row that gets touched again while my extract is still running could end up being picked up inconsistently, or picked up twice across two runs. Fourth, I update the control table with the new watermark value, but that update is the very last thing that happens, and only runs if I've confirmed the extract and load actually succeeded. The reason that ordering is non-negotiable is that moving the watermark forward is effectively telling the next run 'everything before this point is already handled' - if that's not true because this run failed partway through, those rows are gone for good, since the next run will never ask for anything before the watermark again.
questions.example:
DECLARE @OldWatermark DATETIME2, @NewWatermark DATETIME2;

-- Step 1: read the stored watermark
SELECT @OldWatermark = LastWatermarkValue
FROM   control.WatermarkTable
WHERE  TableName = 'SalesOrderHeader';

-- Step 2: read the current max ModifiedDate in source
SELECT @NewWatermark = MAX(ModifiedDate)
FROM   Sales.SalesOrderHeader;

-- Step 3: extract only rows in the bounded window
SELECT *
FROM   Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE  ModifiedDate > @OldWatermark
  AND  ModifiedDate <= @NewWatermark;

-- ... load succeeds and is validated here ...

-- Step 4: persist the new watermark ONLY after confirmed success
UPDATE control.WatermarkTable
SET    LastWatermarkValue = @NewWatermark
WHERE  TableName = 'SalesOrderHeader';
commonMistakes: Leaving the extract's upper bound open (only WHERE ModifiedDate > @OldWatermark), risking inconsistent or duplicate pickup
Updating the watermark before the load is confirmed successful
Using wall-clock time instead of the source's own max ModifiedDate, risking clock-skew gaps
Not persisting a separate watermark per source table
Forgetting that a watermark only detects new/changed rows, never physical deletes
keyPoints: Four-step cycle: read old watermark, read new max value, extract the bounded window, persist new watermark
Bound both the lower and upper edge of the extraction window
Only persist the new watermark after the load is confirmed successful
Store watermark values per source table in a control table
A watermark alone never detects hard deletes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides correct SQL for all four steps
Correctly bounds both edges of the extraction window and explains why
Explains why the watermark update must happen only after confirmed success
Notes the limitation around detecting deletes
