questions.title: Redesigning the Physical Storage of a Billion-Row Fact Table
questions.prompt: Fact_Sales has grown past 2 billion rows. It currently has a traditional clustered rowstore primary key index on SalesOrderKey, aggregate reporting queries are taking minutes, and the nightly load window is starting to miss its SLA because purging 7-year-old data with row-by-row DELETEs takes hours. Propose a physical redesign and explain how each change addresses one of the three symptoms.
questions.modelAnswer: All three symptoms trace back to the table being physically designed like an OLTP table instead of a warehouse fact table, and the fix is a clustered columnstore index combined with date-based partitioning. For query slowness: replace the rowstore clustered index on SalesOrderKey with a clustered columnstore index. Aggregate reporting queries (SUM/GROUP BY across millions of rows touching a handful of columns) are exactly the workload columnstore is built for - it stores and compresses data column-by-column, so the engine reads only the compressed segments of the columns actually touched, and processes rows in batch mode instead of one at a time, which is dramatically less I/O than a rowstore scan. Row-level uniqueness, if still needed, can live as a nonclustered rowstore index or be enforced in ETL instead. For the load-window SLA: partition the table on the integer DateKey (CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION/SCHEME on DateKey, e.g. monthly or yearly boundaries). Partitioning doesn't just help maintenance - combined with columnstore, new data can be loaded into a staging table with the same columnstore structure and switched into the live partitioned table as a near-instant metadata operation rather than a row-by-row insert into one monolithic structure competing with the rest of the table. For the purge SLA: with the same date-based partition scheme in place, retention purging becomes ALTER TABLE ... SWITCH PARTITION to move the oldest partition out to an archive table (or straight to DROP), which is a metadata-only operation regardless of how many rows that partition holds - a world away from a billion-row-scanning, heavily-logged DELETE. I'd also flag that adding more rowstore nonclustered indexes to 'help' performance is the wrong instinct here; it fights the columnstore conversion and doesn't address the real workload mismatch. As a further optimization once the base redesign is in place, I'd consider a complementary aggregate table (via CTAS) for the warehouse's most commonly queried rollups, to reduce scanned volume even further on the heaviest reports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat all three symptoms as one root cause: this table is physically built like an OLTP table, and at 2 billion rows that design works against every workload it actually has. For the slow aggregate queries, I'd convert the clustered index to a clustered columnstore index - that's the standard, recommended storage format for a fact table doing SUM-and-GROUP-BY work across millions of rows, because it only reads the compressed columns a query actually touches and processes data in batches instead of row by row. For the load window, I'd partition the table by the integer date key, typically by month or year, which lets a nightly load build a new partition and switch it into the table as a near-instant metadata operation instead of inserting straight into one giant structure. And that exact same partitioning is what fixes the purge problem - instead of a multi-hour, heavily-logged DELETE against a billion rows, dropping seven-year-old data becomes switching the oldest partition out and dropping it, which again is basically instant regardless of row count. The one thing I'd specifically avoid is reaching for more rowstore indexes to try to speed up queries - that's an OLTP-tuning instinct that actually works against converting the table to columnstore, which is the real fix here. Once the base redesign is stable, I'd also look at whether an aggregate table built from a CTAS query could take some of the heaviest, most repeated reports off the detailed fact table entirely.
commonMistakes: Adding more rowstore nonclustered indexes to try to speed up the fact table
Proposing columnstore alone without partitioning, missing the load/purge SLA fixes
Using DELETE instead of SWITCH PARTITION even after partitioning is in place
Choosing a partitioning column other than the date key, losing the natural load/purge boundary
Not recognizing that creating a clustered columnstore index replaces the table's entire storage format, not adds to it
keyPoints: Clustered columnstore index matches the aggregate-scan workload and fixes query slowness
Date-based partitioning enables fast loads and purges via SWITCH PARTITION
SWITCH PARTITION is a near-instant metadata operation, unlike row-by-row DELETE
Don't apply OLTP rowstore-indexing instincts to a fact table
Aggregate tables are a complementary, not alternative, optimization

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes clustered columnstore index and ties it to the query-slowness symptom
Correctly proposes date-based partitioning and ties it to load/purge SLA symptoms
Explains SWITCH PARTITION as the mechanism replacing slow DELETE
Avoids OLTP-style rowstore-indexing anti-patterns for a fact table

questions.title: Designing a Full SSIS-to-Warehouse-to-Reporting Pipeline for a New Business Process
questions.prompt: A manufacturing client wants a BI pipeline for tracking work orders: each work order has a planned quantity, moves through production with a start date, a due date, and an end date, and can have units scrapped along the way with a reason code. Design the end-to-end architecture - from raw source table to the dimensional model to how SSRS and Power BI would both consume it - and justify your fact table type and date-dimension design.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline starts by landing the raw source table into a loosely-typed staging table unchanged, via an SSIS Data Flow Task doing pure extraction with no transformation - that keeps a bad row's failure contained to a table I can inspect and fix, rather than failing against the live source or a warehouse table reports are already querying. A second Data Flow Task reads from staging and resolves surrogate keys via Lookup transformations against the product and scrap-reason dimensions; the scrap-reason Lookup specifically needs to be configured to redirect unmatched rows to a no-match output rather than fail, because most work orders scrap nothing at all, and a missing scrap reason there is a legitimate NULL, not an error condition. I'd classify the fact table as an accumulating snapshot, not a transaction fact, because a work order isn't a single event - it has a defined lifecycle (started, in progress, completed) and its measures (quantity stocked, quantity scrapped) get revisited and updated as production actually happens, which means the load pattern is insert-at-start-then-update-at-each-milestone, not insert-once. For the dates, I'd use three role-playing foreign keys - StartDateKey, EndDateKey (nullable until the work order finishes), and DueDateKey - all pointing at one single physical Dim_Date table, rather than building three separate date dimensions; building three copies would triple the ETL and maintenance burden of a dimension that never actually changes shape. The work order's own identifying number becomes a degenerate dimension column directly on the fact table, since it has no other attributes worth a separate table. I'd deliberately leave out any attribute that lives at a finer grain than one-row-per-work-order (for example, which physical location within the plant handled each step) rather than forcing a false one-to-one relationship that would silently misreport a multi-location process. Downstream, both the SSRS paginated report (through a shared data source, grouped by product, with any ratio like scrap rate wrapped in SUM() at the group level) and the Power BI dashboard (Import mode, with scrap rate as a DIVIDE()-based measure to avoid divide-by-zero errors) read these exact same warehouse tables directly - neither tool restates or recomputes the underlying business logic independently, which is what guarantees the two never quietly disagree on a number. I'd close the design with the standard validation checklist: row-count parity from source through staging to the fact table, and an orphaned-key check against every foreign key, run every time the pipeline changes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start the pipeline at a staging table, loading the raw work order source as-is with no transformation, because that gives me a safe place for a bad row to fail without touching the live source or any table a report is already reading. From there, a second step resolves surrogate keys through Lookup transformations against the product and scrap-reason dimensions, and I'd specifically make sure the scrap-reason Lookup redirects unmatched rows instead of failing, since most work orders don't scrap anything and a blank scrap reason there is expected, not an error. For the fact table itself, I'd model it as an accumulating snapshot rather than a transaction fact, because a work order has a real lifecycle - it starts, it's due by some date, and it eventually finishes - and the quantities on that same row get updated as production moves forward, which is a fundamentally different load pattern than a one-and-done transaction. I'd give it three date keys - start, end, and due - but all pointing at one single date dimension table, played in three different roles, rather than building three near-identical date tables I'd have to maintain forever. The work order number itself just rides on the fact table as a degenerate dimension since it doesn't need its own table. And I'd be upfront about leaving out anything that actually lives at a finer grain, like a specific production location, rather than forcing it onto this grain and quietly misreporting work orders that touched more than one location. On the reporting side, I'd make sure SSRS and Power BI are both reading the exact same warehouse tables and computing things like scrap rate with the same underlying logic, so there's never a scenario where the two tools show different numbers for the same question. And I wouldn't call any of this done without running the standard checks - row counts matching at every stage, and no orphaned foreign keys - every single time something in the pipeline changes.
questions.example:
stg.WorkOrder -> (SSIS Lookup: Product, ScrapReason - redirect no-match) -> dw.FactWorkOrder

CREATE TABLE dw.FactWorkOrder (
    WorkOrderKey   INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    ProductKey     INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dw.DimProduct(ProductKey),
    ScrapReasonKey INT NULL     REFERENCES dw.DimScrapReason(ScrapReasonKey),
    StartDateKey   INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dw.DimDate(DateKey),
    EndDateKey     INT NULL     REFERENCES dw.DimDate(DateKey),
    DueDateKey     INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dw.DimDate(DateKey),
    WorkOrderID    INT NOT NULL,          -- degenerate dimension
    OrderQty       INT NOT NULL,
    StockedQty     INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    ScrappedQty    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
-- SSRS: =Sum(Fields!ScrappedQty.Value)/Sum(Fields!OrderQty.Value)
-- Power BI: ScrapRate = DIVIDE(SUM(FactWorkOrder[ScrappedQty]), SUM(FactWorkOrder[OrderQty]))
commonMistakes: Modeling the fact table as a plain transaction fact, losing the ability to update progress in place
Building three separate date dimensions for start/end/due instead of one role-played Dim_Date
Forcing a finer-grained attribute (like location) onto the chosen work-order grain
Letting SSRS and Power BI independently define the same business ratio with different logic
Configuring the scrap-reason Lookup to fail on no-match instead of redirecting legitimate nulls
Skipping the staging layer and transforming directly from source into the warehouse
keyPoints: Staging-first ETL discipline isolates bad rows from source and warehouse
Accumulating snapshot classification fits a process with milestones and in-place updates
Role-playing Dim_Date avoids tripling maintenance for multiple date roles
Degenerate dimension for the work order's own identifier
Deliberate grain-mismatch scoping decision for finer-grained attributes
Single source of truth: SSRS and Power BI read the same tables and logic
Standard validation checklist (row-count parity, orphaned keys) after every pipeline change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent staging-to-warehouse-to-reporting pipeline with correct component roles
Correctly classifies and justifies the accumulating snapshot fact type
Correctly designs role-playing date dimension and degenerate dimension
Addresses the grain-mismatch scoping decision explicitly
Explains how single source of truth is preserved across SSRS and Power BI

questions.title: Presenting a Technical BI Project to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: You just finished building an end-to-end BI pipeline - SQL Server staging, an SSIS ETL package, a dimensional warehouse, an SSRS report, and a Power BI dashboard - for a plant manager who has no data background. Walk me through how you would present this finished project to them.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd lead with the business outcome, not the architecture - what question can they now answer that they couldn't before, like 'which products have the highest scrap rate, and is it getting better or worse.' I'd open the Power BI dashboard first, not a schema diagram or a slide about SSIS, because the dashboard is the thing they'll actually use. I'd describe everything in their vocabulary - scrap rate, on-time versus late - never warehouse jargon like 'accumulating snapshot,' 'surrogate key,' or 'grain,' since those terms add nothing for this audience and just signal that I'm not translating for them. I'd explain data freshness in plain terms - 'this refreshes every night after production data comes in, and if a number looks stale, here's exactly where to check' - without walking through SSIS's internal mechanics unless they ask. If they push on a scope decision, like why a production location breakdown isn't in the dashboard, I'd frame it in business terms: 'we left that out deliberately, because a single work order can touch more than one location, and showing just one would have given you a wrong number instead of no number' - not 'there's a grain mismatch between the fact table and WorkOrderRouting.' Throughout, I'd be honest about what's out of scope rather than overselling the pipeline as covering everything, and I'd invite questions rather than treating the presentation as a one-way readout.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always start these with the business question the project actually answers, not the pipeline that answers it - so I'd open by saying something like, 'now you can see exactly which products are scrapping the most material, and whether that's trending up or down,' and then pull up the dashboard itself as the first thing they see, not a diagram. I keep my language in their world the whole time - scrap rate, on time versus late - and I deliberately leave out terms like surrogate key or accumulating snapshot, because those don't help a plant manager and just create distance. When it comes to how fresh the data is, I keep it simple: it updates overnight after production data comes in, and here's where to check if something looks off, without getting into SSIS internals unless they specifically want that. If they ask about something I left out on purpose, like location-level detail, I explain the business reason, not the technical one - that showing a single location for something that actually touched several would have given them a wrong number, which is worse than not showing it at all, and that I'm happy to scope that properly as a next step. The whole presentation is built around trust - being clear about what the numbers mean, what they don't cover yet, and making sure they leave knowing exactly what decisions this new dashboard can actually support.
questions.example: Opening line: 'This dashboard answers the question you asked me about three weeks ago - which products are scrapping the most, and is it getting better. Let me show you.' (Then: dashboard screen, not architecture diagram.)
commonMistakes: Opening with the schema or architecture diagram instead of the dashboard and the business question it answers
Using warehouse jargon (grain, surrogate key, accumulating snapshot) without translation
Being defensive about scope decisions instead of framing them as deliberate choices protecting data accuracy
Not confirming up front which business question matters most to this stakeholder
Overselling the pipeline as covering more than it actually does
keyPoints: Lead with business value and the specific question the project now answers
Use the stakeholder's vocabulary, not technical/warehouse jargon
Show the dashboard/output first, not the architecture
Explain data freshness and limitations in plain, honest terms
Frame scope decisions as deliberate choices protecting accuracy, not gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with business value rather than technical architecture
Demonstrates translating technical concepts into stakeholder-appropriate language
Addresses honesty about limitations/scope without being defensive
Shows awareness of audience and invites dialogue rather than a one-way readout

questions.title: Communicating During a Production ETL Failure
questions.prompt: It's 7 AM. The nightly SSIS job that feeds your warehouse failed overnight, and the Power BI dashboard plant managers check every morning is showing yesterday's stale data. Walk me through what you do in the first 30 minutes, including what you communicate and to whom.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd triage and communicate in parallel, not sequentially - going silent for an hour while debugging, even with good intentions, erodes trust faster than an honest 'I don't know yet.' Within the first few minutes, I'd check the SSISDB catalog's Dashboard and All Executions reports to see where and why the package failed, and check SQL Server Agent's job history to confirm whether the job fired at all versus fired and failed partway through - that distinction changes where I look next. At roughly the same time, I'd send a short, specific status message to whoever relies on that dashboard: acknowledge the data is stale, state the plain-English reason if I already know it ('the nightly load failed partway through - investigating now'), and give a concrete time I'll follow up, rather than speculating publicly about root cause before I'm sure. Once I find the actual cause - say, a Lookup transformation failing on an unresolved dimension key, or an unannounced source schema change - I'd fix it, re-run the load, and then run the standard validation checklist (row-count parity, orphaned-key checks, and a spot-check that SSRS and Power BI agree on a number) before telling anyone it's resolved, because a successful re-run isn't the same claim as a correct one. I'd close the loop with a final message once I've actually verified it's fixed, and afterward write a short note on what caused it and what safeguard I'm adding (for example, a row-count threshold that fails the batch loudly) so the same failure is less likely to happen silently again.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is actually two things happening at once, not one after the other - I start checking the SSISDB catalog and the Agent job history to understand what actually happened, and within that same first few minutes I send a short message to the people who check that dashboard every morning, letting them know it's stale and that I'm on it, with a real time I'll check back in. I don't go quiet while I dig in, and I don't guess out loud about the cause until I actually know it. Once I've found the real issue - whether that's a failed Lookup, a schema change nobody told us about, or something else - I fix it and rerun the load, but I don't tell anyone it's resolved the moment the job finishes successfully. I run through my validation checks first - row counts matching across the pipeline, no orphaned keys, and a quick spot check that the report and the dashboard agree on a number - because a rerun that succeeded isn't automatically a rerun that's correct. Only after that do I send the all-clear. And I don't consider the incident actually closed until I've written down what caused it and put some kind of safeguard in place, like a validation check that would make this fail loudly next time instead of quietly succeeding the way it apparently did last night.
commonMistakes: Debugging silently for an extended period before communicating anything to stakeholders
Declaring the issue resolved the moment the job reruns successfully, without re-validating correctness
Giving a vague status update with no concrete follow-up time
Speculating publicly about root cause before confirming it
Skipping a postmortem or preventive safeguard after resolving the immediate issue
keyPoints: Triage technically and communicate to stakeholders in parallel, not sequentially
Give specific, honest, time-boxed status updates rather than silence or vague reassurance
Verify correctness (row counts, orphaned keys, cross-tool agreement) after a rerun, not just success
Close the loop with stakeholders only after confirming the fix is actually correct
Follow up with a root-cause note and a preventive safeguard

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Demonstrates triaging technically and communicating with stakeholders in parallel
Gives specific, honest, time-boxed communication rather than silence or vague updates
Distinguishes 'ran successfully' from 'verified correct' before declaring resolution
Includes a postmortem/preventive safeguard as part of closing the incident

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Stakeholder's Modeling Request
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks you to add a CurrentRegion overwrite directly onto the sales fact table (instead of modeling it properly as a Type 2 dimension change) because 'it's simpler and faster to build.' You believe this will quietly corrupt historical reporting. How do you handle this disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't just comply, and I wouldn't just refuse - I'd translate the technical risk into a consequence they can see the business impact of. I'd explain concretely: if region gets overwritten in place rather than versioned, every historical sale tied to that customer or salesperson will retroactively show the new region as if it had always been true, so a 'sales by region last year' report will quietly change numbers that may have already gone into a board deck or a commission calculation, with no error or warning anywhere that it happened. I'd then offer the actual alternative plainly - a Type 2 versioned dimension - and be honest that the real cost difference is smaller than it sounds; a Type 2 load isn't dramatically harder to build, and the cost of not doing it is a much more expensive, much harder to trace data-quality incident discovered later, probably by someone other than me. If, after understanding the tradeoff, the stakeholder still prefers the simpler overwrite because they've decided history genuinely doesn't matter for this attribute, that's a legitimate business call and ultimately theirs to make - but I'd document the decision and its known limitation clearly, so it isn't a mystery to whoever investigates a discrepancy six months from now.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try not to just say yes or just say no in a moment like this - I explain what actually happens to their numbers if we go the simple route. In this case, I'd walk them through exactly what overwriting region in place does to history: every past sale from that customer or rep would suddenly show the new region as if it had always been that way, which means a report someone already presented using last year's numbers could silently change under them. Then I'd offer the real fix - versioning the dimension properly - and I'd be upfront that it's not actually that much more work to build, especially compared to the cost of someone discovering six months from now that last year's regional numbers have been quietly wrong. If they hear all that and still want the simpler approach because they've decided this attribute's history genuinely doesn't matter to them, that's their call to make, not mine to override - but I make sure it's written down clearly what we decided and why, so it's a known tradeoff, not a surprise someone finds later.
commonMistakes: Silently implementing the requested change without flagging the risk at all
Being combative or dismissive instead of explaining the business-visible consequence
Refusing outright without offering a concrete, correctly-modeled alternative
Not documenting the final decision and its known limitation once the stakeholder decides
Overstating the cost difference between the two approaches instead of being accurate about it
keyPoints: Translate the technical risk (lost history) into a concrete, business-visible consequence
Propose a specific, correctly-modeled alternative (Type 2) rather than just objecting
Be honest about the actual cost tradeoff, not an exaggerated one
Respect the stakeholder's final decision once they're genuinely informed
Document the decision and its known limitation for future reference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the technical risk in concrete, business-visible terms rather than jargon
Offers a specific, correct alternative rather than simply objecting
Shows willingness to defer to an informed stakeholder decision
Mentions documenting the final decision and its tradeoff

questions.title: Defending a Scope Decision Under Stakeholder Pressure
questions.prompt: During a capstone-style project review, a stakeholder pushes back: 'Why didn't you include production location in the work order dashboard? We need that.' You deliberately left it out because it lives at a finer grain than the fact table and modeling it naively would have produced misleading numbers. How do you respond in the room?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't get defensive, and I wouldn't just say 'it was out of scope' and leave it there - I'd explain the concrete reason in terms they can verify for themselves: a single work order can pass through multiple production locations as it moves through its routing steps, so attaching one location to the work order would mean picking just one and silently misreporting the rest - that's not a missing feature, it's a wrong number dressed up as a feature. I'd frame the omission as protecting the accuracy of every other number already on the dashboard, not as something I simply didn't get to. Then I'd immediately pivot to the real path forward, because stopping at 'no' isn't useful to them: this is a legitimate, larger piece of work - either a second fact table at the finer operation/routing grain, or a many-to-many bridge between work orders and locations - and I'd offer to scope that properly as a follow-up phase rather than bolt it on incorrectly right now under review pressure. That response shows both that I made a deliberate, defensible technical decision and that I'm not just blocking their actual need - I'm giving them a correct way to get it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't treat this as a gotcha and get defensive about it - I'd just explain plainly why it's not there: a work order can touch more than one location as it moves through production, so if I'd forced a single location onto this table, I'd have been guessing for every work order that touched more than one, and that's worse than not showing it at all. I'd make sure they understand this was a deliberate call to protect the accuracy of everything else on the dashboard, not something I overlooked. And I wouldn't stop at explaining why - I'd tell them how we'd actually get what they're asking for correctly, whether that's a second fact table built at the finer production-step grain or a bridge table connecting work orders to the locations they touched, and offer to scope that as the next piece of work rather than trying to cram it in incorrectly just to check a box in this meeting.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or dismissive instead of explaining the technical reason clearly
Saying only 'it was out of scope' without explaining why, leaving the stakeholder unconvinced
Agreeing on the spot to bolt the attribute on incorrectly just to satisfy the room
Not offering a concrete, correctly-scoped path to deliver what they actually need
Being overly technical (grain mismatch, fan-out) without translating it into a consequence they can verify
keyPoints: Explain the grain-mismatch reasoning in plain, verifiable terms
Frame the omission as protecting accuracy, not as a gap or oversight
Offer a concrete, correctly-scoped follow-up path rather than stopping at 'no'
Balance confidence in the technical decision with genuine collaboration
Avoid bolting on an incorrect fix under review pressure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the technical reasoning clearly and in verifiable terms
Frames the decision as deliberate and accuracy-protecting, not a gap
Offers a concrete, correctly-scoped follow-up path
Maintains composure and collaboration rather than defensiveness

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Developer Who Over-Applies SCD Type 2
questions.prompt: A junior BI developer on your team has started applying SCD Type 2 to every attribute on every dimension 'to be safe,' and the warehouse's dimension tables are ballooning with versions from trivial changes like typo corrections. How do you coach them?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd treat this as a teaching moment rather than a correction of carelessness, because the instinct behind it - don't lose history, don't throw anything away - is a reasonable one to start from, so I'd validate that intent before correcting the approach. I'd walk through their own warehouse with them and show the concrete cost: how many extra dimension rows a single typo fix or formatting cleanup is generating, and how that affects both storage and the usability of the semantic model report authors actually browse, since versions with no real analytical meaning clutter what should be a clean dimension. Then I'd teach the actual decision rule rather than just telling them to stop: for each attribute, ask whether any report needs this value exactly as it was at the time a related fact occurred. I'd walk through two or three real attributes on their dimension together and classify them live - a typo correction becomes Type 1, something fixed at insert becomes Type 0, something that actually drives historical rollups becomes Type 2. I'd have them go back and reclassify the dimension attribute by attribute themselves, rather than me rewriting it for them, and review the result together. I'd also follow up again later rather than treating this as a one-time correction, since internalizing a judgment call like this usually takes more than a single conversation.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to just tell them to stop - the impulse to preserve history instead of losing it is actually a good one, so I'd start by acknowledging that before getting into what's going wrong with how they're applying it. I'd pull up their actual dimension table and show them concretely how many rows a simple typo fix is generating, so the cost isn't abstract to them - it's sitting right there in their own warehouse, and it's also making the semantic model messier for whoever's building reports off it. From there I'd walk them through the real question to ask for every attribute: does any report actually need this value exactly as it was when a related fact happened? And I'd do a couple of real examples with them live, sorting attributes into Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 out loud so they see the reasoning, not just the answer. Then I'd have them redo the classification on their own dimension themselves, and review it with them afterward rather than just fixing it myself, because the goal is for them to internalize the judgment call, not just get this one dimension corrected. And I'd check back in on it again later, since this kind of thing usually takes more than one conversation to really stick.

Fixing the dimension yourself instead of coaching them through reclassifying it
Not acknowledging the reasonable instinct (preserving history) behind the overcorrection
Treating it as a one-time fix rather than following up to see if the judgment call stuck
Being overly critical in a way that discourages them from flagging uncertainty in the future

questions.title: Why MERGE Doesn't Guarantee Atomicity Under Concurrent Sessions
questions.prompt: Your team uses a single MERGE statement to upsert a staging table's changes into a dimension table every hour, and until now it's always run alone. A new requirement means two different SSIS packages can now trigger that same MERGE concurrently against the same target table. Explain why MERGE is not automatically safe under concurrent execution the way its single, all-in-one syntax suggests, what actually goes wrong, and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
MERGE's single-statement syntax makes it look atomic, but under the hood it still has to evaluate WHEN MATCHED/WHEN NOT MATCHED by reading the target first and then writing based on what it read -- and under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, that read-then-write gap is exactly where two concurrent sessions can collide. If two sessions both run the same MERGE against overlapping keys at nearly the same moment, both can evaluate a given key as "not matched" before either one has actually inserted it, because neither session's read sees the other session's not-yet-committed insert. Both then attempt WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET's INSERT for the same key, and the second one to commit either throws a primary key/unique constraint violation or, if there's no such constraint protecting the key at all, silently creates a duplicate row -- the exact inconsistency MERGE was supposed to prevent.

The fix has two parts. First, close the actual race: wrap the MERGE in an explicit transaction and add a HOLDLOCK (equivalent to SERIALIZABLE) hint on the target table reference, which forces the session to hold its lock on the examined key range until the transaction commits, so a second concurrent session can't slip a conflicting insert into the same gap. Second, add a defensive safety net regardless: a unique constraint or primary key on the natural/business key the MERGE matches on, so that even if the locking discipline is ever missed somewhere, a duplicate fails loudly with a constraint violation instead of silently landing as two rows.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd want someone to understand here is that MERGE looking like one atomic statement doesn't make it safe just because two packages might fire it at the same time. Underneath, it's still checking whether a row matches and then deciding what to do, and under the normal isolation level SQL Server runs with by default, two sessions can both check the same key, both decide it's new, and both try to insert it -- and now you've either got a duplicate key error or, if there's nothing stopping it, an actual duplicate row sitting in your dimension table. The fix I'd put in place is wrapping the MERGE in an explicit transaction with a HOLDLOCK hint, which basically makes the first session to touch a given key hold onto it until it's done, so the second session can't sneak in underneath it. And on top of that, I'd always want a real unique constraint on whatever natural key we're matching on, so even if that locking discipline ever slips somewhere, we get a loud failure instead of a silent duplicate.
questions.example:
-- Without protection: two concurrent MERGE executions against the same
-- staging batch can both see 'NOT MATCHED' for the same key.

BEGIN TRANSACTION;

MERGE dbo.DimCustomer WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS target
USING dbo.StagingCustomer AS source
    ON target.CustomerNaturalKey = source.CustomerNaturalKey
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET target.Region = source.Region
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (CustomerNaturalKey, Region)
    VALUES (source.CustomerNaturalKey, source.Region);

COMMIT TRANSACTION;

-- Defensive safety net regardless of locking discipline:
ALTER TABLE dbo.DimCustomer
ADD CONSTRAINT UQ_DimCustomer_NaturalKey UNIQUE (CustomerNaturalKey);
commonMistakes: Assuming MERGE's single-statement syntax means it's automatically safe under concurrent execution
Not adding a unique constraint on the natural key, so a race condition can land as an actual silent duplicate instead of a loud error
Not using HOLDLOCK/SERIALIZABLE, leaving the read-then-write gap open between concurrent sessions
Only testing the MERGE running alone, never under concurrent load, so the race condition never surfaces until production
keyPoints: MERGE still performs a read (match check) followed by a write, which is not inherently atomic against concurrent sessions
Default READ COMMITTED isolation doesn't prevent two sessions from both seeing 'not matched' for the same key
HOLDLOCK (SERIALIZABLE) on the target closes the race by holding the lock until commit
A unique constraint on the natural key is a cheap, essential defensive safety net
This class of bug only appears under real concurrent load, so it needs to be tested that way, not just run alone

Identifies the specific failure mode (duplicate key violation or duplicate rows)

questions.title: Building a Dynamic PIVOT for a Report Dataset With a Variable Number of Months
questions.prompt: A regional manager wants an SSRS report with one row per product and one column per month, showing total sales -- but which months appear has to adapt automatically to whatever date range the report parameter picks, so a fixed PIVOT column list won't work. Write the dynamic SQL that builds and executes a PIVOT query whose column list is generated at runtime, and explain why a static PIVOT can't solve this on its own.
questions.modelAnswer:
A static PIVOT's column list -- the values named inside FOR Color IN ([Red],[Blue],[Black]) -- has to be known and written out at parse/compile time; PIVOT does not discover its own output columns from a query at runtime, which is exactly why every PIVOT example uses literal, hardcoded values. A report whose date range parameter can produce a different set of months each time it runs can't satisfy that requirement with a plain PIVOT, because there's no way to hand PIVOT a variable or a subquery in place of that literal list.

The fix is to generate the column list as a string at runtime, then build and execute a complete PIVOT statement as dynamic SQL. First, query the distinct months actually present in the selected date range and build a comma-separated, bracket-quoted list of them using STRING_AGG and QUOTENAME -- QUOTENAME is not optional here, since a month label could otherwise be used to break out of the generated SQL. Then concatenate that column list into the full PIVOT statement as a string, and execute it with sp_executesql rather than EXEC on a raw concatenated string, passing the actual report parameters (the date range) as real parameters to sp_executesql rather than concatenating their values into the string -- the column list is the only part that has to be built as text, because it has to become identifiers, not data.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem is that PIVOT wants its list of output columns spelled out literally when the query is written, and this report's months change depending on whatever date range someone picks -- so a plain PIVOT just can't flex to that. What I'd do is build the column list myself, first: query the distinct months inside the selected range, use QUOTENAME to safely bracket each one, and glue them together with STRING_AGG into one comma-separated string. Then I take that string and drop it into a full PIVOT statement that I'm building as text, and run the whole thing through sp_executesql. The one thing I'm careful about is that I only build the column list as a string -- the actual filter parameters, like the start and end date, I pass into sp_executesql as real parameters instead of pasting their values into the SQL text, so I'm not opening an injection hole on the one part of this that actually comes from user input.
commonMistakes: Trying to pass a variable or subquery directly as PIVOT's column list, which T-SQL doesn't allow
Forgetting QUOTENAME around each generated column value, opening a SQL injection risk through the data itself
Hardcoding a fixed set of months even though the report parameter range is variable, defeating the point of the report
Concatenating the date-range filter values directly into the dynamic SQL string instead of passing them as sp_executesql parameters
keyPoints: PIVOT's column list must be known at parse/compile time, so a variable range requires dynamic SQL
Build the column list from the actual distinct values using STRING_AGG plus QUOTENAME
Execute the generated statement with sp_executesql, not EXEC on a raw concatenated string
Pass genuinely variable filter values (like the date range) as sp_executesql parameters, never by string concatenation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a static PIVOT can't adapt to a variable column set
Builds a correct dynamic column list using QUOTENAME
Executes the generated statement safely via sp_executesql
Parameterizes filter values rather than concatenating them

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'nobody changed the code' rules out a regression, missing that growing data volume is itself the real cause
Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with STATISTICS TIME/IO or direct timing, not assumption
Cursor cost scales with fixed per-row overhead that compounds as row counts grow month over month
Check the cursor's own driving query for separate degradation (stale stats, scan vs. seek)
Rewrite as one set-based UPDATE ... FROM statement
Validate the rewrite produces identical results before replacing the original in production

Explains why cursor cost compounds as data grows

questions.title: A Script Component Is Silently Dropping Rows in Production
questions.prompt: An SSIS data flow uses a Script Component to parse a semi-structured text field and extract three values from it before loading to the warehouse. Row counts between the source and the destination have quietly stopped matching -- no error, no failed package, just fewer rows landing each week. Walk through how you'd confirm the Script Component is where rows are disappearing, the specific coding mistake inside it that's the classic cause, and how you'd fix it so bad rows are visible instead of invisible.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd confirm the location first, not guess: add a Row Count transformation (or a data viewer) immediately before and immediately after the Script Component in the data flow, run the package against a known batch, and compare the two counts. If rows vanish exactly across that one component, it's confirmed.

The classic cause inside a Script Component used as a transformation is a try/catch wrapped around the parsing logic in Input0_ProcessInputRow -- splitting the semi-structured field and indexing into the result -- where the catch block does nothing, or simply returns without ever calling the output buffer's AddRow(). Unlike a built-in data flow component (a Lookup, a Derived Column), a Script Component has no automatic error output; you only get one if you explicitly add it yourself. So when a row's text doesn't parse the way the code expects, the exception gets caught, nothing gets written to any output, and that row simply disappears from the pipeline with the package still reporting success, because no exception ever escaped the component to actually fail anything.

The fix: add a dedicated error output to the Script Component, and inside the catch block, write the failing row's original data plus the exception message to that error output buffer's AddRow() instead of silently returning. Route that error output to a table or file so failed rows become visible and countable going forward, and only let the main output's AddRow() fire for rows that genuinely parsed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd do is actually pin down where the rows are disappearing instead of assuming -- drop a Row Count transformation right before and right after the Script Component and compare the numbers on a real run. Once that confirms it's the Script Component, I'd go looking for the classic bug: a try/catch around the parsing code that catches the exception and just does nothing, or returns without calling AddRow on any output. People forget that a Script Component doesn't get an error output the way a normal transformation does -- you have to build one yourself -- so if nobody did that, a row that fails to parse just vanishes with the package still reporting success, because nothing ever actually threw past the component to fail it. The fix is to add a real error output to the component, and in that catch block, write the row and the error message to it instead of swallowing it, then point that output at an error table so failures become something you can actually see and count, instead of a silent, slowly growing gap between source and destination.
commonMistakes: Trusting that a Script Component has a built-in error output the way other data flow components do -- it doesn't, you must add it yourself
Catching an exception and returning silently instead of redirecting or logging the failing row
Not instrumenting row counts across the data flow to localize exactly where rows are being lost
Only checking the package's overall success/failure status, which says nothing about silently dropped rows
keyPoints: Script Components don't get automatic error outputs like built-in transformations do
Isolate the problem with row counts before and after the component before assuming a cause
The classic bug is a try/catch that swallows a parsing exception without redirecting or logging the row
Fix by adding an explicit error output and writing failed rows to it inside the catch block
Row-count-based monitoring across the data flow is the only reliable way to catch this kind of silent data loss going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly isolates the Script Component as the source using row counts
Identifies the swallowed-exception pattern as the cause
Explains that Script Components lack automatic error outputs
Designs a concrete fix with an explicit error output

questions.title: A Partition SWITCH Load Fails With a Schema Mismatch Error
questions.prompt: Your nightly load builds a new staging table for the day's fact rows and then runs ALTER TABLE ... SWITCH PARTITION to swap it into the partitioned Fact_Sales table as a near-instant metadata operation. Tonight's load fails with an error saying the source and target tables don't match. Nothing about the load logic changed. Walk through what SWITCH actually requires to succeed, the most likely reason it just started failing, and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
SWITCH PARTITION is a metadata-only operation, and SQL Server enforces that strictly: the source table (or partition) and the target partition must be structurally identical -- same columns, same order, same data types and nullability, the same clustered index definition -- and the source table must carry a CHECK constraint that provably confines its data to exactly the target partition's boundary values, or SQL Server rejects the switch before it ever looks at a single row.

With no change to the load logic itself, the most likely cause is schema drift between Fact_Sales and the staging/switch table: someone added a new column (a new attribute or measure) to Fact_Sales without making the identical change, in the identical column position, to the script that builds the staging table. That drift is invisible day to day -- the staging table still loads fine on its own -- and only surfaces the next time SWITCH compares the two structures.

The fix: regenerate the staging table's definition directly from Fact_Sales's current structure (a SELECT ... INTO ... WHERE 1=0, or a CREATE TABLE script kept in source control and updated in lockstep with any Fact_Sales schema change), rebuild the matching clustered index, and re-add a CHECK constraint on the partitioning column that proves the staging data fits exactly the partition boundary being switched into. Keeping the staging table's build script generated from or synchronized with Fact_Sales going forward is what prevents this from recurring the next time a column is added.
questions.professionalAnswer: SWITCH only works if the two tables are structurally identical -- same columns in the same order, same index, and a CHECK constraint on the staging table that proves its data actually fits inside the specific partition boundary it's switching into. If none of that changed in the load logic itself, the most likely thing that happened is someone added a new column to Fact_Sales and the script that builds the staging table didn't get updated to match -- that kind of drift just sits there quietly until the next SWITCH actually compares the two structures and fails. The fix is to regenerate the staging table's definition straight from Fact_Sales's current structure instead of maintaining it by hand, rebuild the clustered index to match, and put the CHECK constraint back on confirming the data fits the boundary. And going forward, I'd want that staging table build tied to Fact_Sales's definition so it can't drift out of sync again the next time someone adds a column.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that any Fact_Sales schema change has to be mirrored in the staging/switch table build immediately, not eventually
Assuming SWITCH fails because of bad data when it's almost always a metadata/structure mismatch
Omitting the CHECK constraint that proves the staging table's data fits the target partition boundary, which SWITCH requires
Mismatched index structure (missing or differently-defined clustered index) between the source and target
keyPoints: SWITCH requires identical table structure, matching indexes, and a CHECK constraint proving the data fits the partition boundary
Schema drift between Fact_Sales and the staging/switch table build is the classic silent cause
Keep the staging table's definition generated from or synchronized with Fact_Sales so they can't drift apart
Re-verify the CHECK constraint boundary matches exactly the partition being switched into

Identifies schema drift as the likely cause

Gives a concrete, safe fix

questions.title: Orphaned-Looking Fact Rows After Fixing a Late-Arriving Dimension Bug
questions.prompt: Your warehouse's customer dimension load was supposed to insert inferred members for loyalty signups whose fact rows arrive before their full customer details, flipping IsInferredMember to FALSE once real details show up. A bug meant that flip never happened -- inferred rows just piled up, duplicated under the same natural key every time new details arrived. You've fixed the bug going forward. Now you need to clean up the backlog. Walk through how you'd identify the duplicated inferred members already in the warehouse, the risk in just deleting them outright, and the safe cleanup approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd identify the duplicates by grouping DimCustomer on the natural key (the loyalty number) and finding any natural key with more than one surrogate key -- specifically, a stale row still marked IsInferredMember = TRUE sitting alongside a later row that was supposed to replace it but, because of the bug, got inserted as a new row instead of updating the original in place.

The risk in just deleting the stale inferred rows outright is referential integrity: fact rows already reference those stale surrogate keys through a foreign key. Deleting the dimension row either orphans that fact history if the foreign key isn't enforced, or fails outright on the constraint if it is -- either way, you can't clean this up by touching the dimension table alone.

The safe approach: for each duplicated natural key, identify the surviving, fully-detailed surrogate key, then UPDATE every fact row currently pointing at the stale duplicate key to point at the surviving key instead. Only once no fact row references the stale key is it safe to delete it from the dimension. I'd do the whole remap inside a single transaction, validate fact row counts before and after to confirm nothing was lost or double-counted, and keep an audit log mapping each stale key to its surviving replacement in case anything needs to be traced back later.
questions.professionalAnswer: To find these, I'd group the customer dimension on the natural key -- the loyalty number -- and look for any key that has more than one surrogate key, specifically a stale row still flagged as inferred sitting next to a newer row that should have updated it in place instead of getting created as a separate row. The thing I'd be careful about is that I can't just delete the stale rows, because fact rows already point at those surrogate keys -- deleting them either breaks referential integrity or orphans history, depending on whether the foreign key is actually enforced. So the real fix is: for each duplicate, figure out which surrogate key is the one that actually has real data, update every fact row pointing at the stale key to point at that surviving key instead, and only delete the stale dimension row once nothing references it anymore. I'd do that whole remap in one transaction, check the fact row counts before and after to make sure nothing got lost, and keep a log of which old key mapped to which new one in case I need to trace it back later.
commonMistakes: Deleting the stale inferred dimension rows before repointing fact table foreign keys, breaking referential integrity or orphaning history
Assuming the newest row for a natural key is always the correct one without checking which one actually has real attribute values versus placeholders
Not wrapping the remap in a transaction, risking a half-finished cleanup
Forgetting to re-verify the forward-going fix (the IsInferredMember flip) actually works before declaring the backlog closed
keyPoints: Find duplicates by grouping on the natural key and spotting multiple surrogate keys, including stale inferred rows
Fact rows already reference the stale surrogate keys, so cleanup order matters
Remap fact table foreign keys to the surviving surrogate key before deleting anything from the dimension
Wrap the remap in a transaction and keep an audit trail
Confirm the forward-going fix actually works before declaring the backlog closed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies how to find the duplicated inferred members
