questions.title: Deciding Whether an Order Number Belongs on the Fact Table or in Its Own Dimension
questions.prompt: You're designing a new Fact_ServiceTickets table at the grain of one row per ticket. Each ticket has a TicketNumber that's unique, carries no descriptive attributes of its own, and is used constantly by support staff to look up a specific ticket. A junior developer on your team proposes building a DimTicket table with just a surrogate key and TicketNumber. Walk through how you'd evaluate that proposal, what you'd recommend instead, and how you'd still make the ticket number easy to filter and report on.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd run the two-question test on TicketNumber: does it sit at exactly the same grain as the fact row (yes -- one ticket number per ticket), and does it carry any descriptive attributes of its own worth joining out to (no -- it's a bare identifier with nothing to look up alongside it)? Two yeses means this is a textbook degenerate dimension, and a DimTicket table holding nothing but a surrogate key and TicketNumber is pure overhead -- it adds a join to every query that needs the ticket number, and buys nothing in return, since the fact table already has every value that table would ever contain.

My recommendation: keep TicketNumber directly as a column on Fact_ServiceTickets, not in a separate dimension table. To keep it just as easy for support staff and report authors to filter and group on without them needing to know it's technically a fact column, I'd expose it through a view that presents it as if it were a dimension -- CREATE VIEW DimTicket AS SELECT DISTINCT TicketNumber FROM Fact_ServiceTickets -- so the field list in Power BI or any ad hoc query tool looks and behaves the same as a real dimension, without the warehouse actually storing or maintaining a second, redundant copy of the same data.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I look at this, I'd ask two things about TicketNumber: is it at the same level of detail as one fact row, and does it have any real descriptive attributes attached to it. Here the answer to both is basically yes and no in the way that makes this a degenerate dimension -- it's just an identifier, there's nothing to look up alongside it. So building a whole separate DimTicket table with just a surrogate key and that number doesn't actually buy us anything; it's an extra join every time someone needs it, for zero payoff. What I'd suggest instead is leaving TicketNumber right on the fact table, and if we want support staff and report authors to still be able to browse it like a normal dimension, I'd wrap it in a view that presents just the distinct ticket numbers -- so it looks and filters exactly like a real dimension table without us actually having to build and maintain one.
commonMistakes: Building a real dimension table for an identifier with zero descriptive attributes, adding a join with no payoff
Assuming every identifier-looking column needs its own dimension table 'to be safe'
Forgetting to give report authors a dimension-like way to access the degenerate attribute, making it harder to use than it needs to be
Not checking grain alignment before deciding -- an identifier only qualifies as degenerate if it matches the fact row's exact grain
keyPoints: Test any identifier against two questions -- same grain as the fact row, and zero descriptive attributes -- to spot a degenerate dimension
A real dimension table for a bare identifier is overhead, not safety
Keep the identifier on the fact table itself
Expose it to report authors via a view so it still looks and filters like a dimension
Order numbers, ticket numbers, and invoice numbers are the classic real-world examples

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies the grain plus no-attributes test to identify a degenerate dimension
Explains concretely why a separate table is pure overhead
Recommends keeping it on the fact table
Proposes the view-based exposure for report authors

questions.title: Consolidating Four Low-Cardinality Order Flags Into a Single Dimension
questions.prompt: Fact_Orders currently carries four separate foreign keys for low-cardinality flags: OrderPriority (3 values), IsGift (2 values), PaymentMethod (4 values), and IsBackordered (2 values) -- four tiny dimension tables, four joins, for a report that frequently filters on combinations of them. Walk through whether these are good candidates for a junk dimension, how you'd build it, and the one condition that would make you stop and NOT consolidate them.
questions.modelAnswer:
These four flags fit the textbook profile for a junk dimension: there are several of them, each has only one attribute, and each is genuinely low cardinality. I'd build it as the Cartesian product of every combination -- 3 x 2 x 4 x 2 = 48 rows -- with one surrogate key per unique combination of OrderPriority, IsGift, PaymentMethod, and IsBackordered, then replace the four existing foreign keys on Fact_Orders with a single OrderAttributes_FK. That collapses four joins into one for any report filtering on these flags, and narrows the fact table from four FK columns down to one.

The one condition that would stop me from consolidating: if the combined cardinality were large enough that the Cartesian product explodes. If PaymentMethod grew to 15 values and a fifth flag with 10 values got added later, the row count could jump into the tens of thousands, at which point the junk dimension becomes a bigger, harder-to-maintain table than the four small ones it replaced, and the consolidation has stopped paying for itself. I'd calculate the actual projected row count before committing to the design, not just assume it stays small because it started small.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at these four flags, they're a good fit for a junk dimension -- there are several of them, each one is basically a single low-cardinality column, which is exactly the profile where this pattern pays off. What I'd do is build the table as every combination of the four flags, which comes out to 48 rows here, give each combination its own surrogate key, and then replace those four separate foreign keys on Fact_Orders with one single key pointing at this new table. That turns four joins into one for any report filtering on these, and the fact table gets narrower too. The one thing that would make me stop and not do this is if the combined row count were about to blow up -- if one of these flags grew to a lot more values, or we kept adding more flags to the same dimension, that Cartesian product can get out of hand fast, and at that point we've built something harder to manage than the four small tables we were trying to get rid of.
questions.example:
-- Cartesian product row count: 3 x 2 x 4 x 2 = 48 rows
SELECT op.OrderPriority, g.IsGift, pm.PaymentMethod, bo.IsBackordered,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY op.OrderPriority, g.IsGift, pm.PaymentMethod, bo.IsBackordered) AS OrderAttributesKey
INTO dbo.DimOrderAttributes
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT OrderPriority FROM StagingOrders) op
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT IsGift FROM StagingOrders) g
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT PaymentMethod FROM StagingOrders) pm
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT IsBackordered FROM StagingOrders) bo;
commonMistakes: Consolidating attributes that actually have independent business meaning analysts need to slice on their own (those belong as real dimensions, not junked together)
Not calculating the actual Cartesian product row count before deciding, missing a combinatorial explosion
Junk-dimensioning a single flag alone, which isn't a consolidation problem worth solving
Forgetting that the fact table's foreign keys need to be rebuilt and remapped to the new single surrogate key as part of the migration
keyPoints: Good junk dimension candidates are several, low-attribute-count, low-cardinality flags
Rows are built as the Cartesian product of every combination, one surrogate key per combination
Consolidating collapses multiple joins into one and narrows the fact table
Stop consolidating once combined cardinality would explode the row count past what's manageable
Don't junk-dimension attributes with independent business meaning that analysts need to filter on their own

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly evaluates the four flags against junk dimension candidate criteria
Correctly computes and explains the Cartesian product construction
Explains the fact table impact
Identifies the cardinality-explosion stopping condition

questions.title: Choosing Between a Periodic Snapshot and an Accumulating Snapshot Fact for Order Fulfillment
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to track order fulfillment performance: how long orders sit at each stage (placed, picked, shipped, delivered), plus a daily view of how many orders are currently sitting in each stage. One developer on your team proposes a single fact table to cover both needs. Walk through why that's the wrong grain for at least one of these questions, which fact table type(s) you'd actually design, and how they'd work together.
questions.modelAnswer:
These are two different business questions with two different natural grains, and forcing them into one fact table only serves one of them well. 'How long did this order sit at each stage' is a per-process-instance question -- one row per order, updated as it reaches each milestone -- which is exactly what an accumulating snapshot fact table is built for: OrderDate_FK, PickDate_FK, ShipDate_FK, DeliverDate_FK as role-playing references to the same Date dimension, with duration measures like DaysToPickAfterOrder.

'How many orders are sitting in each stage right now, as of today' is a different shape entirely -- it needs a row per day regardless of whether anything happened that day, which is what a periodic snapshot fact table is for: one row per day per stage, loaded on a fixed schedule, with a semi-additive count measure that's valid to sum across stages on a given day but never valid to sum across days. Trying to answer the daily-stage-count question from the accumulating snapshot alone would mean re-deriving 'which orders were in stage X on day Y' by inference from milestone dates every time a report runs, which is slow and fragile compared to a dedicated snapshot built for exactly that question.

My recommendation is to build both: an accumulating snapshot for the duration/timing question, a periodic snapshot for the daily-stage-count question, sharing the same conformed Order, Product, and Date dimensions so the two reports stay consistent with each other even though they're built from different fact tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: These really are two separate questions even though they sound related, and they each want a different shape of table. The duration question -- how long an order sat at each stage -- is a per-order thing, one row that gets updated as the order moves along, which is exactly what an accumulating snapshot is for. The daily count question -- how many orders are sitting in each stage right now -- needs a row every single day regardless of whether anything happened, which is a periodic snapshot's job, not the accumulating snapshot's. If we tried to answer the daily-count question off the accumulating snapshot alone, we'd be reconstructing 'who was in which stage on which day' from milestone dates every time someone runs that report, which is slow and honestly fragile compared to just building the table that's meant for it. So my recommendation is build both -- they're not competing designs, they answer two different questions -- and have them share the same Order, Product, and Date dimensions so the two reports never disagree with each other.
commonMistakes: Trying to answer both questions from a single fact table, picking a grain that only really serves one of them well
Using an accumulating snapshot to answer 'how many are in each stage today' by deriving it from milestone dates at query time instead of building a dedicated periodic snapshot
Forgetting the accumulating snapshot needs an UPDATE-based load, not insert-only, which is operationally different from most other fact tables
Summing a periodic snapshot's count measure across days instead of treating it as semi-additive
keyPoints: 'Duration at each stage' and 'how many are in each stage right now' are different business questions with different grains
An accumulating snapshot (one row per order, updated per milestone) answers the duration question
A periodic snapshot (one row per fixed interval) answers the daily-count question
The two fact table types can and should share the same conformed dimensions
Don't force two different grains into one fact table just to avoid building a second one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that the two questions need different grains
Correctly designs the accumulating snapshot for the duration question
Correctly designs the periodic snapshot for the daily-count question
Explains how they share conformed dimensions

questions.title: Designing an Aggregate Fact Table to Speed Up a Slow Executive Dashboard
questions.prompt: An executive dashboard built directly against your 400-million-row Fact_Sales table takes 30+ seconds to render 'revenue by month by region' -- the exact kind of summary query that gets run constantly and never changes shape. Walk through the aggregate table design you'd build to fix this, how you'd keep it from going stale, and the trade-off you're accepting by building it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd build an aggregate fact table that rolls Fact_Sales up to exactly the grain the dashboard needs -- one row per order-month and region, summing Revenue -- using CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (or SELECT INTO), grouping the detailed fact by those dimension keys. I'd point the dashboard's query at this small aggregate table instead of the 400-million-row detail table; because it's a rollup to a coarser grain, the row count drops by orders of magnitude, and the same 'revenue by month by region' query that took 30 seconds against the detail runs against a table with a few thousand rows instead.

Keeping it from going stale: the aggregate isn't a one-time snapshot, it's a derived table that needs refreshing every time Fact_Sales gets new rows. I'd build the rollup logic into a stored procedure and schedule it as its own step in the nightly ETL orchestration, right after the Fact_Sales load completes -- the same dependency-ordering discipline as loading dimensions before facts -- and make sure any failure in that refresh step is visible, since a stale aggregate quietly disagreeing with the detail table is worse than no aggregate at all.

The trade-off I'm accepting: this is deliberate data duplication, not a free win. It's another table the orchestration has to process and keep in sync, and if that refresh job is ever skipped or fails silently, the dashboard will show numbers that don't match the detail table underneath it.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd build is a table that rolls Fact_Sales up to exactly the level the dashboard actually needs -- month and region -- using a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT that groups the detail and sums revenue. Then I point the dashboard at that small table instead of the 400-million-row one, and because it's a much coarser grain, the same query that used to take 30 seconds runs against a table with maybe a few thousand rows instead. The part people forget is that this table doesn't stay correct on its own -- every time Fact_Sales gets new data, this one needs to be refreshed too, so I'd build that into a stored procedure and run it as a scheduled step right after the nightly Fact_Sales load, and make sure if that step ever fails, it's loud about it, because a stale aggregate quietly disagreeing with the real numbers underneath it is worse than not having the shortcut at all. And I'd be upfront that this is a trade-off, not a free performance win -- it's duplicated data and one more thing the pipeline has to keep in sync, in exchange for a dashboard that actually loads fast.
questions.example:
CREATE TABLE agg_sale_by_month_region AS
SELECT
    DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d.FullDate), MONTH(d.FullDate), 1) AS OrderMonth,
    r.Region,
    SUM(fs.Revenue) AS TotalRevenue
FROM dbo.Fact_Sales fs
JOIN dbo.Dim_Date d ON d.DateKey = fs.OrderDateKey
JOIN dbo.Dim_Region r ON r.RegionKey = fs.RegionKey
GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d.FullDate), MONTH(d.FullDate), 1), r.Region;

-- Scheduled nightly, immediately after the Fact_Sales load step completes:
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.usp_RefreshAggSaleByMonthRegion AS
BEGIN
    TRUNCATE TABLE dbo.agg_sale_by_month_region;
    INSERT INTO dbo.agg_sale_by_month_region
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d.FullDate), MONTH(d.FullDate), 1), r.Region, SUM(fs.Revenue)
    FROM dbo.Fact_Sales fs
    JOIN dbo.Dim_Date d ON d.DateKey = fs.OrderDateKey
    JOIN dbo.Dim_Region r ON r.RegionKey = fs.RegionKey
    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d.FullDate), MONTH(d.FullDate), 1), r.Region;
END;
commonMistakes: Treating the aggregate table as a one-time build instead of something that needs a scheduled refresh tied to the detail table's load
Not making aggregate refresh failures visible, letting the dashboard silently drift out of sync with the detail
Building the aggregate at a grain finer than the dashboard actually needs, losing most of the performance benefit
Not considering Power BI's own user-defined aggregations or DirectQuery-over-the-aggregate as alternatives before committing to a new physical table
keyPoints: An aggregate fact table is a rollup of the detail fact to a coarser grain, built with CTAS
It should be built at exactly the grain the dashboard needs, not finer
It must be refreshed on a schedule tied to the detail table's own load, in dependency order
A stale, out-of-sync aggregate is worse than not having one, so refresh failures need to be visible
The trade-off being accepted is deliberate duplication and an extra table to maintain, not a free performance win

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correctly-grained aggregate table using CTAS
Explains the performance mechanism
Addresses keeping it refreshed and in sync
Names the real trade-off (duplication/maintenance cost)

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Environment Promotion Strategy for a 30-Package SSIS Project
questions.prompt: You're the senior developer on a 30-package SSIS project that currently runs fine in development but has never been deployed anywhere else. The team is about to add a test server and a production server, and several packages hardcode connection strings today. Walk through the environment strategy you'd design in the SSIS Catalog so the same deployed project runs correctly on all three, and the one rule you'd make sure the whole team understands before anyone runs a production execution.
questions.modelAnswer:
First, every hardcoded connection string across the 30 packages has to become a project parameter or connection manager property exposed for environment mapping -- that's a prerequisite, not optional, since environments only work by overriding parameters and connection manager properties that already exist as such.

Then, in the SSISDB catalog, I'd create three environments -- Dev, Test, Production -- each containing the same-named variables (server name, database name, file-share paths, anything that differs by server), with values appropriate to that tier, marking anything sensitive (like a connection password) as Sensitive so SSISDB encrypts it. I'd deploy the project once, add environment references to all three environments on the project's References page, then map each relevant parameter and connection manager property to the matching environment variable on the Parameters and Connection Managers tabs -- the same mapping, pointed at different environments depending on which one is active for a given execution.

The one rule every team member needs to internalize before running anything in production: a single execution can reference only one environment, never a mix. So when SQL Server Agent job steps are set up for the production schedule, each step's execution must explicitly specify the Production environment reference, and nobody should ever manually run an execution without double-checking which environment reference is selected -- that's the only thing standing between a routine run and a production job accidentally pulling a dev connection string.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing that has to happen before any of this works is getting rid of the hardcoded connection strings -- they have to become real parameters or connection manager properties, because environments can only override something that's already set up to be overridden. Once that's done, I'd create three environments in the catalog -- Dev, Test, Production -- each with the same-named variables but different values for things like server name and file paths, and I'd mark anything sensitive so SSISDB encrypts it properly. Then I deploy the project once and reference all three environments from it, and map the actual parameters and connection manager properties to those environment variables. The one thing I'd make absolutely sure the whole team understands before anyone touches production: a single execution can only pull from one environment, never a mix of two. So every Agent job step for the production schedule has to explicitly name the Production environment reference, and nobody should ever kick off a manual execution without checking which environment is selected first -- that's genuinely the only thing stopping a production run from accidentally using dev settings.
questions.example:
-- Conceptual mapping, not literal T-SQL:
-- Environment 'Dev':        ServerName = 'dev-sql01'
-- Environment 'Test':       ServerName = 'test-sql01'
-- Environment 'Production': ServerName = 'prod-sql01'
--
-- Project parameter 'TargetServer' mapped to environment variable 'ServerName'
-- on each of the three environment references.
--
-- SQL Server Agent job step for the nightly production run:
--   /ISSERVER "\SSISDB\Finance\MyProject\MyPackage.dtsx" /ENVREFERENCE Production
commonMistakes: Leaving some connection strings hardcoded instead of converting all of them to parameters/connection manager properties first, which environments can't override
Creating the environments but forgetting to actually map parameters to them, leaving the project still running on its fixed defaults
Not marking sensitive values (passwords, connection secrets) as Sensitive in the environment variables
Letting a scheduled job or a manual execution run without explicitly specifying which environment reference to use, risking a production run against dev settings
keyPoints: Hardcoded connection strings must become parameters/connection manager properties before environments can override them
Create one environment per tier (Dev/Test/Production) with matching variable names and tier-appropriate values
Mark sensitive values as Sensitive so SSISDB encrypts them
Map parameters and connection manager properties to environment variables via project References and Configure
The one-environment-per-execution rule is the guardrail against a production run accidentally using the wrong tier's settings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies hardcoded connection strings as the real prerequisite to fix
Correctly designs three environments with mapped variables
Addresses sensitive value handling
Correctly explains and emphasizes the one-environment-per-execution rule

questions.title: Designing a Composite Model to Mix a Live Fact Table With Stable Dimensions in Power BI
questions.prompt: Your Power BI model has a 200-million-row Sales fact table in DirectQuery (too large to import, and the business wants it close to real-time) alongside small, rarely-changing Customer, Product, and Date dimension tables that are currently also set to DirectQuery, just because that's how the Sales connection defaulted. Report authors are complaining that slicers and cross-filtering feel sluggish. Walk through the storage-mode redesign you'd make, why it fixes the slowness, and the one conversion direction you need to warn the team is irreversible.
questions.modelAnswer:
The dimension tables don't need to be DirectQuery at all -- they're small and rarely change, so there's no real-time requirement forcing them to stay live-queried, and every slicer and cross-filter interaction against them is paying a round-trip to the source for data that barely ever changes. The fix is a composite model: convert Customer, Product, and Date to Dual storage mode rather than plain Import.

Dual lets each of those tables behave as Import when that's faster -- serving slicer and filter-pane interactions from memory instead of a live query -- while still behaving as DirectQuery when a query needs to join against the still-live Sales fact table, which is what keeps relationships and cross-filtering consistent between a cached dimension and a live fact table.

Plain Import on the dimensions would be the wrong choice here despite being fastest, because once you convert a table to Import you cannot convert it back to DirectQuery -- if the business later decides a dimension attribute also needs to be live (say, a loyalty tier that changes in near-real-time), an Import table would have to be reconnected from scratch, while a Dual table keeps that option open. So: Sales stays DirectQuery because it has to, by requirement and size, the three dimensions move to Dual, and Sales itself is left alone since DirectQuery-to-Import is a one-way door you don't want to walk through accidentally on the one table you can't take back.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dimension tables here really don't need to be DirectQuery -- they're small, they barely change, and right now every slicer click is paying for a live round-trip to the source for data that's basically static. What I'd do is convert Customer, Product, and Date to Dual mode instead of plain Import. Dual lets them act like Import for fast, cached interactions like slicers, but still behave like DirectQuery when they need to join against the Sales table, which is what keeps everything consistent since Sales has to stay live. The reason I wouldn't just convert them to plain Import, even though that's fastest, is that converting to Import is a one-way door -- you can't go back to DirectQuery later without reconnecting the table from scratch. So if the business ever wants one of these dimensions to be more real-time down the line, Dual keeps that option open and Import would have closed it off. Sales itself I'd leave alone entirely, since that's the one table where an accidental, irreversible conversion would actually hurt.
questions.example:
-- Model view storage modes after the redesign:
-- Fact_Sales   -> DirectQuery  (200M rows, real-time requirement)
-- Dim_Customer -> Dual         (small, rarely changes)
-- Dim_Product  -> Dual         (small, rarely changes)
-- Dim_Date     -> Dual         (small, rarely changes)
commonMistakes: Converting the small dimensions straight to Import instead of Dual, closing off the option to ever make them live again without reconnecting from scratch
Leaving everything in DirectQuery 'to be safe,' which is what caused the sluggish slicer experience in the first place
Not recognizing that the fact table's size and freshness requirement is the actual constraint, not a reason to also force the dimensions into DirectQuery
Forgetting that converting DirectQuery to Import is irreversible, and applying it somewhere that might need to go back later
keyPoints: Small, rarely-changing dimension tables don't need to inherit DirectQuery just because the fact table does
Dual mode lets a table serve fast cached reads for its own interactions while still joining correctly against a live DirectQuery fact table
This composite model (one DirectQuery fact, Dual dimensions) directly fixes sluggish slicers and cross-filtering
Converting a table to Import is one-way -- Dual preserves future flexibility that plain Import would close off
The fact table's size and freshness requirement, not laziness, should be the only reason anything in the model stays DirectQuery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies Dual mode as the fix for the dimension tables
Explains why it resolves the slicer/cross-filter slowness
Correctly distinguishes Dual from plain Import for this scenario
Flags the Import conversion as irreversible

questions.title: Resolving a Design Disagreement With Another Senior Developer Over Star vs. Snowflake
questions.prompt: You and another senior developer disagree about a new Product dimension: you want a star schema (one denormalized Product table), they want to snowflake it out into Product, Category, and Subcategory tables for what they call 'proper normalization.' The disagreement has stalled the sprint for two days. Walk me through how you'd resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd first separate the technical question from the stalled-sprint problem, because two days of disagreement is itself the more urgent issue. I'd bring the trade-off back to our specific warehouse, not an abstract preference: snowflaking buys normalized storage and easier updates to category names, at the cost of extra joins on every query and more clicks for report authors browsing a wider field list; a star schema's denormalized Product table costs a little redundant storage and a slightly more complex load (propagating a category rename to every product row instead of one category row), but it's faster to query and simpler for the Power BI models downstream that this team is accountable for performance on.

I'd frame it as 'which cost are we more willing to pay,' not 'who's right about normalization in the abstract,' and bring concrete evidence -- how often category and subcategory names actually change for us, and how many joins snowflaking adds to the reports we already know are being built. If we still can't agree after that, I'd propose a tiebreaker that isn't just seniority: prototype both against a realistic query the Power BI team actually needs, and let the measured difference decide it, with an explicit time box so the disagreement doesn't cost the sprint a third day.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try not to let two senior people disagreeing turn into a standoff, so the first thing I'd do is name that the two-day stall is actually the bigger problem right now, separate from who's got the better modeling argument. Then I'd pull the conversation back to our actual data, not textbook normalization theory -- how often do category and subcategory names really change for us, and how many extra joins does snowflaking add to the Power BI reports we already know are coming. I'd lay out the real trade-off plainly: a star schema is faster to query and simpler for report authors, a snowflake is more normalized and slightly easier to update category text, and ask which of those we actually care more about for this specific warehouse. And if we're still stuck after that honest conversation, I'd rather settle it with a quick prototype -- build both, run the query the downstream team actually needs, and let the real numbers decide instead of two opinions. I'd also put a time box on it, because letting this run a third day costs the team more than either design choice would.
questions.example: "Let's time-box this to one more conversation: I'll prototype both against the actual sales query Power BI needs, we compare, and whichever wins, we both commit to it by end of day."
commonMistakes: Letting the disagreement run indefinitely without naming the sprint cost
Arguing from abstract normalization theory instead of this warehouse's actual query and change patterns
Pulling rank instead of proposing an objective tiebreaker
Not setting a time box, letting a two-day stall become a three- or four-day one
keyPoints: Name the stalled sprint as an urgent problem separate from the technical disagreement
Ground the argument in this warehouse's actual query patterns and data change frequency, not textbook theory
Frame it as a trade-off to choose, not a right-or-wrong question
Propose an objective tiebreaker (a quick prototype against a real query) if discussion alone doesn't resolve it
Time-box the resolution so the disagreement doesn't keep costing the sprint

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the stalled sprint as a problem to address directly
Grounds the disagreement in concrete trade-offs rather than abstract theory
Proposes a fair resolution mechanism (prototype/evidence-based)
Shows awareness of timeliness and time-boxing

questions.title: Justifying a Dimensional Model to Leadership That Wants a Single 'Simple' Flat Table
questions.prompt: You've designed a proper star schema for a new reporting initiative -- fact table, conformed dimensions, surrogate keys. A director who isn't technical pushes back: 'Why can't we just have one big flat table in Excel that has everything in it? That sounds simpler.' Walk me through how you'd respond.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't argue dimensional modeling theory with a director -- I'd translate the trade-off into outcomes they already care about: cost, speed, and correctness. A single flat table repeats every customer and product attribute on every transaction row; for a company doing millions of transactions a year, that's a table that grows enormous fast, takes longer to refresh, and is slower for anyone filtering or summarizing it. Worse, if a customer's region is ever corrected, a flat table means updating that value on every one of their past transaction rows, or risking the same customer showing two different regions depending on which row you look at -- exactly the kind of inconsistency that erodes trust in a report.

A star schema keeps one clean, authoritative copy of each customer and product's attributes, and transactions just reference them, so a correction happens in one place and is instantly correct everywhere, and the fact table stays lean and fast. I'd be honest that 'simpler to look at' and 'simpler to maintain and trust at scale' aren't the same thing, and offer a concrete comparison if it would help -- the flat-table size projection versus the star schema's, or a side-by-side on how long a correction takes to propagate in each.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always try to meet a non-technical stakeholder where they actually live, which is outcomes, not architecture vocabulary. So instead of explaining normalization, I'd say something like: if we flatten everything into one big table, every customer's name and region gets copied onto every single transaction row they ever make -- and if that region is ever wrong and needs fixing, we'd have to go find and fix it on thousands of old rows instead of one. The design I built keeps one clean record for each customer, and every transaction just points back to it, so a fix happens once and is correct everywhere immediately. I'd also point out that the flat table gets huge fast and gets slower to refresh and query as it grows, while this design stays lean on the transaction side. I try to be upfront that 'looks simpler' and 'is actually simpler to trust and maintain' aren't the same thing, and I'd offer to show them a quick side-by-side if that would help make the trade-off concrete instead of abstract.
questions.example: "If we ever have to correct one customer's region, with my design that's one UPDATE statement. With one flat table, it's potentially thousands of rows to find and fix -- and until we do, the same customer shows two different regions depending on which row you're looking at."
commonMistakes: Explaining normal forms, surrogate keys, or star-vs-snowflake terminology to a non-technical director instead of translating to cost/speed/correctness
Being dismissive or defensive about the 'simpler' framing instead of taking it seriously and addressing it
Not giving a concrete, relatable example of the real cost, like a correction propagating to thousands of rows
Failing to acknowledge that the flat table does look simpler on the surface, which is why the pushback feels reasonable to begin with
keyPoints: Translate the technical trade-off into cost, speed, and correctness outcomes a director already cares about
The concrete failure mode of a flat table is that a single correction has to propagate across every repeated row, or risks inconsistency
A star schema keeps one authoritative copy of each dimension's attributes so corrections happen once
Acknowledge honestly that 'looks simpler' and 'is simpler to maintain and trust at scale' are different things
Offer a concrete comparison or example rather than staying abstract

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Translates the technical justification into business-relevant outcomes
Gives a concrete, correct example of the flat-table failure mode
Avoids technical jargon inappropriate for the audience
Acknowledges the stakeholder's perspective respectfully

questions.title: Owning a Mistake After an SCD Type 1 Overwrite Destroyed Historical Data
questions.prompt: You deployed a dimension update last week that was supposed to be a Type 2 change for customer region, but a copy-paste mistake left it running as a Type 1 overwrite instead. You just discovered that a month of historical region values for every customer who moved has been silently overwritten and can't be recovered from the warehouse itself. Walk me through how you'd handle this -- who you'd tell, in what order, and what you'd actually say.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd move fast and tell people before they find out from a report looking wrong, not after. First, my direct manager or team lead, immediately -- I'd state plainly what happened (a Type 1 ran where a Type 2 should have), what the actual impact is (a month of historical region values on moved customers is gone from the warehouse, not corrupted in a recoverable way), and what I'm already doing about it, rather than waiting until I have a full fix to say anything.

Second, whoever owns the reports that depend on historical region accuracy -- if region-based trend or territory reports went out during that window, they need to know those specific numbers may be wrong, so they can decide whether to re-run or caveat anything already delivered. For recovery, I'd check whether the source system still has the point-in-time region values even though the warehouse doesn't -- a source audit table, a backup, or an upstream change log -- and if so, backfill the dimension's historical rows from there; if genuinely nothing survives, I'd say so plainly rather than overstating what can be recovered.

Throughout, I'd own the mistake directly -- it was my code, I wouldn't frame it as 'the deployment process' or soften it -- while being equally direct about the fix: the Type 2 logic itself, plus a test that specifically checks history is preserved on a sample customer, so the same class of bug can't ship again unnoticed.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct here is to say something immediately, before anyone else notices a report looks off. I'd go straight to my manager and lay it out simply: a copy-paste error made a Type 2 change run as a Type 1, and a month of customer region history got overwritten, not safely preserved somewhere I can just restore from. I wouldn't wait until I had the whole fix figured out to say something -- better they hear 'here's the problem and here's what I'm doing' today than find out from a stakeholder next week. Then I'd flag it to whoever owns the reports that lean on region history, because if anything went out during that window, they deserve to know it might be affected. On the recovery side, I'd check if the source system has the values I need even though my warehouse doesn't -- sometimes there's a backup or an audit trail upstream that saves you -- and if there genuinely isn't, I'd say that clearly instead of promising a recovery I can't deliver. And I'd take ownership of it as my mistake, not hide behind 'the process' -- while also being specific about what I'm changing so it can't happen the same way twice, like adding a test that actually verifies history gets preserved before this kind of deploy ships again.
questions.example: "I made a mistake in last week's deployment -- a copy-paste error ran a Type 1 overwrite where it should have been Type 2, and a month of customer region history is gone from the warehouse. Here's what I'm checking for recovery, and here's what report owners need to know in the meantime."
commonMistakes: Delaying disclosure until a full fix or recovery plan is ready, letting someone else discover the problem first
Softening or diffusing ownership of the mistake instead of stating plainly what went wrong and that it was your error
Overstating what can realistically be recovered instead of being honest about what's genuinely lost
Fixing the immediate bug without adding a safeguard (like a history-preservation test) that would catch the same class of mistake next time
keyPoints: Disclose promptly, before stakeholders discover it through a wrong-looking report
Tell your manager first, directly and specifically, not vaguely or late
Notify whoever owns affected downstream reports so they can assess real impact
Be honest about what can and can't actually be recovered
Take direct ownership of the mistake and pair the fix with a safeguard against the same class of error recurring

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Prioritizes prompt, direct disclosure over delay
Correctly identifies who needs to know and in what order
Takes clear personal ownership without deflecting
Proposes a concrete recovery approach plus a forward-looking safeguard

questions.title: Telling a Stakeholder Their Mid-Sprint Report Change Will Push the Deadline
questions.prompt: You're two days from delivering a Power BI dashboard that's been scoped and committed to for three weeks. A stakeholder asks, mid-sprint, for a new breakdown that requires adding a dimension to the model and reworking several measures -- not a quick tweak. The delivery date was already communicated to their leadership. Walk me through how you'd handle the conversation.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd treat this as a scope and timeline decision the stakeholder should make with real information, not something I quietly absorb by working a weekend or quietly drop from the dashboard. I'd be specific about why this isn't a quick add: it requires a new dimension in the model and rework across several existing measures, not a cosmetic change, and I'd give an honest estimate of what that actually costs in time.

Then I'd lay out the real options plainly: ship the committed scope on the original date and add this breakdown as a fast follow-up right after, or push the delivery date to absorb the new work now, or find a smaller version of what they're asking for that fits in the two days remaining. I wouldn't make that call for them -- it's their deadline commitment to leadership that's on the line, so I'd frame it as 'here's the trade-off, which one matters more to you,' and whatever they choose, I'd follow up in writing so there's a clear record of what was requested, when, and what we agreed to do about the date.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I try hardest not to do here is just silently absorb the extra work and hope I can still hit the date -- that usually ends with either a late delivery nobody saw coming or a rushed, lower-quality dashboard. So I'd be straightforward: this isn't a two-minute change, it means adding a new dimension and reworking several measures, and here's roughly how long that actually takes. Then I'd give them real choices instead of just saying no -- we can ship what we committed to on time and add this right after, we can push the date to include it now, or maybe there's a smaller version of the ask that fits in the time we have left. I'd let them pick, since it's their commitment to their leadership that's at stake, not mine to unilaterally decide, and I'd always follow up with a quick written summary of what we agreed, so nobody's surprised later about what shifted and why.
questions.example: "This breakdown needs a new dimension and changes to several measures -- it's not a quick add. I can ship what we committed to on Thursday and add this as the first thing next sprint, or we push Thursday to include it now. Which matters more to you?"
commonMistakes: Silently absorbing the extra scope without surfacing the real time cost, risking a late or rushed delivery
Making the scope-vs-deadline trade-off decision unilaterally instead of giving the stakeholder real options
Downplaying the actual effort involved to seem accommodating, setting up a worse conversation later
Not following up in writing, leaving the agreed trade-off undocumented
keyPoints: Name the real cost of the change honestly instead of silently absorbing it
Give the stakeholder genuine options -- ship on time plus fast-follow, push the date, or scope down -- rather than a flat no
Let the stakeholder make the final call since their commitment to leadership is what's actually at stake
Document whatever is agreed to in writing so there's no ambiguity later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Surfaces the real scope/time impact honestly rather than absorbing it silently
Presents concrete trade-off options instead of a flat refusal
Correctly defers the final decision to the stakeholder
Addresses documentation and follow-up

questions.title: Giving a Peer Critical Feedback on an SSIS Package's Missing Restartability
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's new SSIS package before it goes to production. It works correctly end to end, but it has no checkpoints and no restart logic -- if task 4 of 6 fails, there's no way to resume without re-running the whole thing, including tasks that already succeeded and shouldn't run twice. The teammate is proud of the package and eager to ship it. Walk me through how you'd give this feedback.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start from what's actually true and positive -- the package works end to end, which is real, meaningful progress -- before raising the gap, so the feedback lands as 'here's one more thing before this is production-ready,' not as a takedown of their work. I'd be specific and concrete about the restartability gap rather than vague: walk through exactly what happens if task 4 fails tonight at 2 AM -- someone has to manually re-run tasks 1 through 3, which may not be safe if they're not idempotent (duplicate inserts, re-triggered side effects), and there's no checkpoint file to tell SSIS where to resume from.

I'd frame it as a production-readiness requirement we apply to every package, not a personal preference of mine, and I'd offer to pair with them on adding checkpoints and restart logic rather than just handing back a list of required changes and walking away -- partly because it genuinely helps them learn the pattern faster, and partly because it keeps the conversation collaborative instead of adversarial. I'd also ask whether there's a reason they skipped it, since sometimes there's a real constraint I'm not aware of, rather than assuming the omission was carelessness.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always lead with what's genuinely working before I bring up a gap, because this package running correctly end to end is real progress and I don't want that to get lost. Then I'd get specific instead of vague about what's missing -- I'd walk through what actually happens if task 4 fails at 2 AM: someone has to rerun everything from task 1, and if those early tasks aren't safe to run twice, that's its own problem on top of the failure. I'd frame checkpoints and restart logic as something we require on every production package, not my personal preference, so it doesn't feel like I'm singling out their work. And I'd offer to sit down and add it together rather than just sending back a review with a required-changes list, both because that helps them pick up the pattern for next time and because it keeps the whole thing feeling like we're solving it together instead of me grading their work.
questions.example: "This runs correctly end to end, which is great. One thing before this ships: if task 4 fails at 2 AM, there's no checkpoint, so someone has to rerun everything from task 1 -- and I want to make sure that's safe before we go to production. Want to pair on adding checkpoints this afternoon?"
commonMistakes: Leading with the gap instead of acknowledging what's genuinely working first, making the feedback feel like a takedown
Being vague about the restartability problem instead of walking through the concrete 2 AM failure scenario
Framing the required change as a personal preference instead of a team production-readiness standard
Not offering to help close the gap, leaving the teammate to figure out an unfamiliar pattern alone
keyPoints: Acknowledge genuine, working progress before raising the gap
Make the restartability risk concrete with a specific failure scenario, not an abstract rule
Frame checkpoints and restart logic as a team production standard, not a personal preference
Offer to collaborate on the fix rather than just listing required changes
Check whether there's a reason the gap exists before assuming it was an oversight

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with genuine acknowledgment of what works
Makes the restartability risk concrete and specific
Frames the standard as objective/team-wide rather than personal
Offers collaborative help closing the gap

questions.title: Triaging Two Stakeholders Who Both Say Their Request Is Top Priority
questions.prompt: On the same afternoon, the sales director tells you her regional pipeline report is 'the most important thing you could be working on' and needs to be done by Friday, and separately the finance director tells you his month-end reconciliation dashboard is 'the most important thing you could be working on' and also needs Friday. You can't do both well by Friday. Walk me through how you'd handle it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't quietly pick one and hope the other doesn't notice, and I wouldn't try to split my time evenly between both and risk delivering two mediocre results by Friday. I'd surface the conflict explicitly and quickly, to whoever can actually resolve a priority call between two directors -- usually my manager, or whoever both directors report into if that's clearer -- and lay out the situation factually: both requests landed today, both are scoped as Friday deliverables, and I physically can't deliver both at full quality by then, so I need a decision on sequencing, not permission to work harder.

I'd come with the actual facts that help that decision: a rough effort estimate for each, what happens if either slips a few days, and whether a partial version of either -- a smaller slice done well by Friday, the rest next week -- is an acceptable middle option. Once there's a decision, I'd personally tell the director whose request is being pushed, rather than letting them find out secondhand -- acknowledging their request is genuinely important, explaining honestly why the other one is going first, and giving them a real date for theirs, not a vague 'soon.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I wouldn't do is just quietly decide which director to disappoint and hope it doesn't blow back on me, and I also wouldn't try to make both happy by splitting my time and risk doing a weak job on both. I'd flag the conflict right away to whoever can actually make a priority call between two directors -- my manager, usually -- and just lay out the facts: both of these landed today, both are asking for Friday, and I can't do both well by then, so I need help deciding which goes first. I'd bring enough information to make that an easy decision -- roughly how long each takes, what happens if either one slips, and whether there's a smaller version of either that could realistically land Friday with the rest following next week. And once there's a decision, I make a point of telling the deprioritized director myself, directly, rather than letting them find out some other way -- I'd acknowledge that their ask matters, be honest about why the other one is going first, and give them a specific date instead of something vague.
questions.example: "Both of these landed on me today as Friday deliverables and I can't do both well by then. I need a priority call -- here's roughly what each takes, and here's what a partial version of either could look like if that helps."
commonMistakes: Silently choosing one priority without escalating, leaving the deprioritized director blindsided
Trying to deliver both by splitting effort, risking two weak deliverables instead of one strong one
Escalating vaguely ('I'm overloaded') instead of bringing concrete facts that make the decision easy
Letting the deprioritized stakeholder find out secondhand instead of telling them directly and respectfully
keyPoints: Don't silently pick a priority between two stakeholders who both outrank that decision
Escalate the conflict explicitly and quickly to whoever can actually resolve it
Bring concrete facts (effort estimates, slip impact, partial-scope options) to make the decision easy, not just a complaint
Personally and respectfully inform whichever stakeholder is deprioritized, with a real new date, not vague reassurance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids silently choosing or silently overcommitting
Escalates the conflict appropriately and promptly
Brings concrete, decision-useful information
Handles the deprioritized stakeholder communication respectfully

questions.title: Updating Your Manager on a Production Performance Regression Before You've Found the Cause
questions.prompt: A warehouse load that normally finishes by 5 AM is still running at 9 AM, and report refreshes across the company are stale. You've been investigating for an hour and have ruled out a few things, but you don't yet know the actual cause. Your manager messages asking for a status update. Walk me through what you'd say.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't wait until I have the root cause to say something, and I also wouldn't speculate out loud about a cause I haven't confirmed -- both of those erode trust in different ways. I'd give a status update structured around what's known, what's not, and what happens next: the load that normally finishes by 5 AM is still running at 9, company-wide reports are stale as a result, I've ruled out specific things I've actually checked, I don't yet have a confirmed root cause, and here's exactly what I'm checking next and roughly when I'll have another update.

I'd also flag the business impact honestly rather than downplaying it -- which reports are affected and since when -- so my manager can decide whether anything needs to be communicated further up or sideways to report consumers, which isn't my call to make alone. I'd commit to a specific time for the next update rather than 'I'll let you know when I know,' because an open-ended silence is worse for everyone than a short, honest 'still working on it, next update at 10.'
questions.professionalAnswer: My rule for a status update like this is to be clear about what I actually know versus what I'm still guessing at, instead of either staying silent until I have the answer or throwing out a theory I haven't confirmed. So I'd say something like: the load's been running four hours past normal, reports are stale company-wide, here's specifically what I've already ruled out, I don't have a confirmed cause yet, and here's what I'm checking next. I'd also be upfront about the actual business impact -- which reports, since when -- because that's information my manager needs to decide if anyone else needs to hear about this, not something I should quietly sit on. And I always try to commit to a specific time for the next update instead of leaving it open-ended, because 'I'll check back when I know something' leaves everyone hanging, while 'next update at 10' at least gives people something concrete.
questions.example: "Still investigating -- load's 4 hours past normal, company-wide reports are stale since 5 AM. Ruled out blocking and disk space so far, no confirmed cause yet. Checking the data flow buffer settings next. Next update by 10."
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the root cause is confirmed instead of giving an honest in-progress update
Speculating about an unconfirmed cause as if it were established fact
Downplaying or omitting the actual business impact to avoid looking bad
Leaving the next update open-ended instead of committing to a specific time
keyPoints: Give a structured update -- what's known, what's not, what's next -- rather than staying silent or guessing
Clearly separate confirmed findings from unconfirmed theories
Report the actual business impact honestly so leadership can decide on further communication
Commit to a specific time for the next update instead of an open-ended 'I'll let you know'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides a timely, honest update rather than waiting for full resolution
Clearly separates confirmed facts from speculation
Accurately communicates business impact
Commits to a concrete next-update time

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Deadline That Would Require Skipping Data Validation
questions.prompt: Your lead tells you to skip the data quality validation step on tomorrow's warehouse load -- just this once -- to hit a leadership demo deadline, since the validation step 'always passes anyway.' You're not confident it always will. Walk me through how you'd respond.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd push back, but specifically and with a reason, not just reflexively refusing. I'd point out exactly what the validation step actually catches -- row count mismatches, null keys, referential breaks -- and that 'it always passes' is true until the one day it doesn't, which is the entire reason the step exists in the first place; skipping it doesn't make tomorrow's data more trustworthy, it just means we wouldn't know if it isn't.

I'd also reframe the actual risk for the demo: showing leadership a dashboard built on unvalidated data that turns out to have a broken join or a null-key row is a worse outcome for that demo than a short delay, because it damages trust in the data itself rather than just the schedule. Rather than a flat no, I'd offer an alternative that still protects the deadline: run the validation in parallel with final load steps so it doesn't block the critical path, or validate a representative subset fast if a full validation genuinely can't finish in time, so there's at least a real signal before the demo rather than none. If my lead still insists on skipping it entirely after hearing that, I'd ask them to make that call explicitly and own it as a conscious risk decision, not something I quietly agreed was fine.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just refuse outright, but I also wouldn't quietly go along with it -- I'd explain specifically what that validation step actually catches, things like row count mismatches or broken keys, and point out that 'it always passes' is exactly why people forget it's protecting against the one time it doesn't. Skipping it doesn't make the data better, it just means we're flying blind on whether it's good. I'd also make the real trade-off clear for the demo specifically: showing leadership something built on data we didn't check, and having it turn out wrong in front of them, is a worse outcome than asking for a little more time. Instead of just saying no, I'd try to offer something that still protects the deadline -- running validation in parallel with the rest of the load instead of after it, or checking a smaller representative sample fast if a full check won't finish in time, so we're not going in with zero signal. And if my lead still wants to skip it entirely after all that, I'd ask them to make that call explicitly themselves, so it's a decision somebody owns on purpose, not something that just quietly happened.
questions.example: "I'd rather not skip it blind -- can I run validation in parallel with the final load steps instead, so it doesn't block tomorrow but we still have a real signal before the demo?"
commonMistakes: Silently complying without raising the risk, leaving an unvalidated load to speak for itself at a leadership demo
Refusing flatly without offering any alternative that still respects the deadline pressure
Not articulating specifically what the validation step actually protects against, making the pushback sound like process for its own sake
Letting an informal 'just this once' become the de facto new standard without anyone consciously deciding that
keyPoints: Push back with a specific reason (what the validation actually catches), not a reflexive no
Reframe the real risk -- bad data in front of leadership is worse than a short delay
Offer a concrete alternative that still respects the deadline, like parallelizing validation or checking a representative subset
If overridden, make sure the decision to skip it is made explicitly and owned by whoever makes that call, not absorbed silently

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Pushes back with a specific, substantive reason rather than reflexively
Correctly reframes the real risk to the business/demo
Offers a concrete deadline-respecting alternative
Handles being overridden professionally if it comes to that

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Developer Through Their First Production Incident
questions.prompt: A junior developer on your team just got paged for the first time -- their SSIS package failed overnight, and they're visibly rattled when they message you at 6 AM asking for help before their manager notices. Walk me through how you'd handle both the technical problem and the junior developer's state in this moment.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd deal with both halves of this, because a rattled junior developer trying to debug under panic will move slower and make more mistakes than a calm one, so settling them down isn't a soft distraction from the technical work -- it's part of fixing it efficiently. First, I'd say plainly that a package failing isn't a crisis and isn't a reflection on them -- this happens to everyone, and the fact that they're asking for help instead of either panicking alone or trying to hide it is exactly the right instinct, not something to be embarrassed about.

Then I'd walk the actual triage with them rather than just taking over and fixing it myself -- read the error message together, figure out which of the recurring SSIS failure categories it falls into, check the obvious first things -- because they learn the pattern by doing it with support, not by watching me solve it while they take notes. On their manager finding out: I'd be straightforward that hiding an incident is worse than a manager hearing about it calmly after it's handled, and I'd offer to be there with them if they want to give that update, so they're not facing it alone, but I wouldn't suggest trying to quietly fix it before anyone notices -- that pattern, if it became a habit, is worse for them long-term than owning an early-career incident openly. Once it's resolved, I'd suggest a short, blame-free walk-through afterward -- not right at 6 AM when they're still rattled -- so the incident turns into something they actually learn from rather than just survive.
questions.professionalAnswer: There are really two things happening here at once -- an actual technical problem, and a junior developer who's scared -- and I treat the second one as just as real as the first, because someone panicking is going to debug worse, not better. So I'd start by just telling them plainly that this happens to everyone, it's not a reflection on them, and reaching out for help at 6 AM instead of spiraling alone is exactly the right move, not something to feel bad about. Then I'd work through the actual triage with them rather than taking the keyboard away and fixing it myself -- read the error together, figure out what kind of failure this is, check the first obvious things -- because that's how they actually build the instinct for next time instead of just watching me do it. On telling their manager, I'd be honest that trying to quietly fix it before anyone notices is a worse habit to build than just handling it and letting their manager know calmly once it's resolved -- and I'd offer to be there with them for that conversation if it would help, so they don't feel like they're facing it completely alone. Once we've actually fixed it, I'd want to circle back later, not right then while they're still rattled, for a quick no-blame look at what happened and what we'd watch for next time.
questions.example: "First -- this happens to everyone, you did the right thing messaging me instead of panicking alone. Let's read the error together and figure out what we're actually looking at before we touch anything."
commonMistakes: Taking over and fixing the package solo instead of walking through it with the junior developer, missing the teaching opportunity
Treating the junior developer's anxiety as irrelevant to the technical task instead of addressing it directly and early
Encouraging or tacitly allowing them to hide the incident from their manager instead of handling it openly and calmly
Doing the post-incident debrief immediately while they're still rattled instead of after things have settled
keyPoints: Address the junior developer's emotional state directly and early, since panic makes debugging slower and more error-prone
Walk through triage together rather than taking over, so they build the skill instead of just watching it happen
Be honest that hiding an incident from a manager is a worse long-term habit than handling it openly and calmly
Offer to be present for the manager conversation if that would help, without suggesting avoidance
Schedule the learning debrief for after things have settled, not in the middle of the panic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explicitly addresses the junior developer's emotional state as part of resolving the incident
Walks through triage collaboratively rather than taking over
Gives sound, honest guidance on manager communication
Proposes a later blame-free debrief for learning
